alerting.summary: A managed layer of rules and notifications: it evaluates conditions over telemetry on a schedule and wakes the on-call. Added in wave v2, when metrics and logs already exist but incident response still relies on somebody watching a dashboard. It is the only observability block whose real bound is human rather than technical.
alerting.capacity: Formally there are two bounds: rule-evaluation at maxEvaluationsPerSec = 20000000 and ingest-bandwidth at maxIngestMbs = 50 MB/s. In practice the first is unreachable: rules = 400 at evaluationIntervalSec = 30 s produce 13.3 evaluations per second, six orders of magnitude of headroom, so the real limit becomes noiseRatio and the onCallSeats = 8 count.
practices: Measure the load on the on-call: 400 rules × firingsPerRuleMonth = 2 give 800 firings per month, that is 100 for each of the 8 seats, about 3.3 alerts per person per day.
noiseRatio = 0.6 by default is above the realistic ceiling of 0.5: on the defaults 480 of the 800 firings are false, and that is the first thing to fix, not the number of rules.

Detection delay is the sum of evaluationIntervalSec = 30 s and lookbackWindowSec = 300 s, so up to 330 s; against rtoTargetSec = 900 s on multi-region-policy a third of the budget goes to merely noticing.
lookbackWindowSec = 300 s is protection against flapping: shortening the window speeds up the reaction and raises noiseRatio at the same time.
The bill is modest and should not drive decisions: 8 seats × 21 USD plus 800 notifications × 0.01 USD is 176 USD per month.
pitfalls: Growing rules as a sign of maturity: 5000 rules at the same noiseRatio = 0.6 produce 6000 false firings per month, and the on-call stops reading alerts.

Alerting on the symptoms of every block instead of alerting on the user-facing SLO: probe-slo with targetP99Ms = 300 ms and targetAvailability = 0.999 yields three or four meaningful rules instead of hundreds.
availability = 0.999 of alerting itself means about 43 minutes per month when nobody will wake you: duplicate critical paths with a second channel.
Feeding raw telemetry into alerting: maxIngestMbs = 50 MB/s here is ten times lower than in logs, the block is designed for aggregates.

api-gateway.summary: A single entry point for the API: authentication, limits and quotas, request transformation, an optional response cache and telemetry. It differs from lb-l7 in carrying application logic, which makes it more expensive both in latency and in money. Place it after the load balancer and in front of the services.
api-gateway.capacity: The limits are gateway-rps and network. gateway-rps equals instances=3 × maxRpsPerInstance=10,000 RPS = 30,000 RPS, and with serviceTimeMs=3 ms plus authLatencyMs=0.5 ms its own contribution to latency is 3.5 ms. The network side counts request and response volume plus logging: logLinesPerRequest=2 × logBytesPerLine=500 B = 1 KB per request, that is 30 MB/s and about 2.6 TB of logs per day at full capacity.
practices: authMode=jwt-local verifies the signature locally and costs authLatencyMs=0.5 ms; introspection turns every request into a network call and shifts the full 30,000 RPS onto the auth service.
Reconcile rateLimitRpsPerClient=1000 RPS with quotaPerDay=5,000,000 requests: at a sustained 1,000 RPS the daily quota is burned in 5,000 s, about 83 minutes.
timeoutMs=29000 ms is deliberately just under the typical 30,000 ms on the load balancer; keep that gap so the client receives a meaningful gateway error instead of a connection drop at the proxy.
responseCacheEnabled=false by default; enabling it with responseCacheTtlSec=30 s takes load off the services, but it is only suitable for non-personalised responses.
Connect the telemetry port to an observability block: 2 log lines per request is 2.6 TB per day, and that stream has to land somewhere.
pitfalls: Piling all the business logic onto the gateway and running into 30,000 RPS, while the lb-l7 right next to it handles 75,000 RPS: the gateway is almost always the narrowest point of the edge chain.
costPerMillionRequests=3.5 USD is the most expensive line among the edge blocks: 1 billion requests costs 3,500 USD against 600 USD on glb.
payloadLimitMb=10 MB cuts off large uploads, which should instead bypass the gateway and go straight to object storage via signed URLs.
Raising logLinesPerRequest to 5-10 for debugging and ending up with a multi-terabyte daily log stream that costs more than the gateway itself.

apm.summary: A managed observability platform from an external provider: host agents, custom metrics and log ingest in a single SaaS. Taken instead of the logs plus metrics plus traces trio when time to launch matters more than control over cost and data. The block is marked managed, so it scales through plan limits rather than through nodes.
apm.capacity: Two bounds apply and both are set by the provider: a rate-limit of providerLimitRps = 50000 RPS for API and agent calls, and ingest-bandwidth at maxIngestMbs = 200 MB/s. You cannot add resources of your own, so the only lever is reducing the telemetry stream; serviceTimeMs = 5 ms sets the cost of a call to the platform.
practices: Read the bill as three lines: 200 hosts × 31 USD = 6200 USD, plus 20000 custom metrics as 20 batches of a thousand series × 5 USD = 100 USD, plus 5000 GB of logs × 0.1 USD = 500 USD, for about 6800 USD per month.
costPerThousandSeries = 5 USD here is 5.5 times more expensive than the 0.9 USD of your own metrics block: custom metrics in APM only pay off at small volumes.
Tie hostsMonitored = 200 to the real fleet: with autoscaleNodes on k8s-cluster the host count floats, and the bill floats along with it.
costPerGbIngest = 0.1 USD against 0.5 USD in your own logs block makes APM a cheap log sink exactly as long as the host count stays low.
Use APM either as your only observability layer or as a supplement, but do not duplicate your own logs, metrics and traces with it: you will pay twice.
pitfalls: Hitting providerLimitRps = 50000 shows up not as a service outage but as silent telemetry loss and gaps on the charts.
hostsMonitored growth caused by autoscaling: 200 hosts at 31 USD is 6200 USD, while a sudden 600 hosts at peak is 18600 USD for the same month.
A managed block gives you no reliability knobs: availability = 0.999 is about 43 minutes per month, and nothing can change it except a second source.
logIngestGb = 5000 GB per month is set as a parameter rather than derived from the diagram: reconcile it with the real log stream or the estimate will drift away from reality.

audit-log.summary: An immutable journal of significant actions: who did what and when, retained to satisfy regulators and investigations. It differs from ordinary logs through immutable = true and a horizon of retentionYears = 7 instead of days. Added once the diagram involves money, personal data or administrator access.
audit-log.capacity: Two bounds apply: ingest-bandwidth at maxIngestMbs = 200 MB/s and ops at maxOpsPerSec = 200000 RPS. On the defaults both are far away: eventsPerSec = 5000 at eventBytes = 1200 bytes is 6 MB/s, that is 3 percent of the bandwidth and 2.5 percent of the operations limit, so the real bound turns out to be storage volume.
practices: Compute volume over the entire horizon: 6 MB/s at compressionRatio = 4 is 1.5 MB/s stored, about 47 TB per year and 331 TB over retentionYears = 7, which at costPerGbMonth = 0.023 USD gives roughly 7600 USD per month at full term.
Keep eventBytes = 1200 bytes within the realistic range of 500 to 4000: recording the whole request body instead of identifiers easily quadruples both volume and bill.
immutable = true is a commitment, not a checkbox: a record cannot be deleted or rewritten before retentionYears expires, so decide on the field set before launch.
availability = 0.9999 against 0.999 in logs was not chosen by accident: about 4.3 minutes per month versus 43, because a missed audit record is a violation, not an inconvenience.
Write identifiers and references into audit-log and keep the personal data itself in the primary store, where it can be deleted on request.
pitfalls: Writing audit records synchronously on the user path: the availability of the operation becomes no higher than the journal's own 0.9999, and its response time is added to p99.
The conflict between immutable = true with retentionYears = 7 and the right to erasure: if events carry personal data, there is no way to wipe it.
Mixing audit with ordinary logs: logs have retentionDays = 30 and samplingRate, that is a sample and a horizon incompatible with journal requirements.
eventsPerSec is set by hand rather than derived from the diagram: when traffic doubles the parameter stays the same and the estimate will still show the old volume.

aurora.summary: A managed relational database whose storage is moved into a distributed layer with quorumN = 6 copies and quorumW = 4. Replicas read that same storage, so readReplicas = 3 lag by only replicaLagMs = 20 ms, and a write costs iopsPerWrite = 1 instead of the four postgres needs. It is taken at the v1 stage when self-hosted postgres hits the disk ceiling and a long failover.
aurora.capacity: The limits are cpu, connections and iops. cpu binds first: cpuCores = 16 / readServiceMs = 0.6 ms ≈ 26,600 reads/s and 16 / writeServiceMs = 1.8 ms ≈ 8,900 writes/s. iops at provisionedIops = 60,000 and iopsPerWrite = 1 is not in the way, and connections at maxConnections = 3000 with connectionPooler = proxy-managed also leave plenty of headroom.
practices: quorumW = 4 out of quorumN = 6 together with quorumR = 3 gives an intersection (4 + 3 is greater than 6), so a write is visible to any quorum read; below quorumW = 4 that guarantee is lost.

readFromReplica = 0.6 is safer here than on self-hosted: replicaLagMs = 20 ms against 200 ms in postgres, yet consistencyModel = linearizable still requires stickyReadShare above zero for read-your-writes.
connectionPooler = proxy-managed is already enabled, and that is exactly what you pay managed for; maxConnections = 3000 supports thousands of service instances without a separate pgbouncer.
costPerMillionIo = 0.2 USD means heavy queries are billed separately from the instance: queryProfile = point-read is cheap, a full scan over rowCount = 500 million is not.
failoverSec = 30 s at availability = 0.9999 (about 53 minutes of downtime per year) means the service needs retries with backoff sized for exactly those 30 seconds.
pitfalls: Writes still go to a single writer: readReplicas = 3 do not raise the write ceiling, which stays at 16 cores / 1.8 ms ≈ 8,900 operations/s.

rowCount = 500 million × 400 bytes × indexOverhead = 0.4 is 280 GB out of storageGb = 2000, but you pay costPerGbMonth = 0.1 for what is actually allocated, and that does not shrink back when rows are deleted.
replicationMode = async applies at the replica level: during a failover, commits inside the replicaLagMs = 20 ms window may never reach the promoted replica.
isolationLevel = read-committed by default brings the same lost updates under read-modify-write as postgres; being managed does not fix that.

auth.summary: The authentication and authorization block: in mode jwt-local-verify it issues tokens and serves JWKS, while the services verify signatures themselves in verifyMs 0.05 ms. It sits at the entrance to the system next to the gateway; a login costs loginServiceMs 150 ms and mfaShare 0.25 of logins go through a second factor. It has no out ports — it is a leaf dependency of the design.
auth.capacity: The limiters are rps-ceiling and cpu. rps-ceiling = instances 3 × maxRpsPerInstance 3000 = 9000 RPS. cpu is derived from serviceTimeMs 4 ms for an ordinary operation and loginServiceMs 150 ms for a login: these are different worlds, because a login is almost 38 times more expensive, and 9000 token checks are not the same as 9000 logins.
practices: mode jwt-local-verify takes auth off the hot path: with jwksCacheSec 3600 s a service calls the block once an hour rather than on every request.
tokenTtlSec 900 s is the window during which a revoked token still works; if you need it shorter you need a session lookup or a blacklist in session-store.
refreshTokenTtlSec 2,592,000 s (30 days) sets how often users log in again; shortening it without cause is expensive — every login costs 150 ms against 4 ms for an ordinary operation.
sessionStore redis requires a separate session-store block: connect the two, otherwise there is nowhere to keep session state.
Build availability 0.9995 (22 minutes a month) straight into the product SLO: without auth nothing that requires a user works.
pitfalls: Switching to mode introspection makes auth a synchronous dependency of every request: introspectionMs 6 ms is added to all calls, and the rps-ceiling of 9000 becomes the ceiling of the entire system.
jwksCacheSec 3600 s during key rotation: if the old key is removed immediately, services will reject valid tokens for up to an hour.
Capacity planning against average RPS: the login peak in the morning or after a mobile release is a spike of 150 ms operations specifically, not of 4 ms ones.
mfaShare 0.25 adds an external channel (SMS, push) to a login — its limits and cost belong in the notification or email-smtp blocks, not here.

autocomplete.summary: A suggestion service over a prefix tree (Trie or FST): it returns candidates in single-digit milliseconds for every keystroke in the search box.
autocomplete.capacity: memory is the limit: the prefix dictionary has to live in RAM. 400 million prefixes at 56 B (4× FST compression) is 22 GB against memoryGb = 8, only 36% resident, which cuts capacity threefold.
practices: Keep memoryGb at no less than prefixCount × (keySizeBytes + valueSizeBytes) / 4, otherwise the dictionary stops being resident.
queryServiceMs = 2 ms is not arbitrary: a suggestion is produced on every keystroke, and the typing budget is tens of milliseconds.
updateLagMin 1–60 decides when a new query shows up in suggestions; 15 minutes is the default compromise.
Derive RPS from typing, not from searches: an eight-letter word means eight requests.
pitfalls: 400 million prefixes with memoryGb = 8 is the classic underestimate of the dictionary: trim the long tail by frequency first.
Autocomplete without client-side debouncing multiplies traffic several times over the search itself.
updateLagMin = 15 min means yesterday's trend will not reach suggestions right away.

az.summary: An availability zone container inside a region: an isolated failure domain with its own power and network. Blocks placed in the same az talk over the internal network, blocks in different az are connected through link-cross-az. Use at least two or three of them, otherwise any discussion of fault tolerance is pointless.
az.capacity: hasModel = false: the zone serves no requests and does not enter the capacity calculation. It sets two values for everything inside it: intraAzLatencyMs = 0.25 ms per call between blocks of the same zone, and failureProbability = 0.0001 as the probability that everything in the zone fails at once.
practices: The gap between an intra-zone and a cross-zone call is fourfold: 0.25 ms against latencyMs = 1 ms on link-cross-az, so a chain of six hops costs 1.5 ms inside a zone against 6 ms between zones.
Keep the synchronous chain of one request inside a single zone, and spread replicas and standby capacity across zones, since they are not on the hot path.
failureProbability = 0.0001 for a single zone means a ceiling of 0.9999 for a design without redundancy; two independent zones give 1e-8 for a simultaneous failure, three give 1e-12.
Place quorum systems across an odd number of zones: three zones survive the loss of one, two do not.
pitfalls: Stretching one synchronous path across three zones for a prettier picture: every crossing adds 1 ms to p99 and 0.01 USD per GB at the costPerGb of link-cross-az.
Standby capacity in the same zone as the primary block: failureProbability = 0.0001 applies to both at once, and the availability of the design does not improve.
Forgotten cross-zone replication traffic: it travels over link-cross-az and is billed, even though on the diagram it looks like an internal detail of the database.

batch.summary: Batch processing of a large dataset: datasetGb 2000 is pushed through cores 32 at throughputMbPerCoreSec 8. Use it for nightly ETL, data-mart rebuilds, migrations and training sets, where volume matters and latency does not. The only input is consume — the job is started by an event or a signal.
batch.capacity: The limiters are cpu and job-window. cpu = cores 32 × 8 MB/s = 256 MB/s, while the amount of work = datasetGb 2000 × shuffleFactor 2 = 4000 GB, so a run takes about 15,600 s ≈ 4.3 h. windowHours 4 (14,400 s) no longer holds at the defaults: fitting inside it needs at least 35 cores.
practices: Size the window with headroom for retries 1: a single restarted stage on a 4.3-hour run pushes the job well past 4 hours.
shuffleFactor 2 is the main work multiplier: joins and grouping move the data twice, and shuffleFactor 5 on the same dataset means 10,000 GB and nearly 11 hours.

cores 32 at costPerCoreHour $0.04 is $1.28/hour and about $5.5 per run; doubling the cores halves the time at the same cost per run, which is why the window is usually fixed with cores rather than with optimization.
rowSizeBytes 2000 across 2000 GB implies roughly 1 billion rows — check that number against the expected table size, otherwise the whole calculation rests on the wrong dataset.
Read from object storage or from a data mart, not from a live OLTP database: 256 MB/s of reads will flatten it.
pitfalls: windowHours 4 against a computed 4.3 h is the classic 'it almost fits': 10% growth in the dataset turns a nightly job into a morning incident.
availability 0.99 means roughly every hundredth run fails; without checkpoints a retry costs a full window.
Linear scaling with cores breaks down on shuffle: above shuffleFactor 3 the bottleneck becomes network and disk, not CPU.
Batch and online load on the same cluster: 32 cores busy for 4 hours knock latency-sensitive services out of their SLO.

bff.summary: Backend-for-frontend: a thin aggregator that makes downstreamCalls 5 calls per client request and stitches the response together in aggregationMs 8 ms. It sits between the client and the domain services so that a mobile or web client does not make five round trips itself. It holds almost no business logic of its own — serviceTimeMs 25 ms is mostly serialization.
bff.capacity: The limiters are inflight, cpu and network. inflight = instances 4 × concurrencyPerInstance 64 = 256 slots divided by the hold time: with callMode parallel that is 25 + 40 + 8 ≈ 73 ms and ~3500 RPS, with sequential it is 25 + 5 × 40 + 8 = 233 ms and only ~1100 RPS. cpu gives 4 × cpuCores 4 ÷ (0.025 s × cpuShare 0.15) ≈ 4300 RPS, network gives 4 × 1000 = 4000 Mbps.
practices: callMode parallel is the right default for a BFF: five calls of downstreamCallMs 40 ms each cost 40 ms rather than 200 ms and triple the inflight capacity.
partialFailureMode degrade returns a partial response instead of an error — it is the only way to stop availability 0.999 across five dependencies from becoming 0.995 at the client.
timeoutMs 800 ms has to cover the downstream tail: with parallel and a 40 ms median there is headroom, but switching to sequential pushes the median to 200 ms, already close to the limit.
Remember the fanout: downstreamCalls 5 turns 3500 client RPS into 17,500 RPS on the domain services — size their capacity against that number.
concurrencyPerInstance 64 is deliberately lower than a service's 200: a BFF mostly waits, and the slots exist to cap the surge onto downstream, not to saturate CPU.
pitfalls: Raising downstreamCalls from 5 to 12 (the top of the realistic range) with sequential pushes the hold time to 25 + 480 + 8 = 513 ms and drops capacity to ~500 RPS on the same 256 slots.
A BFF with business logic in it: cpuShare 0.15 stops being true, and the cpu ceiling of 4300 RPS turns out to be two or three times lower than calculated.
One slow downstream under parallel with fail-fast kills the whole response: without degrade the BFF's p99 equals the p99 of the worst of the five dependencies.
There is no cache here: if the same five calls repeat on every screen, put a cache block in front of them, otherwise the domain services take the full fanout.

bigquery.summary: A managed warehouse billed by bytes scanned: SQL over petabytes with no cluster to administer. Made for batch analytics and reporting, not for point lookups.
bigquery.capacity: query-slots is the limit: one query takes 200 slots, so slotCount = 2,000 allows 10 concurrent queries; concurrency (100) and ingest-bandwidth bind later. The scanned volume drives both the latency and the bill.
practices: partitioning day leaves 12% of the scan, hour leaves 2%, and clustering cuts up to another 55%. Together that is 6.6% of a full scan.
Compute the money directly: TB scanned × $6.25. On defaults that is about $50,000 a month.
Reserve slotCount 500–20,000 for peak query concurrency, not for the average load.
An auto-refreshing dashboard is billed like a stream: the model takes max(queriesPerDay, λ × 86400).
pitfalls: A query without a partition filter is equivalent to partitioning = none and multiplies both the scan and the bill by roughly 8.
BigQuery on an interactive path: 13 GB of scan is about 0.8 s per query even with 2,000 slots.
Storing 400 TB at $0.02/GB adds $8,000 a month before the first query even runs.

block.summary: A block volume attached to a single node: raw blocks on which file systems and databases live. The attach port makes the point — this is not a shared resource but the disk of one specific machine. Use it for databases, brokers and anything that needs latency in the hundreds of microseconds (latencyUs 200).
block.capacity: The limiters are iops and throughput. provisionedIops 12000 is consumed with the weights iopsPerRead 1 and iopsPerWrite 2: pure writes give 6000 operations/s, pure reads give 12000. throughputMbs 500 at 12000 IOPS puts the break-even point around 42 KB per operation: small random operations hit the IOPS wall, large sequential ones hit the bandwidth wall.
practices: volumeType gp3 is the baseline; io2 is taken for consistent latency and high IOPS, and nvme for local speed at the cost of losing the data when the instance stops.
Work out the profile before choosing: 12000 IOPS at 4 KB is only 48 MB/s, and the 500 MB/s of bandwidth will go unused.
One volume, one node: fault tolerance is built through replication at the database or broker level, not by the disk itself.
latencyUs 200 (realistically 100-500) is exactly why a block disk is chosen over nfs with its 2.5 ms.
diskGb 2000 at costPerGbMonth 0.08 USD is 160 USD a month, and you pay for the provisioned capacity rather than for what is actually used.
pitfalls: availability 0.999 (about 8.8 hours a year) applies to the volume, not to the data: a volume failure stops the entire node, so snapshots and replicas are mandatory.
Growing the volume does not add IOPS automatically: on gp3 they are set separately through provisionedIops, and you can hit 12000 on a nearly empty disk.
Write amplification in databases and brokers (log plus data plus compaction) pushes the real iopsPerWrite above the assumed 2 — plan for a realistic 1-4.

cassandra.summary: A masterless wide-column store: nodes = 6, replicationFactor = 3, any node accepts a write, and a write costs writeServiceMs = 0.3 ms, five times cheaper than a read at readServiceMs = 1.5 ms. consistencyModel = eventual with conflictResolution = lww, while strictness is tuned through the quorums quorumR = 2 and quorumW = 2. It is chosen at mvp for a write stream with a read pattern known in advance by partitionKey.
cassandra.capacity: The limits are node-ops, cpu and iops. node-ops: maxOpsPerSecPerNode = 20,000 × 6 nodes = 120,000 operations/s, but writes are multiplied by replicationFactor = 3 (about 40,000 client writes/s) and reads by quorumR = 2 (60,000). On reads cpu binds earlier: 6 × 16 cores / readServiceMs = 1.5 ms = 64,000 operations/s, that is roughly 32,000 client reads/s.
practices: quorumR = 2 and quorumW = 2 at quorumN = 3 give 2 + 2 greater than 3, that is strict quorum consistency on top of consistencyModel = eventual; dropping either one to 1 brings genuinely eventual behaviour back.
Keep partitionSizeMb = 64 inside the realistic 1–100 MB band: a gigabyte-sized partition means a single query reads a gigabyte from one node.
The data model is built from the query: partitionKey = userId must appear in the WHERE clause of every read, while secondary indexes and ALLOW FILTERING are a hidden full scan across the cluster.
compactionStrategy = stcs suits writes that are rarely overwritten; use twcs for time series with TTL and lcs for read-heavy workloads, otherwise writeAmplification = 4 grows.
hintedHandoff = true repairs short outages but does not replace repair: without regular repair at tombstoneRatio = 0.05 deleted rows come back from the dead.
pitfalls: conflictResolution = lww with concurrencyControl = none: of two concurrent updates to the same cell one simply disappears, and the winner is decided by clock skew between nodes.
Read-modify-write is impossible in principle: counters, increments and uniqueness checks are either lightweight transactions with their cost, or a design mistake.

rowCount = 5 billion × 200 bytes = 1 TB, with replicationFactor = 3 that is 3 TB, and after compressionRatio = 3 it is 1 TB again, that is 167 GB per node — but compaction needs free space of the same order.
A read is five times more expensive than a write (1.5 ms against 0.3 ms): a profile with ten reads per write will hit cpu long before the advertised 120,000 operations/s.

cdc.summary: Capturing changes straight from the database log (WAL, binlog, oplog) and publishing them as a stream of events. Unlike outbox it requires no application code changes, but it also yields no domain events — only row-level insert, update and delete. Use it to feed analytics, search indexes and caches when the source system must not be touched.
cdc.capacity: The limiters are source, workers and depth. source: changesPerSec 20000 is the rate the log of sourceDb postgres delivers. workers: instances 2 parsing and publishing the stream. depth: walRetentionGb 16 is the lag buffer; at 20000 changes/s of messageSizeKb 1 that is about 20 MB/s, so a stopped connector eats the entire WAL reserve in roughly 13 minutes.
practices: snapshotMode initial takes a full snapshot on the first start — on a large table that means hours of load on the source, so the first start is scheduled into a maintenance window.
lagMs 500 is a freshness SLO: measure it as the difference between commit time and publish time, not by the number of unprocessed messages.
Keep the replication slot under monitoring: an inactive slot holds WAL and, in the extreme, stops writes to the source database entirely.
Publish with the key set to the primary key of the row: then changes to one row keep their order within a partition on the receiving side.
The consumer must be idempotent and apply upserts: after a restart the connector resumes from the last committed position and replays what it already sent.
pitfalls: CDC exposes your table schema to the outside world: changing a column breaks every consumer, which is why outbox is the safer choice for contracts between services.
A single bulk update over a million rows produces a million events at once and instantly hits both changesPerSec 20000 and walRetentionGb 16.
Deletes arrive as an event with an empty state, while truncate and ddl may not arrive at all — the consumer quietly drifts away from the source.
instances 2 does not speed up capture: reading the log is sequential by nature, so the second instance is a standby rather than scaling.

cdn.summary: A caching delivery network at the edge: it serves static assets and cacheable responses from the nearest PoP, taking both load and bandwidth off the origin. A managed block that scales with the PoP count and the configured cacheHitRatio. Place it right after DNS, ahead of the origin chain, whenever part of the traffic is cacheable.
cdn.capacity: The limits are pop-rps and pop-network, both computed per PoP, so popCount=300 spreads the incoming RPS across the points of presence. The network limit is driven by response size: at avgObjectKb=120 KB every 1,000 RPS is about 120 MB/s, roughly 1 Gbps. The origin receives the miss share 1 − cacheHitRatio=0.92, that is 8%: out of 10,000 RPS arriving at the edge, 800 RPS reach the origin.
practices: cacheHitRatio=0.92 is realistic for static assets (range 0.7-0.98); for personalised responses set it closer to the lower bound, otherwise the origin comes out under-loaded in the calculation.
originShield=true adds an intermediate layer between the 300 PoPs and the origin: without it every PoP misses independently and the origin gets up to 300 identical requests for a single object.
staleWhileRevalidateSec=60 s allows serving a stale object while it is being refreshed; this is the main mechanism protecting the origin at the moment ttlSec=3600 s expires.
Latency works out as follows: a hit costs edgeLatencyMs=20 ms, a miss costs 20 ms plus originLatencyMs=80 ms, about 100 ms; at a hit ratio of 0.92 the average comes to roughly 26 ms.
maxObjectSizeMb=50 MB excludes large objects from caching; for video and big files keep rangeRequests=true, which is enabled by default.
pitfalls: Setting cacheHitRatio=0.98 simply because it is a CDN, forgetting that with cacheableShare=0.6 on client-web 40% of the requests are uncacheable in principle and will pass through to the origin regardless.
costPerGbEgress=0.085 USD is invisible per request, but 1 TB served costs about 87 USD, and a terabyte accumulates after roughly 9 million deliveries of a 120 KB object.
Forgetting signedUrls=false: with that setting private content is cached and served to everyone.
Applying ttlSec=3600 s to all content at once, which stretches invalidation of dynamic responses out to an hour.

clickhouse.summary: A columnar DBMS for analytics: wide scans, aggregates and reports over event data. Deploy it as a sink for the event stream, not as a replacement for the OLTP database.
clickhouse.capacity: disk-scan binds first: 6 nodes give 12 GB/s, while a single query reads rowsIngestedPerSec × 3600 s × rowSize / compressionRatio × the share of columns, roughly 10 GB. The cpu scan (28.8 GB/s) and query-slots bind later.
practices: The scan shrinks with the share of columns: 6 out of 40 is 15%. Drop unneeded fields from the SELECT before you add nodes.
compressionRatio is realistically 5–15×: at the default of 8 a 300 B row is stored as 37 B.
insertBatchRows 10,000–1,000,000: insert in batches so that partsPerPartition stays within 10–300 at a merge rate of 200 MB/s.
materializedViews compute aggregates at insert time — cheaper than scanning raw data for every dashboard.
pitfalls: concurrencyControl = none together with conflictResolution = lww: writing one key from two places silently loses updates.
ttlDays = 90 with a longer reporting horizon: the data disappears before anyone asks for it.
replicas = 2 doubles the disk: growth is rows × rowSize / compressionRatio × replicas.

client-api.summary: A load source representing external integrators that call the public API with a key or a token. Unlike user-facing clients it has a small number of sources with high and uneven RPS, plus daily quotas. Place it in front of api-gateway or rate-limiter, where those limits are actually enforced.
client-api.capacity: hasModel=false, the block defines the inbound stream and does not constrain capacity. clients=200 × rpsPerClient=5 RPS gives 1,000 RPS at baseline and about 2,000 RPS at peak with peakFactor=2, plus burstiness=2 over short intervals. quotaPerDay=1,000,000 requests per client is equivalent to 11.6 RPS sustained, so at rpsPerClient=5 RPS the quota is not the binding limit.
practices: authMode=jwt-local is verified locally and is almost free; introspection adds a call to the auth service on every request, which is another 1,000 RPS on that service with the defaults.
Reconcile rpsPerClient=5 RPS with rateLimitRpsPerClient=1000 RPS on api-gateway: with that much headroom the limit will never trigger and the scenario will never exercise it.
burstiness=2 models bursts, so burst on rate-limiter must be at least twice the client's per-second limit.
avgResponseKb=12 KB at 1,000 RPS is about 12 MB/s, roughly 95 Mbps; that is a noticeable share for API traffic and belongs in the network limits at the edge.
Integrators almost always have retries=2 and their calls are rarely idempotent: turn on retryPolicy=idempotent-only on lb-l7 or api-gateway.
pitfalls: Setting clients=200 and treating the stream as smooth while ignoring burstiness=2: the one-second peak from a single client is twice rpsPerClient=5 RPS.
quotaPerDay is expressed per day while the gateway limit is per second: at rateLimitRpsPerClient=1000 RPS the daily quota of 1,000,000 requests is burned in 1,000 s, about 17 minutes.
Choosing authMode=introspection for security and ending up with the auth service in the critical path of every request, with the client's retries=2 stacked on top.

client-bot.summary: A load source representing crawlers, scrapers and bots: reads only (readWriteMix=1), with a deliberate share of requests bypassing the cache. It exists to show the difference between useful and parasitic traffic and to gauge its impact on the origin and on the egress bill. Place it alongside the user-facing clients, on the same cdn or waf entry point.
client-bot.capacity: hasModel=false, the block only generates load. rps=500 RPS at baseline and 750 RPS at peak with peakFactor=1.5; at avgResponseKb=60 KB that is about 29 MB/s, roughly 235 Mbps of outbound traffic. cacheBusting=0.2 means 20% of the requests miss the cache and reach the origin: roughly 150 RPS out of the 750 RPS peak.
practices: Route this block into waf: botScore=0.6 and rulesCount=250 on waf exist precisely to cut part of this traffic off before the origin.
avgResponseKb=60 KB is higher than the 45 KB users generate on client-web, so bots take a disproportionately large share of the cdn egress cost (costPerGbEgress=0.085 USD).
respectRobots=true reduces the volume but is not a defence: model aggressive bots with a separate instance of the block with respectRobots=false.
Keep cacheBusting=0.2 non-zero: this is exactly the parameter that shows why originShield is needed on cdn.
pitfalls: Bot traffic is left out of the cdn calculation, and the origin picks up an extra 150 RPS or so because of cacheBusting=0.2.
750 RPS looks trivial next to the user-facing thousands, but at 60 KB per response it is hundreds of megabits per second and a visible egress bill.

Assuming that with readWriteMix=1 the block is harmless to storage, when the unique requests bots make wash out reverse-cache, where only about 437,000 objects out of uniqueKeys=5,000,000 fit in memory.

client-internal.summary: A load source representing other internal services rather than external users: east-west traffic inside the perimeter. It exists to account for service-to-service calls that bypass cdn and waf but still load lb-l7, service-mesh and the services themselves. Attach it directly to an internal entry point.
client-internal.capacity: hasModel=false, no capacity is modelled; the block defines a stream. rps=2000 RPS at baseline and 4,000 RPS at peak with peakFactor=2; at avgResponseKb=8 KB that is about 31 MB/s, roughly 250 Mbps at peak. slaTier=standard governs how strictly degradation of this stream should be treated relative to user-facing traffic.
practices: Route the block past cdn and waf: internal traffic does not go through the public edge, and wiring it there inflates the edge load in the calculation.
timeoutMs=5000 ms here is shorter than the 15,000 and 20,000 ms of the clients, and that is correct: an internal call must fail before the external request waiting on it does.
retries=2 with timeoutMs=5000 ms gives up to 15 s across three attempts; check that the caller is prepared to wait that long.
Set slaTier=critical only where a failed internal call means a failed user scenario; for best-effort streams it is reasonable to allow shedding on rate-limiter.
pitfalls: The internal 2,000 RPS is left out of service sizing because it is invisible on the client-facing chart, and the service saturates under load nobody expected.
retries=2 inside the perimeter multiplies across hops: with hopsPerRequest=2 on service-mesh the amplification reaches 9x (3 attempts on each of the two hops).
Marking every internal stream slaTier=critical, leaving no traffic in the diagram that can be sacrificed under overload.

client-iot.summary: A load source representing a fleet of devices that send telemetry on a schedule rather than in response to user actions. The traffic is almost entirely writes (readWriteMix=0.1) and very even (peakFactor=1.3). Place it in front of the ingest chain: ws-gateway or lb-l4 plus api-gateway, and on to a queue or a time-series store.
client-iot.capacity: hasModel=false, the block constrains nothing; it defines the inbound stream. deviceCount=500,000 with reportIntervalSec=60 s and batchSize=1 gives about 8,330 messages per second on average and roughly 10,800 at peak with peakFactor=1.3. At payloadBytes=200 B that is on the order of 1.7 MB/s, about 13 Mbps: the network is almost never the bottleneck here, unlike the connection count and the write operations.
practices: alwaysConnected=true means 500,000 persistent connections: at connectionsPerInstance=100,000 on ws-gateway you need at least 5 instances just to hold them.
Raise batchSize if you are limited by operation count: at batchSize=10 the stream drops from 8,330 to 833 requests per second, while the payload grows to 2 KB per request.
readWriteMix=0.1 means 90% of the traffic is writes; put a queue or a time-series store behind this block, not a read cache.
timeoutMs=30000 ms must not exceed reportIntervalSec=60 s, otherwise stuck attempts start overlapping the next reporting cycle.
geoDistribution=global requires either a global entry point (glb or anycast) or an explicit ingest path in every region.
pitfalls: Devices restart in lockstep after an outage and peakFactor=1.3 does not reflect that: the real reconnect surge across 500,000 devices is many times higher.
retries=3 is usually harmful for telemetry: resending a stale reading pushes writes to 33,300 messages per second instead of 8,330 with no benefit to the data.
Sizing by bandwidth, where 13 Mbps looks harmless, and missing the real constraints: 500,000 concurrent connections and 8,330 write operations per second.

client-loadtest.summary: A synthetic load generator for exercising the diagram: it sets the load shape and a target RPS without being tied to any audience. Use it to run a ramp or spike scenario and see which limit binds first. Attach it where the real clients attach, usually only temporarily.
client-loadtest.capacity: hasModel=false, the block does not count as capacity; it only applies load. targetRps=5000 RPS over durationSec=600 s produces 3,000,000 requests per run, and the shape is set by pattern=constant, with ramp, spike and sawtooth as the alternatives. retries=0 by default, so the load is not distorted by the generator's own repeats, which is exactly what a clean measurement needs.
practices: To find the breaking point use pattern=ramp with a gradual increase of targetRps rather than 5,000 RPS straight away in constant mode: that way you can see at which value the limit kicked in.
pattern=spike is useful against blocks with cold starts and autoscaling; it exposes the gap between an instant surge and the time it takes to add instances.
Leave retries=0 at zero, otherwise the test starts amplifying its own overload and the result stops being reproducible.
durationSec=600 s (10 minutes) is enough to warm the caches; do not go shorter if you want to verify cacheHitRatio=0.85 on reverse-cache.
geoDistribution=europe is the default: if you are testing glb with regions=2, spread the generators across regions, otherwise the second region gets no traffic at all.
pitfalls: Running constant at 5,000 RPS and concluding the system is resilient, even though the real client profile has peakFactor=3 and a completely different shape.
The generator's timeoutMs=10000 ms is shorter than timeoutMs=30000 ms on lb-l7: the test records a client error while the request is in fact still being processed.
Forgetting to remove the block from the diagram after the run, so its 5,000 RPS stays in the calculation as permanent load.

client-mobile.summary: A load source representing mobile apps, accounting for network quality, background polling and offline sync. It differs from client-web in having shorter and more frequent sessions plus a noticeable channel RTT. Place it at the entry of the diagram wherever the bulk of the traffic comes from an app.
client-mobile.capacity: hasModel=false, no capacity is computed; the block only generates load. dau=3,000,000 × sessionsPerUserDay=6 × requestsPerSession=25 gives 450 million requests per day, about 5,200 RPS on average and roughly 18,200 RPS at peak with peakFactor=3.5. On top of that, networkProfile=lte with networkRttMs=60 ms adds to the response time, while pollIntervalSec=30 s and offlineSyncBurst=25 requests create background and bursty traffic over and above the session traffic.
practices: diurnalPattern=evening with peakFactor=3.5 produces an evening peak almost four times the average; size the edge against 18,200 RPS specifically.
networkRttMs=60 ms is part of the client-side p99 budget: with a 300 ms SLO only about 240 ms is left for the server side, so this parameter cannot be ignored when you walk the chain.
cacheableShare=0.45 is noticeably lower than the 0.6 of client-web; do not count on the same cdn offload for a mobile API.

pollIntervalSec=30 s means 2 requests per minute from every online device: with 100,000 devices online at once that is another 3,300 RPS of background load, and with pushEnabled=true that share is better moved to ws-gateway.
retries=3 with timeoutMs=20000 ms gives a worst case of 80 s for a single user request; lower one of the two values.
pitfalls: Forgetting that retries=3 multiplies load up to fourfold during degradation: the 18,200 RPS peak turns into a 72,800 RPS retry storm.
offlineSyncBurst=25 models the batch of requests fired when a device comes back online; during a mass connectivity recovery this is an instant spike that is invisible in the average RPS.
Switching networkProfile to nr5g to make the numbers look better while the real audience stays on lte, which makes the p99 estimate optimistic by tens of milliseconds.
avgResponseKb=18 KB looks small, but at 5,200 RPS it is about 90 MB/s of traffic through the edge.

client-web.summary: A load source representing browser users: it defines how many requests per second enter the diagram and what profile they have. It goes first in the chain, and all downstream load on the edge and the services is derived from it. This is the baseline traffic generator of the MVP wave for any web scenario.
client-web.capacity: hasModel=false, so the block takes no part in capacity calculations and constrains nothing; it only produces load. With the defaults dau=2,000,000, sessionsPerUserDay=3 and requestsPerSession=40 you get 240 million requests per day, which is about 2,780 RPS on average and roughly 8,300 RPS at peak with peakFactor=3. The traffic profile for downstream blocks is set by readWriteMix=0.85, cacheableShare=0.6, avgRequestKb=2 KB and avgResponseKb=45 KB.
practices: Connect the output to dns, cdn or an edge entry point (waf, glb, lb-l7, api-gateway); wiring it straight into an internal service bypasses the whole edge and skews the calculation.

peakFactor=3 together with diurnalPattern=business models a daytime office peak; switch to evening for an evening audience and to global for a worldwide one, otherwise the peak is computed for the wrong hour.
cacheableShare=0.6 defines the share of requests that is worth serving from cdn or reverse-cache at all; do not inflate it, or the origin will be modelled with less load than it actually receives.
Use growthPerYear=0.35 (35% growth per year) to check headroom: in two years 240 million requests per day become 437 million (240 × 1.35 × 1.35).
timeoutMs=15000 ms with retries=1 gives a worst case of 30 s per request; align it with timeoutMs=30000 ms on lb-l7 and timeoutMs=29000 ms on api-gateway.
pitfalls: Setting dau in the millions and forgetting peakFactor: downstream capacity has to be sized against the 8,300 RPS peak, not the 2,780 RPS average.
retries=1 doubles the load at exactly the moment the upstream is already degraded, so the edge limit is consumed twice as fast as expected.
keepAlive=false sharply increases the number of new connections: lb-l4 runs into newConnPerSec=100,000 and lb-l7 spends tlsHandshakeMs=1.2 ms of CPU on every single request.
avgResponseKb=45 KB at 2,780 RPS is about 120 MB/s, roughly 1 Gbps of outbound traffic; the network limits at the edge are overlooked more often than the RPS ones.

cockroach.summary: A distributed SQL database on Raft: nodes = 9 across regions = 3, every range in replicationFactor = 3 copies, and isolationLevel = serializable out of the box. It provides distributed transactions (transactionScope = distributed-2pc) and survives a node failure within failoverSec = 10 s. It is chosen at v1 when you need strict transactions across several regions, not just sharding.
cockroach.capacity: The raft-quorum binds first: maxOpsPerSecPerNode = 8000 × 9 nodes = 72,000 operations/s, but every write is replicated replicationFactor = 3 times, which leaves roughly 24,000 client writes/s. cpu is far behind (9 × 16 cores / writeServiceMs = 1.5 ms ≈ 96,000), connections give 500 per node, and iops is provisionedIops = 16,000 at iopsPerWrite = 2.
practices: partitionStrategy = geo-partitioned with partitionKey = region keeps all three replicas of a range inside one region, otherwise every commit pays crossRegionRttMs = 70 ms for its quorum.
replicationFactor = 3 survives the loss of one node and 5 survives two; above 5 the cost of a write grows with no gain in availability.
concurrencyControl = optimistic with isolationLevel = serializable means retries on conflicts, so the application must catch the serialization error and replay the transaction.
partitionSizeMb = 512 over 1.12 TB of logical data yields about 2,200 ranges, which is the right order; below 128 MB metadata bloats, above 1 GB rebalancing suffers.
readFromReplica = 0 by default is correct for linearizable; enable follower reads only alongside a deliberate move to bounded staleness.
pitfalls: A cross-region transaction pays crossRegionRttMs = 70 ms at least twice (prepare and commit in 2PC), which is 140+ ms at p99, and writeServiceMs = 1.5 ms changes nothing there.
serializable together with optimistic on a hot row produces a retry storm: as contention grows, throughput falls instead of rising.
Storage is usually estimated without replicationFactor: 1.12 TB of logical data becomes 3.4 TB on disk, that is 373 GB per node out of storageGbPerNode = 3000.
maxConnections = 500 per node (4,500 per cluster) requires connectionPooler = proxy-managed: a connection here is more expensive than in postgres.

config.summary: A configuration and feature-flag service: clients fetch values every pollIntervalSec 30 s and cache them (clientCache true), while the application performs evaluationsPerRequest 12 local evaluations at evaluationMs 0.02 ms per request. Use it to change behaviour without a deploy. It has no out ports.
config.capacity: The limiters are ops, cpu and connections. ops = maxOpsPerSec 6000 requests/s, connections = maxConnections 20,000 clients. With clientCache true and pollIntervalSec 30 s those 20,000 clients generate only 20,000 ÷ 30 ≈ 667 requests/s — far below 6000; the flag evaluations themselves cost 12 × 0.02 = 0.24 ms and happen inside the application, not in the block.
practices: Never turn clientCache off: without a cache each of the evaluationsPerRequest 12 flags becomes a network call, and just 500 application RPS produces exactly maxOpsPerSec 6000.
pollIntervalSec 30 s is your rollout time: a flag reaches the last instance in half a minute, so plan risky switches around that lag.
pushMode true cuts the lag to seconds but moves the limiter to connections: 20,000 long-lived subscriptions instead of short polls.
Keep default values in the client: if the block is unavailable the application must keep running on its last cache rather than crash.
Connect it to every compute block, but do not put secrets here — that is what the secrets block with encryption, auditing and a rate limit is for.
pitfalls: A flag inside a hot loop: evaluationMs 0.02 ms is harmless across 12 evaluations and noticeable across 1000 — count evaluations per request, not per user.
A synchronous application startup through config: when the block is unavailable instances do not come up, and availability 0.999 turns into an inability to deploy.
All clients polling in lockstep: 20,000 instances with the same pollIntervalSec 30 s and no jitter produce volleys instead of a steady 667 requests/s.
Nobody ever deletes flags: evaluationsPerRequest 12 quietly becomes 40 — the top of the realistic range — and the evaluation cost triples.

couchbase.summary: A document database with a memory-first architecture: memoryQuotaGb = 64 on each of nodes = 6, ejectionPolicy = value-only, replicas = 1. It gives readServiceMs = 0.4 ms on a memory hit and diskFetchMs = 3 ms on a miss, so it behaves as a cache and a store at the same time. It is placed at v2 when you need the access profile of a cache with the durability of a document database.
couchbase.capacity: The limits are memory, ops, connections and iops. memory: with ejectionPolicy = value-only the keys and metadata of all documentCount = 500 million documents stay resident regardless of documentSizeKb = 4, and memoryQuotaGb = 64 × 6 nodes = 384 GB has to cover workingSetGb = 200 on top of that. ops give maxOpsPerSecPerNode = 25,000 × 6 = 150,000 operations/s, of which writes are split across two copies at replicas = 1, connections stop at maxConnections = 10,000, and iops at provisionedIops = 30,000 with writeAmplification = 2.
practices: A memory miss costs diskFetchMs = 3 ms against readServiceMs = 0.4 ms, 7.5 times more, so keep workingSetGb = 200 inside the 384 GB quota with room for metadata growth.
ejectionPolicy = value-only is right for a cache profile; full ejection saves memory on rarely used documents but adds a disk hit even for checking whether a key exists.
bucketCount = 3 splits memoryQuotaGb between the buckets rigidly, so do not create a bucket per entity, scopes and collections exist for that.
replicas = 1 survives a node failure, while raising it to 2 doubles both the cost of a write and the memory with almost no change to availability = 0.9995.
consistencyModel = read-your-writes rests on reading from the active copy: for secondary-index queries state the scan consistency explicitly, otherwise you get staleness of replicaLagMs = 20 ms.
pitfalls: Memory is driven by documentCount, not by volume: 500 million small documents will eat the quota with metadata sooner than 50 million large ones of the same total size.
conflictResolution = lww resolves conflicts by time, and with XDCR between clusters that means losing a write whenever clocks drift.
documentCount = 500 million × 4 KB is 2 TB, and with replicas = 1 it is already 4 TB on disk: counting by documents without the replica is off by a factor of two.
concurrencyControl = optimistic works through CAS: without an explicit CAS check a concurrent document update is lost exactly as in mongodb.

cron.summary: A scheduler for periodic jobs: on scheduleCron '0 * * * *' (the same thing as intervalSec 3600) it starts a job that runs for jobDurationSec 600 s. Use it for regular recalculations, exports, cleanup and reconciliations. The only entry point is the trigger port; the outputs are the usual ones — databases, queues, external APIs.
cron.capacity: The limiters are concurrency and job-window. concurrency = instances 2 × concurrency 16 = 32 slots ÷ processingTimeMs 200 ms = 160 items/s, so within the jobDurationSec 600 s window a job gets through about 96,000 items. job-window requires that 600 s fit inside intervalSec 3600 s — right now the job takes 17% of the period.
practices: overlapPolicy skip is the safe default: if the previous run did not finish within the hour, the next one does not start and you never get two competing recalculations.
spikeFactor 10 honestly describes the nature of cron: once an hour downstream receives 10× the average load, and its capacity is sized against that peak, not against the hourly average.
timeoutMs 60,000 ms per item against jobDurationSec 600 s means 10 stuck items consume the entire window — keep the per-item timeout an order of magnitude below the job duration.
Stagger the schedules of different cron blocks: five blocks all set to '0 * * * *' is a synchronized volley at the top of every hour.
instances 2 exist for availability, not for parallelism: the scheduler has to elect a leader, otherwise the job runs twice.
pitfalls: overlapPolicy allow accumulates concurrent runs as data volume grows: two, then three jobs competing for the same database.
Sizing the load by the average: 96,000 items an hour looks like 27 items/s, but it is really 160 items/s for 10 minutes and zero for the other 50.
retries 2 inside the window triple the job duration on bad data — the job no longer fits into jobDurationSec 600 s, and skip silently drops the following runs.
Cron without observability: a run dropped by skip raises no error, so wire up the telemetry port and alert on the absence of a successful completion.

discovery.summary: A service registry: registeredInstances 900 instances belonging to services 60 services register, pass a health check every healthCheckIntervalSec 10 s and live for ttlSec 30 s. Clients resolve addresses and cache them with resolverCacheHitRatio 0.9. Use it where addresses change dynamically and there is no static load balancer.
discovery.capacity: The limiters are ops and cpu. ops = maxOpsPerSec 5000 requests/s at serviceTimeMs 1.5 ms. Thanks to resolverCacheHitRatio 0.9 only every tenth resolve reaches the block, so 5000 ops/s serve about 50,000 resolves/s; the background load from health checks is 900 ÷ 10 = 90 checks/s.
practices: Keep resolverCacheHitRatio high: dropping from 0.9 to 0.5 raises the share of resolves that reach the block from 10% to 50% and hits the 5000 ops/s wall five times sooner.
ttlSec 30 s is how long a dead instance still receives traffic; shorten it together with healthCheckIntervalSec 10 s, otherwise the TTL dominates anyway.
healthCheckIntervalSec 10 s across registeredInstances 900 produces 90 checks/s of background load; grow to 10,000 instances and that becomes 1000 checks/s — a fifth of the block's entire capacity.
instances 3 and availability 0.9995 are there because discovery is a startup-time dependency: without it new instances cannot find their neighbours.
Clients have to survive the block being unavailable on their own cache: that is the only protection against a cascade, since the block has no out ports and nowhere to degrade to.
pitfalls: Resolving on every call instead of caching: without a client cache, 5000 ops/s becomes the ceiling for every inter-service call in the system.
Treating ttlSec 30 s as a guarantee, when the client cache adds its own time on top — actually pulling an instance out of rotation takes noticeably longer.
Registration without deregistration: after a hard crash an instance hangs in the registry for ttlSec 30 s, and all traffic to it produces errors rather than timeouts.
Conflating discovery with load balancing: the block hands out a list of addresses but does not distribute load — evenness is the client's job.

dist-lock.summary: A distributed lock: it serializes access to a critical section by holding the lock for lockHoldMs 20 ms on backend redis, with fencingTokens true to guard against zombie owners. Use it where two instances must not perform the same operation at once — a debit, issuing a number, starting a job. It has no out ports.
dist-lock.capacity: The limiters are lock-serialization and ops. lock-serialization is the main one: a single key allows 1 ÷ lockHoldMs 20 ms = 50 acquisitions/s no matter how many instances there are. ops = maxOpsPerSec 100,000 operations/s across all keys combined, and that number is only reachable with an even key distribution.
practices: Keep lockHoldMs as small as possible: cutting it from 20 to 5 ms raises the hot-key ceiling from 50 to 200 acquisitions/s — the only way to speed up a serialized section.
fencingTokens true is mandatory: without a token an owner whose lock expired during a GC pause keeps writing and corrupts data that the next owner is already editing.
contentionRate 0.05 means 5% of operations fight over one key: at 10,000 RPS that is 500 requests/s against a single key with a ceiling of 50/s, a tenfold overload.
backend etcd or zk gives linearizability at the cost of latency; redis is faster, but correctness then rests on fencing and a short lockHoldMs.
Make the key as narrow as you can: locking per user instead of per table turns one hot key into millions of cold ones.
pitfalls: Using a lock instead of idempotency: dist-lock does not protect against reprocessing after the owner crashes — you need an idempotency key in the target store.
Waiting for a lock inside an HTTP request: at 50 acquisitions/s per key the queue grows and clients get timeouts instead of an honest contention error.
Sizing capacity by maxOpsPerSec 100,000: that is the ceiling for the whole block, while the real constraint is 50 acquisitions/s on a specific key.
Holding a lock longer than its lease: instances 3 and availability 0.999 will not save you if the application assumes the lock is eternal.

dlq.summary: A dead-letter queue: everything a consumer failed to process within maxRetries 5 attempts ends up here. The job of the block is to take a poison message off the main flow, keep it for investigation and offer a controlled retry. Attach it to the dlq port of any queue or subscription that must not be blocked by one failing message.
dlq.capacity: The limiters are rate-limit and depth. rate-limit is set by the retry loop: reprocessBatchSize 50 messages once every redriveDelaySec 300 s is 600 messages per hour, so an accumulated 100000 will take about 7 days to work through. depth is bounded by maxDepth 100000000 messages and retentionHours 336, that is 14 days: whatever is not handled within two weeks disappears.
practices: alertThresholdMessages 100 together with notifyOnArrival true is the minimum sensible setup: a DLQ without an alert is useless, because people remember it a month later.
reprocessMode manual is the right default: an automatic redrive without fixing the cause sends the same message straight back into the same failure.
Raise reprocessBatchSize and lower redriveDelaySec only once the root cause is understood, otherwise the retry burst takes the consumer down again.
Give every source its own DLQ: a single shared one makes investigation impossible, because the origin context of the message is lost.
Store the failure reason and the attempt counter in the attributes — at messageSizeKb 4 there is enough room for diagnostic metadata.
pitfalls: retentionHours 336 is often shorter than the real reaction time for a rare bug: two weeks pass and the evidence disappears along with the messages.
reprocessMode auto with redriveDelaySec 300 against an unfixed error gives an endless loop and bills every pass at costPerMillionRequests 0.4 USD.
Some messages are invalid forever (a broken schema, a deleted entity): export and drop them instead of cycling them through retries.
Landing in the DLQ usually means a bug rather than overload: raising maxRetries from 5 to 50 only delays the investigation and multiplies the side effects of retries.

dns.summary: Authoritative DNS: it turns a name into an address and acts as the first point where traffic is routed by latency, geography, weights or failover. A managed block whose capacity is set by the provider's quota rather than by an instance count. It goes first, right after the clients and before cdn, glb and the load balancers.
dns.capacity: The only limit is authoritative-qps with maxQps=500,000 RPS. Only a fraction of client requests reaches the authoritative layer because resolverCacheHitRatio=0.9 absorbs 90% of them: at 5,000,000 client resolutions per second the block receives exactly 500,000 RPS. Lowering ttlSec=60 s reduces resolver cache efficiency and directly raises the load on the authoritative layer.
practices: routingPolicy=latency with geoMapping=continent suits an ordinary multi-region setup; use failover for an explicit switch to a standby and weighted for canary traffic shifting.
ttlSec=60 s is a compromise: it sets the lower bound on switchover time, while raising it to 300 s (the top of the realistic 30-300 s range) cuts the load on the authoritative layer fivefold.
Total switchover time is healthCheckSec=10 s × healthCheckThreshold=3 = 30 s to detect plus ttlSec=60 s to propagate, about 90 s in total; that is the lower bound on RTO for a DNS failover.
anycastPops=30 is what delivers resolveMs=18 ms; reducing the PoP count only makes sense if you raise resolveMs in the calculation at the same time.
Wire the resolve output to glb or cdn rather than straight to lb-l7 whenever the diagram has more than one region.
pitfalls: Relying on DNS as a fast failover mechanism, when clients and intermediate resolvers ignore ttlSec=60 s and hold on to the old address for minutes.
Setting ttlSec=1 s for a faster switchover, which wipes out resolverCacheHitRatio=0.9 and sends the entire load straight into maxQps=500,000 RPS.
Forgetting negativeTtlSec=30 s: after one bad negative answer clients keep getting a failure for another half a minute after the fix is in.
availability=0.99999 (about 5.3 minutes of downtime per year) looks like absolute reliability, but a DNS failure takes down all of the diagram's traffic, not just a part of it.

druid.summary: A columnar time-series store fed from a stream: time-based segments, rollup pre-aggregation and sub-second slices for real-time dashboards.
druid.capacity: On writes the first limit is realtime-ingest = 40,000 events/s divided by the write share; on reads it is disk-scan against the volume of segments scanned, then cpu and query-slots.
practices: The scan equals segmentsScannedPerQuery × rowsPerSegment × rowSize / compressionRatio / rollupRatio — the time filter decides everything.
rollupRatio 2–100 compresses both storage and the scan proportionally: at 8 a 300 B row is stored as 6 B.
rowsPerSegment 1–10 million gives segments of about 30 MB — a convenient size for parallel reads.
realtimeIngestRps 10,000–2,000,000 is the ingest ceiling; compare it with the producer that stands in the design.
pitfalls: A query without a time filter takes all segments: 20,000 segments instead of 4 means 625 GB instead of 125 MB.
Rollup is irreversible: detailed rows cannot be recovered after aggregation.
ttlDays = 90 quietly removes the old segments that annual reports rely on.

dynamodb.summary: A managed key-value and document store where capacity is bought in units: capacityMode = on-demand, rcu = 20,000 and wcu = 5000. It delivers a predictable p99 at any volume, but only by partitionKey = userId and gsiCount = 2 secondary indexes. It is taken at mvp when the access pattern is known in advance and nobody wants to operate a database.
dynamodb.capacity: The limits are vendor-units, partitions and hot-partition. vendor-units are counted from itemSizeKb = 2: an eventual read costs 0.5 RCU, so rcu = 20,000 is 40,000 reads/s, while a 2 KB write costs 2 WCU plus 2 WCU for each of the gsiCount = 2 indexes, 6 WCU in total, so wcu = 5000 yields only about 830 writes/s. partitions require at least 7 partitions for 20,000 RCU (maxRcuPerPartition = 3000) and 5 for 5000 WCU (maxWcuPerPartition = 1000), while hot-partition at hotPartitionShare = 0.1 would cap the table at 30,000 RCU and therefore does not bind at the current units yet.
practices: consistencyModel = eventual is twice as cheap as strongly consistent: switching every read to strong turns 40,000 reads/s into 20,000 at the same rcu = 20,000.
gsiCount = 2 triples the cost of a write, so project only the attributes you need into a GSI (KEYS_ONLY or INCLUDE), not the whole item.
partitionKey = userId must have high cardinality: hotPartitionShare = 0.1 already means a tenth of the traffic hits one partition capped at 3000 RCU and 1000 WCU.
streams = true wires up the cdc output into Kafka, and that is the standard way to build projections and search on top of the table, because there are no non-key queries here.
ttlEnabled = true cleans up itemCount = 1 billion without spending WCU, but the deletion is asynchronous, so do not treat it as a guarantee of removal by a deadline.
pitfalls: A write is five times more expensive than a read (costPerMillionWrites = 0.625 against costPerMillionReads = 0.125), and that is before GSIs: a write-heavy profile on DynamoDB costs money, not just units.
readServiceMs = 4 ms and writeServiceMs = 8 ms are an HTTP call over the network, an order of magnitude slower than redis-store at serviceTimeMs = 0.25 ms.
conflictResolution = lww with concurrencyControl = optimistic: without a conditional write a concurrent item update is lost.
itemCount = 1 billion × itemSizeKb = 2 is 2 TB, and every GSI with a full projection adds another 2 TB — at costPerGbMonth = 0.25 three copies come to about 1500 USD per month.

edge-function.summary: Code at the network edge: popCount 300 points of presence run lightweight logic in cpuMsPerRequest 8 ms of CPU — redirects, A/B, personalization, token checks, header rewriting. Put it in front of the origin so that a simple decision does not require a trip across the ocean. It is a managed block with very cheap cold starts: coldStartMs 5 ms.
edge-function.capacity: The limiters are cpu and concurrency. cpu = popCount 300 × cpuCoresPerPop 2 = 600 cores, i.e. 600,000 CPU-ms/s ÷ cpuMsPerRequest 8 ms = 75,000 RPS. concurrency is barely a constraint: 300 × isolatesPerPop 2000 = 600,000 isolates held for serviceTimeMs 25 ms give on the order of 24 million RPS.
practices: Keep cpuMsPerRequest 8 ms far away from cpuMsLimit 50 ms: exceeding the limit does not slow a request down, it kills it, and that is the block's only hard wall.

subrequestsPerInvocation 1 means every invocation goes to the origin; the whole value of the block is finishing part of the requests with zero subrequests — from cache, with a redirect, or with a 304.
Size the load against the hottest PoPs rather than against all 300: 75,000 RPS spread evenly is 250 RPS per PoP, but real traffic concentrates in 5-10 of them.
coldStartMs 5 ms at coldStartShare 0.05 adds just 0.25 ms to the average — unlike serverless, here the cold start can be ignored.
Do not keep state here: isolates are short-lived and scattered across 300 PoPs, and any consistency requires a trip to central storage.
pitfalls: Heavy logic at the edge: raising cpuMsPerRequest from 8 to 30 ms (the top of the realistic range) drops the ceiling from 75,000 to 20,000 RPS without a single change in traffic.
Cost at volume: costPerMillionRequests $0.3 plus 8 CPU-ms × costPerMillionCpuMs $0.02 = $0.16, or $0.46 per million in total; at 10,000 RPS that is 864 million requests a day and about $400 a day.
Raising subrequestsPerInvocation to 5 quietly multiplies the origin load fivefold — the edge stops shielding and starts amplifying.
Debugging is spread across 300 PoPs: logLinesPerRequest 2 × logBytesPerLine 300 bytes looks trivial, but at 10,000 RPS that is 6 MB/s of logs from hundreds of locations.

elasticsearch.summary: A search cluster built on an inverted index: full-text search, filters and aggregations over documents. It sits next to the primary database to offload the queries that database cannot serve.
elasticsearch.capacity: cpu binds first: capacity equals nodes × cpuCores / (S × fanout), where fanout is the number of shards a single request touches. search-threads bind later (24 slots against 16 cores), and indexing is loaded only by writes.
practices: Every read request fans out to all shardsPerIndex shards: 6 shards multiply the CPU cost of a query sixfold. Keep it in the 1–30 range.
Keep heapGb at 31 GB or below — the compressed-pointer boundary; grow with more nodes, not a bigger heap.
queryType sets the cost: term 0.4×, match 1×, aggregation 3× of queryServiceMs = 25 ms.
Freshness rests on refreshIntervalSec = 1 s and a replica lag of 1,000 ms — never promise users anything tighter.
pitfalls: queryConcurrencyPerNode above cpuCores buys no throughput: with 16 cores and 24 slots, cpu remains the limit.
Elasticsearch as the primary store: eventual consistency and lww lose updates when a document is written from two places.
A forgotten replica doubles both volume and indexing traffic: 200 million documents on defaults take about 1.1 TB.

email-smtp.summary: Sending mail over SMTP: messagesPerSec 500 messages/s with dkimSigning true, exponential-backoff on errors and a typical delivery delay of deliveryLagSec 8 s. Use it for transactional mail — confirmations, invoices, password resets. The only outputs are http/grpc/internal to the mail provider.
email-smtp.capacity: The limiters are rate-limit, workers, connections and inflight. rate-limit = messagesPerSec 500 binds first: workers = instances 2 × concurrency 60 = 120 slots ÷ serviceTimeMs 150 ms = 800 emails/s, connections = maxConnections 400 at the same hold time give about 2600 emails/s, and maxInflight 200,000 is 400 s (6.7 minutes) of buffer at 500/s.
practices: dkimSigning true is mandatory alongside SPF and DMARC: without a signature the mail lands in spam, and bounceRate 0.02 quickly grows several times over.
Keep bounceRate below 0.05: providers cut sender reputation on exactly that metric, and messagesPerSec 500 stops being achievable.
Separate transactional and marketing mail across different domains and blocks: complaints about a campaign must not take down password-reset delivery.
retryPolicy exponential-backoff is the right choice for SMTP: temporary 4xx responses are cured by retrying minutes later, while permanent 5xx must never be retried at all.
Put the block behind a queue: deliveryLagSec 8 s and maxInflight 200,000 say outright that mail is asynchronous by nature, and a synchronous call from a service has no place here.
pitfalls: messagesPerEvent 1 quietly becomes 100 (the top of the realistic range) on bulk campaigns: 100 events/s turns into 10,000 emails/s — 20 times above messagesPerSec 500.
concurrency 60 across two instances at serviceTimeMs 150 ms gives 800 emails/s — only 60% headroom over the limit, and losing one instance drops capacity to 400 emails/s, below the limit itself.
Treating maxInflight 200,000 as reliability: if the provider stops, the buffer is exhausted in 6.7 minutes and mail is lost after that unless there is a DLQ.
costPerThousand $0.1 at 500 emails/s is 43.2 million emails and $4320 a day, while the 2 × 0.06 = $0.12/hour for the instances is indistinguishable against that background.

etcd.summary: A replicated key-value store on Raft for metadata: nodes = 3, consistencyModel = linearizable, replicationMode = sync. It holds uniqueKeys = 200,000 small keys, watchers = 5000 subscriptions and leaseCount = 10,000 leases, which is configuration, service discovery and leader election, not user data. It is placed at v1 next to the control plane, not on the user request path.
etcd.capacity: The limits are write-quorum, cpu and memory: every write is a Raft round-trip of writeQuorumMs = 10 ms, and only batchSize = 64 lifts the ceiling to 6,400 writes/s, whereas one-by-one writes give 100/s. cpu works out as cpuCores = 8 × cpuShare = 0.3 = 2.4 effective cores / readServiceMs = 0.5 ms ≈ 4,800 reads/s. memory runs into maxDbSizeMb = 2048, a hard backend quota, while 200,000 keys of 1152 bytes occupy about 230 MB.
practices: nodes = 3 survives the loss of one node and 5 nodes survive two, but every write then waits for a larger quorum: the cluster is not grown for throughput.
consistencyModel = linearizable applies to reads as well: a linearizable read pays its own quorum round-trip, while a serializable read from the local node is cheaper when staleness is acceptable.
valueSizeBytes = 1024 is the right order of magnitude: etcd is not a blob store, the request limit is around 1.5 MB, and large values hurt the Raft log.
watchers = 5000 means 5000 open streams, and every key change is broadcast to all subscribers, so compute the fanout as watchers × the change rate.
leaseCount = 10,000 requires keepalive traffic; an expiring lease is the standard leader-election mechanism, do not invent locks on top of plain keys.
pitfalls: maxDbSizeMb = 2048 is reached not by the size of the data but by MVCC history: without regular compaction and defrag the cluster goes read-only with 230 MB of useful data.
Putting etcd on the user request path is an architectural mistake: 4,800 reads/s and 100 writes/s without batching is orders of magnitude below redis-store.
A slow disk breaks Raft: writeQuorumMs = 10 ms holds only while fsync is fast, and on a network volume leader elections start firing on their own.
cpuShare = 0.3 means etcd shares the node with other processes, and a noisy neighbour turns into a lost quorum, not merely a slowdown.

external-api.summary: An arbitrary external API as a managed dependency: p50Ms 120 ms, p99Ms 900 ms, rateLimitRps 500 and a daily quotaPerDay 5,000,000 calls. Put it in the design to represent someone else's service honestly — maps, exchange rates, data enrichment, antifraud. It is shielded by circuitBreaker true with a threshold of 0.5 and circuitBreakerResetSec 30 s.
external-api.capacity: The limiters are rate-limit and daily-quota. rateLimitRps 500 is the instantaneous ceiling, while quotaPerDay 5,000,000 spread over a day gives only 5,000,000 ÷ 86,400 ≈ 58 calls/s on average. You can hold 500 RPS for just 10,000 s ≈ 2.8 hours a day, so the daily quota is almost nine times tighter.
practices: Plan against quotaPerDay, not against rateLimitRps: a steady 58 calls/s is the real budget, and everything above it has to be cached.
circuitBreakerErrorThreshold 0.5 and circuitBreakerResetSec 30 s protect the quota as well: an open breaker does not spend calls on a service that is already failing.
retries 2 with retryBackoffMs 200 ms triple quota consumption in the worst case: at errorRate 0.005 that is plus 1%, but during an incident retries burn through the daily limit in minutes.
timeoutMs 3000 ms against p99Ms 900 ms is 3.3× headroom, which is reasonable; going below p99 is not an option, and going higher means holding the caller's slots longer.
Put a cache in front of the block: with cacheable responses and a 90% hit ratio, a load of 580 calls/s turns into 58 and the quota question disappears.
pitfalls: costPerCall $0.0005 × 5,000,000 = $2500 a day ≈ $76,000/month if the quota is fully consumed — an external API is usually an order of magnitude more expensive than your own instances.
Exhausting the daily quota at 15:00: for the rest of the day the block returns errors, and it looks like your system failing, not someone else's.
Ignoring idempotencyRequired true on retries: a retry without a key for non-GET operations creates duplicates on the provider's side.
The external API's availability 0.999 is part of your chain: without degrading to a cache or to a default value, its 43 minutes a month become yours.

ftp-legacy.summary: File exchange over FTP or SFTP: sessions, directories, whole-file uploads. A technically obsolete block that is kept for integration with external partners and legacy systems that can do nothing else. In a design it honestly reflects the risk: availability 0.99 is the lowest figure in the whole set.
ftp-legacy.capacity: The limiters are concurrency and throughput. concurrency 50 sessions at perSessionMbs 10 give 500 MB/s in theory, but the shared throughputMbs 100 cuts that by five: roughly 10 sessions run at full speed and the other 40 split what is left. At avgFileSizeMb 8 the ceiling is about 12.5 files per second.
practices: Place the block only at the boundary with an external system, and plan the migration to s3 or minio with the S3 API from the start.
Reconcile concurrency 50 and perSessionMbs 10 with the shared throughputMbs 100: declared parallelism without bandwidth produces a queue, not throughput.
Upload the file under a temporary name and rename it once the transfer completes — otherwise the consumer picks up a partially written file.
Run a separate process that moves files into object storage: storageGb 4000 on an FTP server without rotation runs out silently.
There is no out port and the block emits no events about new files: discovery is done by polling the directory, and that interval becomes part of your SLO.
pitfalls: availability 0.99 is about 87 hours of downtime a year, that is 3.6 days: any SLO above that figure is unreachable on top of FTP.
Polling the directory instead of receiving events brings both latency and races: two consumers pick up the same file unless there is a lock or a move into a processing directory.
latencyMs 40 and the session model make the protocol unsuitable for small frequent files: establishing a session costs more than the transfer itself.

The cost looks deceptively low (costPerInstanceHour 0.1 USD plus 4000 GB at costPerGbMonth 0.1 USD, about 470 USD a month), but manual failure investigations and the absence of built-in retries eat up more than that.

geo-index.summary: A geospatial index: cellCount 5,000,000 cells at precision 6 on backend redis serve 'what is nearby' queries within queryRadiusKm 5 and absorb updatesPerSec 50,000 coordinate updates. Use it in delivery, ride-hailing, maps and nearest-object search. It has no out ports — the block only answers queries.
geo-index.capacity: The limiters are ops and throughput. ops = maxOpsPerSec 200,000 operations/s, but a radius query is not a single operation: at precision 6 a cell is roughly 1.2 × 0.6 km, and a circle with a radius of 5 km covers about 100 cells, so the real ceiling is on the order of 2000 queries/s. throughput = updatesPerSec 50,000 is a separate limit on coordinate writes.
practices: Choose precision to match queryRadiusKm: precision 6 at a 5 km radius gives about 100 cells per query, precision 7 gives roughly 3500, and precision 5 gives a handful of cells at the cost of coarse filtering.
Always filter the result by exact distance after selecting the cells: a geohash gives rectangles, not circles, and false positives appear at the boundary.
updatesPerSec 50,000 sets how often positions can be refreshed: 500,000 moving objects can be updated once every 10 seconds, no more often than that.
cellCount 5,000,000 × rowSizeBytes 256 = 1.28 GB — the whole index fits in memory, which is why backend redis and serviceTimeMs 0.05 ms are realistic.
Choose backend search or database when you need complex filters alongside the geo query; redis only gives you proximity.
pitfalls: Treating maxOpsPerSec 200,000 as queries: one query costs about 100 operations, and the real ceiling is 2000 queries/s — a hundredfold estimation error.
