Growing queryRadiusKm from 5 to 50 km increases the area 100 times, to roughly 10,000 cells per query — the block stops answering in 0.05 ms.
Uneven density: in a city centre a single precision 6 cell can hold tens of thousands of objects, and the query returns all of them.
Keeping movement history in this same block: 50,000 updates/s × 256 bytes is 1.1 TB per day, which needs a separate database rather than a proximity index.

glacier.summary: An archival storage class: storage costs an order of magnitude less than s3 (costPerGbMonth 0.004 against 0.023 USD), but the data is not available straight away — you have to request a restore and wait hours. Use it as the end point of a lifecycle for logs, backups and data that has to be kept for years to satisfy regulatory requirements.
glacier.capacity: The limiters are retrieval and throughput. retrieval: retrievalTier standard gives retrievalHours 4 of waiting before the object appears and concurrency 200 simultaneous restore jobs. throughput: throughputMbs 500 for serving what is already restored, so a terabyte takes 2000 s to pull down (about 33 minutes) — and that is after the four-hour wait.
practices: Pick retrievalTier by deadline: expedited is minutes and expensive, standard is hours, bulk is up to half a day and the cheapest of all; the tier is chosen at request time, not at upload time.
minStorageDays 90 is the minimum billable period: an object deleted on day ten is still billed as if it had been stored for 90.
Pack small files into archives before uploading: objectCount 200000000 means 200 million separate restore jobs, not one.
Test restores regularly: an archive nobody has ever pulled data out of is a hope, not a backup.
Bring the block into the design only through a lifecycle rule from s3, never by writing to it directly from the hot path: the read latency makes it unusable for user requests.
pitfalls: Disaster recovery plans routinely ignore retrievalHours 4: an RTO under a day is unreachable with this block.

costPerGbRetrieval 0.01 USD goes unnoticed in tests and hurts on a mass restore: pulling down 3.2 PB (200 million objects of 16 MB, about 12800 USD a month to store) costs another 32000 USD for a single retrieval.
concurrency 200 limits the number of parallel jobs rather than the volume: a mass restore is stretched out by queueing, not by bandwidth.

glb.summary: A global load balancer: it distributes traffic across regions and shifts it to a healthy region on failure. A managed block with a stated RPS quota and no instances of its own. Place it after DNS and before the regional lb-l7 or api-gateway whenever the diagram has more than one region.
glb.capacity: The only limit is global-rps with maxRps=1,000,000 RPS for the whole block, regardless of regions=2. Its own latency is latencyMs=0.5 ms and its availability=0.99999, that is about 5.3 minutes of downtime per year. The number of regions does not change the block's capacity; it changes how much traffic each region receives and what happens during a failover.
practices: routingPolicy=latency suits an ordinary multi-region setup; failover is for an active-passive design and weighted for gradually shifting traffic.

Reaction time to a regional failure is healthCheckIntervalSec=10 s × healthCheckThreshold=3 = 30 s of detection plus failoverSec=30 s of switching, about a minute in total, plus drainTimeoutSec=60 s for connections that are already open.
With regions=2 each region must sustain 100% of the traffic, not 50%: after a failover the entire stream goes into the single surviving region.
stickyRegion=false is the default; turn it on if there is region-bound state behind the block (sessions, sharded writes), otherwise one user's requests will land in different regions.
Leave drainOnFailover=true enabled, otherwise a switchover kills active connections instead of draining them gracefully.
pitfalls: Sizing each region for 50% of the traffic at regions=2, so when one fails the survivor is instantly overloaded.
Expecting an instant failover, when the minimum is about 60 s of detection plus switching, and more once drainTimeoutSec=60 s is counted.
stickyRegion=false combined with asynchronous replication breaks read-after-write: the write went to one region and the read arrived in another one that is behind by the replication lag.
costPerMillionRequests=0.6 USD looks like pennies, but 1 billion requests per day is 600 USD per day for global load balancing alone.

hazelcast.summary: A distributed in-memory data grid: a partitioned map with backups and a near cache on every node. Shared state for when a single cache is no longer enough.
hazelcast.capacity: memory is the limit: usable capacity equals nodes × memoryGb × 0.7 / (1 + backupCount) against the write stream over the TTL. Next come network (4 KB values) and ops, where every write weighs (1 + backupCount).
practices: A near cache helps only when it is comparable to the key space: 256 MB against 42 GB yields under 1% hits.
backupCount 1–2 divides usable capacity by (1 + backupCount): 6 × 16 GB turn into 33.6 GB of data.
Every write costs (1 + backupCount) operations and broadcasts a near cache invalidation to all nodes.
networkMbps is 1 Gbps per node: with 4 KB values the network binds before grid operations do.
pitfalls: backupCount = 0 turns the grid into a cache with no right to fail: losing a node takes its partitions with it.
A near cache without accounting for invalidation yields stale reads and adds traffic on every write.
The grid as the primary store: the data lives in memory, and a simultaneous restart of the nodes loses it.

hbase.summary: A wide-column store on top of HDFS: regionServers = 12 serve regionsPerServer = 100 regions each, and the data sits with hdfsReplication = 3. Unlike cassandra it gives consistencyModel = linearizable per row, because every region is served by exactly one server. It is placed at v2 under very large tables (rowCount = 20 billion) with range scans over the rowKey.
hbase.capacity: regions bind first: regionServers = 12 × regionsPerServer = 100 = 1200 regions × maxOpsPerSecPerRegion = 25 = 30,000 operations/s, whereas node-ops gives 12 × 8000 = 96,000, and cpu on 192 cores at readServiceMs = 2 ms gives the same 96,000. iops is driven by misses: blockCacheGb = 16 × 12 nodes = 192 GB against workingSetGb = 400 GB, so less than half the working set is in memory.
practices: The rowKey decides everything: a monotonic key such as a timestamp parks every write in a single region capped at maxOpsPerSecPerRegion = 25, so salt the prefix or use a reverse timestamp.
Keep regionsPerServer = 100 inside the 20–300 band: fewer and the cluster is underused, more and the MemStore of each region no longer fits into the server's memory.
Bring workingSetGb down toward the total blockCache: 400 GB against 192 GB means more than half the reads go to HDFS on top of readServiceMs = 2 ms.
A write is five times cheaper than a read (writeServiceMs = 0.4 ms against 2 ms), so HBase is good under a write stream with scans, not under high-RPS point reads.
The cdc output into Kafka is built on WAL replication, and analytical scans should be moved to separate replicas so they do not evict the blockCache.
pitfalls: A RegionServer failure makes its 100 regions unavailable until they are reassigned, hence availability = 0.999, lower than the 0.9995 of cassandra, where a region has no single owner.
hdfsReplication = 3 at 20 billion rows of 200 bytes: 4 TB raw, 1.33 TB after compressionRatio = 3 and 4 TB again on HDFS, that is 333 GB per node out of storageGbPerNode = 8000.
linearizable here holds only within a single row: there are no transactions across rows, and concurrencyControl = pessimistic applies inside a region.
The cluster drags along ZooKeeper, HDFS and HBase at once — three systems to operate for the sake of one table, so at v2 it is worth comparing against cassandra and s3-table.

hdfs.summary: A distributed file system for batch processing: files are cut into blocks of blockSizeMb 128 and spread across data nodes with replication 3, while a single NameNode holds the entire metadata tree in memory. It is optimized for large sequential reads, not for small files and random access. Use it for the classic Hadoop and Spark stack, when data and compute live on the same hardware.
hdfs.capacity: The limiters are namenode-metadata and throughput. Metadata: all fileCount 80000000 entries are held in namenodeMemoryGb 64, and the rate is capped by namenodeHandlers 64 at namenodeServiceMs 1 ms, that is 64000 metadata operations/s — about 21000 writes/s at metadataOpsPerWrite 3. Bandwidth: nodes 20 × throughputMbsPerNode 500 = 10000 MB/s raw, of which writes are divided by replication 3, leaving roughly 3300 MB/s.
practices: The NameNode is the single scaling point for metadata: raise blockSizeMb (realistically 64-512) instead of multiplying the number of files.
Keep the average file noticeably larger than a block: avgFileSizeMb 256 with blockSizeMb 128 gives 2 blocks per file, which is a sensible minimum.
A read costs metadataOpsPerRead 1 and a write costs metadataOpsPerWrite 3: a write-heavy pipeline hits the NameNode wall three times faster than a read-heavy one.
replication 3 serves both durability and compute locality; dropping to 2 saves a third of the capacity at the cost of noticeably worse recovery.
There is no out port: HDFS does not notify anyone when files appear, so batch orchestration is done externally on a schedule.
pitfalls: The small-file problem: millions of files a few megabytes each eat namenodeMemoryGb 64 and bring the cluster down, even though the data nodes still have plenty of space.

The defaults do not add up on capacity: fileCount 80000000 at avgFileSizeMb 256 is about 20 PB, whereas nodes 20 × storageGbPerNode 8000 at replication 3 give only about 53 TB usable; the file count and the file size have to be brought in line with capacity.
namenodeHandlers 64 is the bottleneck under a spike: hundreds of parallel tasks opening files queue up at the NameNode while the data nodes sit idle.
latencyMs 8 and a batch profile: HDFS does not serve user requests, and a separate layer on top is needed for that.

id-gen.summary: An identifier generator: strategy snowflake issues idsPerSec 250,000 monotonic IDs in serviceTimeMs 0.05 ms. Use it where you need unique, time-sortable keys without a trip to the database — orders, messages, events. It has no out ports, and availability 0.9999 here is no accident: without an ID no write goes through.
id-gen.capacity: The limiters are ops and cpu. ops = idsPerSec 250,000 identifiers/s across instances 3; serviceTimeMs 0.05 ms means the block barely computes at all — the ceiling is set by the ID scheme (the number of counter bits within a millisecond), not by the hardware.
practices: strategy uuidv7 is generated inside the application and removes the network call: if time-sortability is all you need, the block can be deleted from the design entirely.
Hand out ranges rather than single IDs: a client that takes a block of 1000 identifiers cuts the load 1000× and survives the block being unavailable.
clockSkewRisk 0.02 is about snowflake: a clock running backwards breaks monotonicity, so NTP and protection against backward jumps are mandatory.
monotonic true gives time-sortability and good insert locality in a B-tree index — that is exactly why snowflake is preferred over a random UUIDv4.
Keep availability 0.9999 (4.4 minutes a month) honest: id-gen sits on the write path, and its unavailability equals the unavailability of writes.
pitfalls: strategy ticket-server turns generation into a database write: 250,000 IDs/s becomes unreachable and the ceiling drops to thousands.
Two snowflake instances sharing the same node identifier produce duplicate IDs while the block looks perfectly healthy — node-id assignment has to be centralized.
A monotonic ID used as a public order number: people measure your business volume from it, and the sequence lets them enumerate other people's records.
Calling id-gen synchronously for every row of a batch: inserting 10,000 rows becomes 10,000 round trips instead of one range request.

influx.summary: A purpose-built TSDB: seriesCardinality = 5 million series, pointsPerSec = 200,000 points, bytesPerSample = 3 bytes after compression, retentionPolicy = month. It stores metrics more compactly than a general-purpose database, paying for it with consistencyModel = eventual and conflictResolution = lww. It is placed at v1 under application metrics and telemetry, where volume matters and transactions do not.
influx.capacity: The first limit is cardinality, and it is also memory: memoryGb = 64 at memoryPerMillionSeriesGb = 4 holds at most 16 million series, while the current 5 million take 20 GB, that is 31% of the ceiling. iops at provisionedIops = 20,000 binds during flushes to disk, and volume works out as 200,000 points/s × 3 bytes = 51.8 GB per day and about 1.56 TB over the retention month.
practices: Cardinality is the one metric you have to watch: a tag with unique values (userId, requestId) multiplies seriesCardinality by its own cardinality and pins memory.
batchSize = 500 points per write is mandatory: sending 200,000 points/s one at a time means 200,000 requests/s to the TSDB.
seriesPerQuery = 1000 at queryServiceMs = 5 ms is a normal dashboard, whereas a query over 100,000 series eats memory and evicts the index.
Set retentionPolicy = month together with downsampling: raw points for a month are 1.56 TB, while aggregates for a year are a few gigabytes.
Write here through a separate pipeline (Kafka or an agent) rather than directly from the services: consistencyModel = eventual and availability = 0.99 must not affect the main request path.
pitfalls: Cardinality explosion: one new tag with 100 values turns 5 million series into 500 million and demands 2 TB of memory instead of 20 GB — that is not degradation, that is an outage.
conflictResolution = lww with concurrencyControl = none: two points with the same timestamp and tags collapse into one, and the second silently overwrites the first.
availability = 0.99 is about 3.6 days per year, and the metrics disappear exactly when you need them if the TSDB runs on the same cluster as the service being observed.
replicaLagMs = 500 ms with replicationMode = async means gaps in the freshest data: a no-data alert must have a margin comfortably larger than the lag.

internet.summary: The link from the client to your entry point: a public network with latency, packet loss and the cost of establishing TLS. It describes the leg you cannot influence with code, yet it is the first thing a user feels. Placed between client blocks and the edge of the design, that is the CDN, the load balancer or the API gateway.
internet.capacity: hasModel = false: the internet serves nothing and has no bounds, bandwidth is not modelled here. What it contributes to the calculation is clientRttMs = 40 ms per leg, tlsHandshakeRtt = 2 round trips to establish a secure connection, and packetLoss = 0.001 as the fraction of lost packets.
practices: A cold connection costs clientRttMs × (1 + tlsHandshakeRtt) = 40 × 3 = 120 ms before the first byte of the request, and all of it happens before your code gets control.
TLS 1.3 reduces tlsHandshakeRtt to 1, cutting the cold start from 120 ms to 80 ms; only session resumption lets you count on 0.
Terminate TLS as close to the client as possible: a CDN or an edge point of presence lowers the effective clientRttMs, because the handshake goes to the nearest site rather than to the region.
packetLoss = 0.001 at an RTT of 40 ms means a lost packet costs a retransmission and adds tens of milliseconds to the tail of the distribution.
Compare server-side p99 with the client-side one: the user sees server time plus at least 40 ms, and plus 120 ms on a cold connection.
pitfalls: Designing an SLO from server-side metrics: targetP99Ms = 300 ms on probe-slo with a 120 ms cold start leaves the code 180 ms, not 300.
Ignoring keep-alive: without connection reuse every request pays the full three round trips of the handshake.
clientRttMs = 40 ms as a value for everyone: the range is 1 to 500 ms, and users from another continent or on a mobile network live closer to the upper bound.

k8s-cluster.summary: A Kubernetes cluster container: the node pool that hosts the services, workers and other compute blocks of the design. It defines how many pods fit in total, how quickly a new pod appears and how much the hardware underneath costs. Appears in wave v1, when there are more services than is convenient to place on separate machines.
k8s-cluster.capacity: hasModel = false: the cluster serves no requests by itself, capacity is computed by the blocks nested inside it. It sets the capacity of nodes × podsPerNode = 6 × 110 = 660 pods, the delay before a new pod appears at schedulingLagSec = 30 s, and a cost of 6 × 0.15 USD per hour × 730 hours = 657 USD plus controlPlaneCostMonth = 73 USD, for 730 USD per month in total.
practices: schedulingLagSec = 30 s is the applicability boundary of autoscaling: a burst shorter than half a minute is served by pods that are already up, so keep the headroom in them rather than in autoscaleNodes.
Choose nodeType to match the profile of the nested blocks: general against memory and compute changes which resource the services inside run out of first.
podsPerNode = 110 is the kubelet upper limit, not a realistic one: compute from memory and from the addresses in the parent vpc cidr, you usually hit those first.
controlPlaneCostMonth = 73 USD is paid per cluster, not per node: three small clusters cost 219 USD for management alone, before the first node.
autoscaleNodes = true does not remove the need to plan: autoscaling smooths the daily profile but does not save you from a peakFactor that arrives faster than 30 s.
pitfalls: Computing capacity from the node count without podsPerNode: 6 nodes is 660 pods, and with hundreds of service replicas the limit is reached before CPU runs out.
Splitting the design into many small clusters for isolation: each one adds a fixed 73 USD per month and its own downtime during upgrades.
Expecting an instant reaction to load: between the decision to scale and the first served request lie schedulingLagSec = 30 s plus application warm-up.
A cluster that sits entirely in one az: the zone's failureProbability = 0.0001 becomes the probability of losing all 660 pods at once.

kafka.summary: A distributed log with retention: producers write to topics, and every consumer reads at its own pace and can replay the history from scratch. Delivery is at-least-once, and strict ordering holds only inside a partition (orderingScope per-partition). Use it when a single event has to reach several independent consumers and when the ability to replay the stream matters.
kafka.capacity: The limiters are partitions and broker-network. Partitions cap parallelism: with partitions 12 a group can usefully run at most 12 consumers, and with consumersPerGroup 6 each one takes two. Bandwidth works out as brokers 3 × throughputMbsPerBroker 250 = 750 MB/s, but every message is written replicationFactor 3 times, so writes top out at roughly 250 MB/s, that is about 62500 messages/s at messageSizeKb 4; reading with four consumerGroups spends the same bandwidth on top of that.
practices: Ordering exists only inside a partition: if you need ordering per entity, set a key and choose orderingScope per-key; global means a single partition and no parallelism at all.
Keep acks all together with minInsync 2 and replicationFactor 3 — then losing one broker does not lose an acknowledged write; acks leader and none change the semantics to possible data loss.
Make the partition count a multiple of the consumer count: 12 divides evenly by 6, while 12 over 5 gives a 3-versus-2 skew and uneven consumer lag.
batchMs 10 ms with compression lz4 is the latency-versus-bandwidth compromise; raising batchMs to 50-100 ms saves network on small messages but adds exactly that much to p99.
The block has no dlq port: route failing messages to the dlq block through a separate topic, otherwise a consumer will spin forever on a poison message.
pitfalls: retentionHours 168 with diskGbPerBroker 2000 and replicationFactor 3 leaves about 2 TB of unique data, that is roughly 3.3 MB/s of sustained flow; above that Kafka deletes unread records and the consumer gets OffsetOutOfRange.
Every extra group in consumerGroups is one more full pass over the stream through the same broker network: the write volume does not grow, yet the bandwidth runs out.
Sprawl adds up: topics 20 × partitions 12 gives 240 partitions, and 720 replicas once replication is counted — that is rebalance time and broker memory, not just a number in the config.
consumer lag grows silently: without an alert on lag you notice the backlog only once retention has already eaten the data you needed.

kinesis.summary: A managed sharded record stream with retention and replay — the closest AWS analogue of kafka without running your own nodes. Ordering is guaranteed within a shard, that is per partition key, and delivery is at-least-once. Use it for telemetry, clickstreams and analytical pipelines that need a buffer you can re-read.
kinesis.capacity: Three limiters. shard-records: shards 8 × recordsPerShard 1000 = 8000 records/s. ingest-bandwidth: shards 8 × mbPerShardIn 1 = 8 MB/s, which at messageSizeKb 2 is only 4000 records/s — bandwidth becomes the wall twice as early as the record limit. broker-network covers reads: with enhancedFanout false both consumerGroups share the same 2 MB/s per shard.
practices: Compute both shard limits at once: at messageSizeKb 2 you get 4000 records/s out of 8000, at 0.5 KB you get all 8000; add shards based on whichever of the two is worse.
The partition key drives both ordering and balance: a key with few distinct values creates a hot shard that hits its own 1 MB/s while its neighbors sit idle.
Turn enhancedFanout true on from three consumers upwards: otherwise every consumerGroup shares the same 2 MB/s per shard and read latency climbs.
retentionHours 24 is your replay window; extend it ahead of time, because the data cannot be brought back retroactively.
publishLatencyMs 20 is noticeably higher than kafka's (5 ms): you do not put such a stream on the synchronous path of a user request.
pitfalls: Resharding is not free: split and merge change the key distribution and break ordering for a while, so shard headroom is planned up front.
The bill combines costPerShardHour 0.015 USD (8 shards is about 88 USD a month) and costPerMillionRequests 0.014: small frequent records are cheaper if you aggregate them before sending.
One hot shard exceeding its limit looks like the whole stream degrading, even though the total load is nowhere near 8000 records/s.

lakehouse.summary: A data lake: raw events in columnar files on object storage, plus a catalog. Cheap storage and a shared source for Trino, Spark and exports.
lakehouse.capacity: throughput and ingest-bandwidth are the limits: bandwidthGbps = 40 gives 5 GB/s against the size of the partition being scanned, maxIngestMbs = 2,000 caps writes, and concurrency = 30 caps parallel queries.
practices: parquet plus zstd leave 8.75% of the raw volume: 1,000 GB/day become 87.5 GB/day of storage.
partitionScheme hour reads 1/24 of the daily partition, day reads the whole one, and month reads thirty.
lifecycleDays 30–3650 is the only brake on a growing bill: storage grows linearly with days.
Queries are billed separately: λ per month / 10⁶ × $0.4, which makes small files expensive in operations.
pitfalls: partitionScheme none forces every query to read the entire lifecycle of the data.
A lake without a query engine returns nothing: Trino, Spark or an external table must stand next to it.
Storage without lifecycleDays grows forever: 87.5 GB/day at $0.023/GB produces a bill nobody ever revisits.

lb-l4.summary: A transport-layer load balancer: it spreads TCP and UDP connections across backends without inspecting request contents. Cheaper and faster than L7 (latencyMs=0.3 ms), but it cannot do path-based routing, retries or TLS termination. Place it in front of lb-l7, ws-gateway or any other block where connection throughput matters more than HTTP logic.
lb-l4.capacity: The limits are new-connections and throughput. newConnPerSec=100,000 new connections per second sits next to maxConnections=500,000 concurrent ones: if a connection lives longer than 5 s, the concurrency limit binds first, because 100,000 × 5 = 500,000. Throughput of throughputGbps=25 with a 45 KB response corresponds to roughly 68,000 RPS.
practices: keepAlive on the clients matters most for exactly this block: without it every request is a new connection and the ceiling drops to newConnPerSec=100,000 per second.
idleTimeoutSec=350 s keeps a connection open longer than a typical client timeout; at a high rate of new connections it is this retention that consumes maxConnections=500,000.
algorithm=round-robin ignores backend load; least-conn or random-2-choices is better when processing time is uneven.
stickiness=none suits stateless backends; source-ip is only needed where state is pinned to an instance, and it is also what breaks even distribution.
healthCheck=true with healthCheckIntervalSec=10 s is the bare minimum of protection: an L4 check only sees a live port, not a working application.
pitfalls: Expecting L7 features from L4: URL-based routing, retries (there simply is no retryPolicy parameter here), TLS termination and compression; those need an lb-l7 behind it.
Sizing capacity in RPS when the block's limits are connections and gigabits: with keep-alive one RPS is not one connection, and the other way round.
instances=2 across azSpread=2 means one instance per zone, so losing a zone leaves half the capacity on both newConnPerSec and throughputGbps.
Backend health is judged by the TCP port, so an instance that is alive but returning errors keeps receiving traffic.

lb-l7.summary: An application-layer load balancer and reverse proxy: it terminates TLS, routes by HTTP, performs retries and holds keep-alive connections to the backends. This is the main regional entry point for HTTP traffic. Place it behind glb, cdn or waf and in front of the services or api-gateway.
lb-l7.capacity: The limits are proxy-rps, cpu and network. The nominal proxy-rps ceiling is instances=3 × maxRpsPerInstance=25,000 RPS = 75,000 RPS, but with tlsTerminate=true and keepAlive off, CPU binds sooner: tlsHandshakeMs=1.2 ms on cpuCores=4 yields about 3,300 handshakes per second per instance, that is roughly 10,000 RPS for the block, 7.5 times less. The network limit depends on response size: 45 KB at 75,000 RPS is already about 27 Gbps.
practices: Leave keepAlive=true and http2=true enabled: they amortise tlsHandshakeMs=1.2 ms across many requests on one connection and take the bulk of the load off the CPU.
retryPolicy=idempotent-only is the right default: none gives up on recoverable failures, while exponential-backoff on all methods produces duplicate POSTs and amplifies storms.
timeoutMs=30000 ms must be greater than timeoutMs=29000 ms on the downstream api-gateway so that the gateway, not the proxy, returns the error; the client timeout in turn must be larger still.
connectionDrainSec=30 s is what makes a rollout possible without cutting connections, so releasing a single backend must take longer than that.
compression=true saves bandwidth but costs CPU: when the cpu limit binds, turning compression off buys more RPS at the price of traffic.
pitfalls: Declaring maxRpsPerInstance=25,000 RPS (realistic range 5,000-60,000) without checking whether cpuCores=4 is enough given the chosen tlsHandshakeMs and the amount of compression.
Setting timeoutMs=30000 ms and retryPolicy=exponential-backoff at the same time: a hung backend holds connections for 30 s each while retries pile new ones on top.
Forgetting that latencyMs=1 ms is added to every request and doubles if lb-l7 sits both at the entrance and internally in front of the services.
availability=0.9999 is about 53 minutes per year, and that figure multiplies with the availability of every block placed in series along the chain.

link-cross-az.summary: A link between availability zones of one region: it describes the leg that carries calls and replication between blocks in different az. Placed wherever the design crosses a zone boundary, it turns a free internal call into a billed and slower one. This is the main instrument for trading latency against fault tolerance.
link-cross-az.capacity: hasModel = false: the link serves no requests and has no bounds of its own. What it contributes to the calculation is latencyMs = 1 ms per crossing, a ceiling of bandwidthGbps = 25 Gbps on volume, and costPerGb = 0.01 USD for every gigabyte that passes through.
practices: Count crossings, not blocks: a chatty service that makes 20 calls to a database in the neighbouring zone adds exactly 20 ms to p99, and that is visible in probe-waterfall with showNetwork = true.
A single leg at 1 Gbps is 324000 GB per month and 3240 USD at costPerGb = 0.01, so treat cross-zone database replication as its own line in the estimate.
latencyMs = 1 ms is the default for a typical region; the 0.1 to 20 ms range covers both dense zones and widely separated sites, and the value is worth refining before you break down p99.
Send asynchronous work over this leg: replication, backups, exchange between clusters, but not the synchronous chain of a user request.
pitfalls: Replication with a factor of 3 across zones triples the bytes written on the wire, and every gigabyte is billed, not just the useful payload.
Counting traffic in one direction only: the return flow is usually billed as well, and the estimate comes out half of what it should be.
bandwidthGbps = 25 Gbps feels infinite right up until somebody routes a cold data migration or a full backup over this leg.

link-cross-region.summary: A link between regions: the leg for geo-replication, failover and global writes. This block is what turns a pretty two-region picture into a set of latency and cost trade-offs. Placed together with multi-region-policy; on its own it makes almost no sense.
link-cross-region.capacity: hasModel = false: the link has no bounds and serves no requests. What it contributes to the calculation is latencyMs = 80 ms one way, that is at least 160 ms for a synchronous round trip, bandwidthGbps = 10 Gbps of capacity and costPerGb = 0.02 USD per gigabyte.
practices: Any synchronous write across a region costs at least 160 ms: that is already more than half of the typical targetP99Ms = 300 ms budget on probe-slo, leaving under 140 ms for the rest of the path.
Keep encryption = true always: the traffic travels over somebody else's infrastructure, and the saving on encryption in the model does not offset the risk.
dedicatedLink = false means public transit with floating latency; a dedicated channel is what you buy when predictable jitter matters more than average latency.
Reconcile bandwidthGbps = 10 Gbps with the replication stream: 10 Gbps is 1.25 GB/s, and if the write volume exceeds that, lag grows without bound.
1 Gbps of steady replication is 324000 GB and 6480 USD per month at costPerGb = 0.02: cross-region traffic is usually the second largest line item after NAT.
pitfalls: A synchronous quorum across regions for the sake of consistency: latencyMs = 80 ms per leg makes write p99 three digits regardless of code quality.
Counting on rpoTargetSec = 60 s from multi-region-policy without checking bandwidth: if the write stream does not fit into 10 Gbps, the declared RPO is unreachable.
Treating latencyMs = 80 ms as a universal default: the range is 5 to 400 ms, and a pair of regions on different continents sits closer to the upper bound.
Saving on encryption and on a dedicated channel while dataResidency = strict: residency requirements usually arrive together with requirements on protecting the channel.

local-cache.summary: A cache inside the process memory (Caffeine, LRU): a fraction of a millisecond per hit and no network hop. The first tier in front of the shared cache and the database.
local-cache.capacity: The only limit is memory: instances × min(sizeMb, maxEntries × entryBytes) against the write stream over the TTL. On defaults maxEntries sets the limit: 100,000 × 616 B = 61.6 MB out of the 256 MB allocated.
practices: sizeMb and maxEntries apply together and the smaller of the two wins: check which one actually constrains you.
TTL must be longer than the interval between repeat accesses: 60 s on defaults drops the hit ratio from 0.84 to 0.26.
Keep stampedeProtection enabled: without it a miss on a hot key sends every concurrent request to the database.
Cache only what tolerates divergence between instances here: coherenceRisk = 0.2.
pitfalls: The cache lives in every instance: a deploy or a scale-out leaves all copies cold at the same time.
There is no event-based invalidation — data refreshes only on TTL, and different pods answer differently.
A local cache on top of Redis doubles the divergence window: the two TTLs add up.

logs.summary: A log store with ingest, compression and indexing: it collects lines from every service and makes them searchable during incident investigation. Placed as a telemetry sink for services, gateways and brokers when metrics are no longer enough and you need the context of one specific request. On the diagram it is a terminal node: it has only the ingest:serve:telemetry inbound port and no outgoing ports.
logs.capacity: Two bounds apply: ingest-bandwidth caps the stream at maxIngestMbs = 500 MB/s measured after samplingRate = 1 is applied, and indexing, which gets more expensive with indexMode (labels-only versus full-text) and indexedFields = 12. At the same time queryConcurrency = 10 limits how many searches run in parallel: the eleventh query waits in the queue.
practices: Budget by ingest, not by storage: 1 MB/s of logs is 2592 GB per month, that is 1296 USD at costPerGbIngest = 0.5 USD per GB, while the same data at compressionRatio = 8, retentionDays = 30 and replicationFactor = 2 occupies 648 GB and costs 19 USD at costPerGbMonth = 0.03 USD.
samplingRate is the main lever: the default value of 1 means you pay for every line, while 0.1 cuts both ingest and storage tenfold.
Keep indexMode at labels-only until full-text is proven necessary: a full-text index inflates both volume and ingest cost, while search across the 12 indexedFields covers most investigations.
hotRetentionDays = 7 against retentionDays = 30 means a query for the third week falls through to the cold tier and will be noticeably slower; plan incident investigation inside the hot window.
ingestLagSec = 15 s sets how long it takes a line to become searchable: never build a reaction on logs when it needs second-level freshness.
pitfalls: Cutting retentionDays to save money at costPerGbIngest = 0.5 and costPerGbMonth = 0.03: on those defaults ingest is roughly 67 times more expensive than a month of storage, so cut samplingRate instead.
flowLogsEnabled turned on for a VPC, or debug level in the services, silently doubles the stream and pushes it against maxIngestMbs = 500 MB/s.
availability = 0.999 is about 43 minutes of downtime per month: if incident investigation depends entirely on logs, you have no backup channel exactly when you need one.
replicationFactor = 2 doubles the stored volume: 30 days of logs on the defaults take twice as much space as a naive calculation shows.

meilisearch.summary: A compact search engine for catalogs and reference data: prefix and typo-tolerant search without tuning analyzers. Chosen over Elasticsearch when the corpus is measured in tens of millions of documents.
meilisearch.capacity: memory is the limit: capacity is multiplied by the share of the index that fits into indexRamGb. On defaults the index is 164 GB against 32 GB of RAM, 20% resident — memory caps throughput noticeably earlier than cpu.
practices: Size the index as docCount × docSizeKb × indexExpansionRatio (realistically 1.2–2.5) and give indexRamGb at least that much.
typoTolerance multiplies query time by 1.4 — turn it off where people search by SKU or code.
A realistic footprint is 1–8 nodes and tens of millions of documents; beyond those bounds reach for Elasticsearch.
Indexing is capped at 30 MB/s per node: plan a bulk catalog load as a separate window.
pitfalls: Availability defaults to 0.99 — roughly 7 hours of downtime per month; do not put it on the critical path without a fallback.
Adding nodes multiplies capacity but does not make the index resident: RAM first, nodes second.

memcached.summary: A simple distributed in-memory key-value cache: reads and writes only, with no data structures, replication or persistence. The cheapest layer for taking reads off the database.
memcached.capacity: memory is the limit: the write stream over the TTL window has to fit into nodes × memoryGb × 0.9. Next come ops (nodes × maxOpsPerSec) and cpu = nodes × threads / S, that is 80,000 rps with 4 threads.
practices: A value larger than slabSizeKb (1 MB by default) gets truncated: keep valueSizeBytes inside the slab page.
threads is realistically 4–16: with 3 nodes and 4 threads the cpu ceiling is 80,000 rps, not the advertised 450,000.
Compare ttlSec = 600 with the interval between repeat accesses: a TTL shorter than that wastes the memory you paid for.
Uniform value sizes keep slab efficiency near 1.0, while a mix of sizes drags it down.
pitfalls: Memcached does not replicate: losing a node hands its share of keys to the database and buries it in load.
Swapping it in for Redis without revisiting the design: there are no counters, no lists and no persistence here.
hotKeyShare = 0.05 with 150,000 ops per node gives a ceiling of 3 million rps — the hot key binds before the cluster does.

metrics.summary: A time-series store: it accepts numeric samples on the scrape schedule and serves them to charts and alerting rules. This is the baseline observability layer, usually deployed first because it is orders of magnitude cheaper than logs and traces for the same coverage. It has a single port, ingest:serve:telemetry, and no outgoing links.
metrics.capacity: Two bounds apply: sample-ingest is computed as activeSeries / scrapeIntervalSec, that is 2000000 / 15 s = 133333 samples per second, and memory, equal to activeSeries × memoryPerMillionSeriesGb = 2 million × 4 GB per million = 8 GB, multiplied by replicationFactor = 2, for 16 GB in total. Capacity here is driven by series cardinality, not by application RPS.
practices: Cardinality matters more than frequency: growth in activeSeries hits both memory and costPerThousandSeries = 0.9 USD, while raising scrapeIntervalSec from 15 s to 60 s cuts the sample stream fourfold and saves not a single byte of memory.
Keep activeSeries within the realistic range of 100 thousand to 20 million; the default 2 million series cost 1800 USD per month at costPerThousandSeries.
cardinalityAlarm = 5000000 gives 2.5x headroom over the default 2 million series: it is your early warning of a label explosion, not a technical limit.
downsampleAfterDays = 30 with retentionDays = 400 means full resolution only for the first month: on the defaults that is 19.6 GB per day and about 588 GB for the month before downsampling.
Treat labelsPerSeries = 8 as a budget: every new label is a multiplier, not an addend.
pitfalls: A high-cardinality label such as userId or requestId: a single label with 50 values turns 2 million series into 100 million, memory from 8 GB into 400 GB, and the bill from 1800 USD into 90000 USD per month.
Trying to keep in metrics what belongs in logs: bytesPerSample = 1.7 bytes only works for numbers, text does not fit into labels.
replicationFactor = 2 doubles both memory and storage but does not raise queryConcurrency = 20 queries.
retentionDays = 400 without downsampling: keeping a year of history at full resolution costs more than the value it brings.

minio.summary: S3-compatible object storage on your own hardware: the same API, but nodes, disks and erasure coding are under your control. People take it to keep data inside the perimeter, to avoid egress charges and for firstByteLatencyMs 8 against 30 for s3. Use it wherever you would use s3 — files, artifacts and cold data — but in your own infrastructure.
minio.capacity: The limiters are node-ops and throughput. Operations: nodes 8 × maxOpsPerSecPerNode 5000 = 40000 ops/s. Bandwidth: throughputGbps 25, that is about 3100 MB/s, which at avgObjectSizeMb 4 gives 780 objects/s — bandwidth becomes the wall long before 40000 ops/s. Capacity: nodes 8 × disksPerNode 8 × diskSizeTb 8 = 512 TB raw, and with storageOverhead 1.5 (exactly what erasureCoding ec-8-4 costs) about 341 TB remains, which lines up with usableTb 300.
practices: erasureCoding ec-8-4 survives the loss of 4 disks out of 12 at the price of a 1.5 multiplier on capacity; ec-4-2 has lower overhead but less resilience.
The operational minimum is 4 nodes, realistically 4-32: below that erasure coding degenerates and a node failure means the data becomes unavailable.
Compute capacity as nodes × disksPerNode × diskSizeTb / storageOverhead and keep headroom: filling above 80 percent breaks rebalancing when you expand.
You expand MinIO with new node pools, not with individual disks: a disk cannot be added to an existing erasure set.
availability 0.999 against 0.9999 for s3 is an order of magnitude more downtime, and availability, replication and backups are your responsibility rather than a provider's.
pitfalls: costPerTbMonth 12 USD at usableTb 300 is 3600 USD a month for capacity alone, excluding people, network and facilities; comparing it with s3 on storage price alone is misleading.
objectCount 20000000 at avgObjectSizeMb 4 is 80 TB; as the average size grows, that very same object count quickly overruns usableTb 300.
Erasure coding protects against disk failures, but not against an accidental delete or the loss of a site: you still need a separate backup.

ml-inference.summary: A GPU model inference service: instances 2 × gpuCount 4 cards of gpuType a10g return predictions in inferenceMs 30 ms in batches of batchSize 8. It sits behind an API or a queue wherever ML logic is needed — recommendations, scoring, embeddings, generation. It is the most expensive compute block in a design: costPerInstanceHour $4.2.
ml-inference.capacity: The limiters are gpu, concurrency and memory. gpu = 2 × 4 = 8 cards × throughputPerGpu 200 = 1600 inferences/s, and that is the real ceiling. concurrency computed from batches gives more: batchSize 8 in inferenceMs 30 ms = 267 requests/s per card, i.e. 2133/s. memory: modelSizeGb 6 against gpuMemoryGb 24 leaves 18 GB for batches and cache.
practices: batchSize 8 is a compromise: a larger batch raises throughputPerGpu but adds batch-accumulation waiting to p99, and timeoutMs 2000 ms does not cover that waiting indefinitely.
quantized false: turning quantization on usually shrinks modelSizeGb 6 by a factor of 2-4 and raises throughputPerGpu at the cost of accuracy — it is the first lever to pull before buying cards.
warmupSec 60 s means a new instance is useless for its first minute: load-based autoscaling cannot keep up, so keep gpuCount headroom in place ahead of time.
Put a queue in front of the block for batch jobs and a cache for repeated inputs: at $4.2/hour per instance a cache pays for itself at any noticeable share of repeats.
Choose gpuType to fit the model: t4 and l4 are cheaper, but with modelSizeGb 6 and large batches they hit gpuMemoryGb before they hit compute.
pitfalls: Sizing by concurrency instead of gpu: the batch formula promises 2133/s while throughputPerGpu caps you at 1600/s — the 33% difference turns into queueing and rising p99.
A model that does not fit into gpuMemoryGb 24: paging weights between calls destroys throughput, and the symptom is inferenceMs several times higher at low card utilization.
2 × 4.2 = $8.4/hour ≈ $6100/month runs continuously: at 1600 inferences/s that is $1.46 per million, but at 10 requests/s it is already $233 per million.
availability 0.995 (3.6 h a month) on a synchronous path: without degrading to a heuristic or to a cache, the model going down becomes the product going down.

mongodb.summary: A document database: replicaSetSize = 3, shardCount = 1, and the schema lives inside the documents themselves at documentSizeKb = 4. writeConcern = majority together with readPreference = primary gives consistencyModel = read-your-writes out of the box. It is chosen at the mvp stage when the shape of the data changes quickly and joins are not needed.
mongodb.capacity: The limits are cpu, connections and iops. cpu yields cpuCores = 16 / readServiceMs = 0.5 ms = 32,000 reads/s and 16 / writeServiceMs = 1.5 ms ≈ 10,700 writes/s, while connections stop at maxConnections = 1000. iops is driven by cache misses: wiredTigerCacheGb = 32 GB against workingSetGb = 40 GB, so every fifth read goes to disk.
practices: Raise wiredTigerCacheGb = 32 GB up to workingSetGb = 40 GB: the missing 8 GB turn into 20% of reads hitting disk and into a higher p99.

writeConcern = majority at quorumW = 2 out of quorumN = 3 waits for one secondary to acknowledge, and that is the cost of a write and it is justified; w1 is faster but loses commits during a primary election.
readPreference = primary keeps read-your-writes honest: switching to a secondary at replicaLagMs = 100 ms breaks the guarantee, because quorumR = 1 and 1 + 2 is not greater than quorumN = 3.
indexCount = 5 at documentCount = 500 million: every index is an extra write per insert and one more chunk of the working set in cache.
shardKey = userId is chosen before the collection grows to 2 TB: changing the shard key means reloading the data.
pitfalls: The 16 MB document limit invites ever-growing arrays inside a document, which is O(n) on every update and a working set that keeps spreading.
concurrencyControl = optimistic with conflictResolution = single-writer-per-key: a concurrent update of the same document without findAndModify silently loses one of the versions.
shardCount = 1 means every write goes to one primary: 10,700 writes/s is the ceiling, and replicas do not move it.
documentCount = 500 million × 4 KB is 2 TB out of storageGb = 3000, and the headroom disappears as soon as 5 indexes, the oplog and fragmentation are added on top.

monolith.summary: A single application in which moduleCount 12 modules live inside one process and share a pool of sharedDbConnections 50 to a common database. Use it as the starting point of a design, or as the legacy core from which services are gradually carved out. It gives you easy in-process consistency at the price of a shared blast radius and startupSec 90 s on every restart.
monolith.capacity: The limiters are workers, cpu and db-pool. workers = instances 4 × concurrencyPerInstance 200 ÷ serviceTimeMs 45 ms ≈ 17,800 RPS, cpu = 4 × cpuCores 8 ÷ (0.045 s × cpuShare 0.25) ≈ 2840 RPS. db-pool runs into sharedDbConnections 50: if a connection is held for the full 45 ms, that is about 1100 RPS per pool.
practices: Reconcile sharedDbConnections 50 with the connection limit of the database itself: four instances at 50 each means 200 sessions, and the database has to survive them.
startupSec 90 s is the price of every step of a rolling deploy: with instances 4 a full cycle takes 6 minutes, which is exactly why there are no autoscale parameters here.
azSpread 2 means losing a zone removes half the capacity — plan for 2× headroom or raise azSpread to 3.
serviceTimeSigma 0.9 produces a heavy tail: p99 will be several times the 45 ms mean, so keep timeoutMs 3000 ms above the p99 of every internal call.
Point the out port at a single database — that is the whole meaning of a monolith; extracting a module starts with taking its traffic out of the shared db-pool.
pitfalls: queueLimit 500 against a capacity of about 2800 RPS is only 180 ms of buffer — a spike longer than a second is simply dropped.
moduleCount 12 in one process: a memory leak or an infinite loop in one module takes down all twelve, hence availability 0.995 = 3.6 hours of downtime a month.

logLinesPerRequest 8 × logBytesPerLine 500 bytes = 4 KB per request: at 2800 RPS that is 11.2 MB/s ≈ 970 GB per day, and the log bill overtakes the 4 × 0.68 = $2.72/hour you pay for the instances themselves.
Adding instances does not cure a db-pool bottleneck: each new instance brings its own 50 connections and finishes off the database instead of raising RPS.

multi-region-policy.summary: A policy block describing how the design operates across several regions: where writes go, how data replicates, how conflicts are resolved and how failover happens. It serves nothing itself but changes the meaning of almost every other block. Placed once per diagram, next to region and link-cross-region.
multi-region-policy.capacity: hasModel = false: the policy has neither ports nor bounds and does not enter the capacity calculation. Instead it decides whether the link-cross-region leg lands on the hot write path, and it declares two commitments: rpoTargetSec = 60 s as the acceptable data loss in a disaster and rtoTargetSec = 900 s as the acceptable recovery time.
practices: mode = single by default means there is no second region in the calculation: until you change the mode, the standby region you drew affects nothing.
read-local-write-global gives fast reads and expensive writes: every write travels to writeRegion and pays at least 160 ms per round trip over link-cross-region.
conflictResolution = lww is safe only with replicationDirection = one-way or with a single writer; for two-way replication use single-writer-per-key or crdt.
rtoTargetSec = 900 s with failoverMode = manual means a human has to react within 15 minutes; check that against the detection delay on alerting, which already eats up to 330 s.
dataResidency = strict is incompatible with active-active over one data set: under strict residency the realistic option is sharded-by-geo, where a region's data never leaves the region.
pitfalls: A single failover with rtoTargetSec = 900 s burns roughly 3.5 times the monthly SLO budget at the 0.9999 level: 900 s against the 259 s allowed per month.
active-active with conflictResolution = lww: concurrent writes to the same key are lost silently, with no errors and no trace in the logs.
An empty writeRegion under active-passive and read-local-write-global modes: the policy is only half described, and the model does not know where to route writes.
failbackPolicy = auto without a consistency check: automatically returning to the primary region after a disaster can overwrite the data accumulated in the standby one.

mysql.summary: A relational database on InnoDB: a primary plus readReplicas = 2, with replicationMode = semi-sync by default, so a commit waits for acknowledgement from at least one replica. Compared to postgres it has cheaper writes (writeServiceMs = 2 ms, iopsPerWrite = 3) and isolationLevel = repeatable-read by default. It is chosen as the main OLTP store at the mvp stage when the team already lives in the MySQL ecosystem.
mysql.capacity: The limits are cpu, connections and iops. cpu yields cpuCores = 8 / readServiceMs = 0.6 ms ≈ 13,300 reads/s and 8 / writeServiceMs = 2 ms = 4,000 writes/s; iops at provisionedIops = 12,000 and iopsPerWrite = 3 gives exactly the same 4,000 writes/s, so both ceilings meet at the same point. connections are maxConnections = 500 with connectionsPerQuery = 1.
practices: bufferPoolGb = 24 GB equals workingSetGb = 24 GB, so the working set fits entirely in memory; as the data grows move both values together, otherwise reads fall through to disk.
replicationMode = semi-sync pays one network round-trip per commit, but it saves you from losing transactions during failoverSec = 60 s; async speeds writes up and opens a data-loss window.
maxConnections = 500 with connectionPooler = none means every connection is a thread; put pgbouncer-transaction or ProxySQL in front of the database.
readFromReplica = 0.4 with replicaLagMs = 500 ms: 40% of the reads see data half a second stale, so keep reports and listings there, but not the check of a just-created row.
The cdc output into Kafka reads the binlog, so enable the row-based format, otherwise consumers cannot reconstruct changes row by row.
pitfalls: consistencyModel = linearizable together with readFromReplica = 0.4 and stickyReadShare = 0 does not hold: 40% of the reads come from replicas that lag 500 ms.
isolationLevel = repeatable-read in InnoDB does not protect against write skew the way serializable does; invariants such as a booking limit need SELECT FOR UPDATE.
shardCount = 1 at rowCount = 300 million: 300 million × 300 bytes × 1.35 = 121 GB, so space is fine, but an ALTER TABLE on a table that size blocks writes for hours.
iopsPerWrite = 3 accounts for the doublewrite buffer and the redo log; counting only logical rows underestimates disk by a factor of three.

nat-egress.summary: An egress gateway: it translates private network addresses to the outside when services call external APIs. A managed block whose capacity is determined by the number of public addresses and ports, not by requests. Place it at the exit of the private segment, between the services and their external dependencies.
nat-egress.capacity: The limits are ports and throughput. The port limit works out like this: publicIps=1 × portsPerIp=64,000 with portHoldSec=30 s gives about 2,130 new connections per second, and at connectionsPerRequest=0.2 that is roughly 10,700 outbound requests per second for the whole block. The second limit, throughputGbps=45 across gateways=2, usually does not bind given that port ceiling.
practices: publicIps=1 is the most common bottleneck: every address you add raises the limit linearly, and four addresses already give about 42,700 outbound requests per second.

connectionsPerRequest=0.2 reflects connection reuse (one connection per five requests); without keep-alive to the external APIs the value drifts towards 1 and the limit drops fivefold, to 2,130 requests per second.
portHoldSec=30 s is how long a port is held after close; shortening it raises the achievable rate of new connections proportionally but increases the risk of collisions.
Keep gateways=2 matched to the number of zones: a NAT gateway is zonal, and losing a zone cuts off outbound traffic for that zone's services entirely.
Route heavy external transfers (exports, backups) around this block so you neither burn ports nor pay costPerGb=0.045 USD for every gigabyte.
pitfalls: Sizing capacity in gigabits and missing the port limit: throughputGbps=45 looks enormous next to the 10,700 requests per second the ports allow.
Not reusing connections to external APIs, so connectionsPerRequest effectively becomes 1 and the block immediately runs into 2,130 connections per second.
costPerGb=0.045 USD for outbound traffic is left out of the estimate: 1 TB through NAT costs about 46 USD, plus costPerGatewayHour=0.045 USD for each of the two gateways.
idleTimeoutSec=350 s holds idle connections along with their ports, so when a large share of external calls is short-lived the ports run out sooner than the calculation suggests.

nats.summary: A lightweight messaging bus with subject-based routing; in JetStream mode it adds persistent streams with acknowledgements. Core NATS is fire-and-forget with at-most-once, while JetStream gives at-least-once and redelivery driven by acks. Use it where internal communication needs minimal latency: publishLatencyMs 0.5 against 5 ms for kafka and 20 ms for kinesis.
nats.capacity: The limiters are throughput and inflight. The operations ceiling is nodes 3 × maxOpsPerSecPerNode 150000 = 450000 ops/s. inflight works in parallel: maxAckPending 2000 unacknowledged messages per consumer at processingTimeMs 5 ms gives 2000 / 0.005 = 400000 messages/s, but with 50 ms of processing the same limit cuts the rate to 40000/s.
practices: Choose streamRetention by the job: limits is a log bounded by time and size, interest deletes once every subscriber has read the message, and workqueue is a queue where a message disappears after the first ack.
Raise maxAckPending in proportion to processingTimeMs: with slow processing the default 2000 becomes the wall long before 450000 ops/s.
retentionHours 24 is a short window: NATS does not replace kafka for long history, and for a week of replay take kafka or pulsar.
messageSizeKb 1 is the target profile: the NATS latency advantage shows up on small frequent messages, and large payloads eat it away.
nodes 3 is the minimum for a JetStream quorum (realistically 3-9); on a single node persistence does not survive a restart.
pitfalls: Without JetStream delivery is at-most-once: a subscriber that goes offline never receives the message and never learns that it missed one.
subjects 200 with wildcard subscriptions easily turn into hidden fanout: a single broad subscription doubles the load on the cluster.
availability 0.999 is about 8.8 hours of downtime a year; on a critical path you need a fallback route or a buffer on the sender side.

neo4j.summary: A graph database: nodeCount = 100 million vertices and edgeCount = 500 million edges, an average degree of 5. It walks pointers between records instead of joining, so queryComplexity = neighbourhood at traversalDepth = 3 is cheap here and expensive in SQL. It is placed at v1 under recommendations, relationship graphs and hierarchy-based access checks.
neo4j.capacity: The limits are cpu, iops and memory. The cost of a query grows as a power of the depth: at an average degree of 5 and traversalDepth = 3 a single traversal touches on the order of 125 vertices, and that is a multiplier on readServiceMs = 0.5 ms across nodes = 3 × cpuCores = 16 cores. iops is the bigger danger: a traversal is random reads, and if the graph does not fit into cacheGb = 32, provisionedIops = 30,000 at 125 hops per query yields only about 240 queries/s.
practices: Size cacheGb = 32 and heapGb = 16 so that the hot part of the graph stays in memory: a miss during a traversal is a random read, the worst case for a disk.
traversalDepth = 3 already touches 125 vertices, and depth 4 gives 625, a fivefold cost increase per extra step, so bound the depth inside the query itself.
queryComplexity = neighbourhood is cheaper than variable-length and shortest-path; move heavy traversals into offline jobs rather than synchronous queries.
readReplicas = 2 with readFromReplica = 0.5 take half the reads away, but writes stay on a single leader at writeServiceMs = 2 ms.

The graph is not the primary store: keep the facts in SQL or a document database and deliver relationships here via cdc, so the block's availability = 0.999 does not become the availability of the product.
pitfalls: consistencyModel = read-your-writes does not hold at readFromReplica = 0.5 with stickyReadShare = 0: half the reads go to replicas lagging replicaLagMs = 100 ms.
A supernode with a million edges breaks the model: a traversal through it expands a million relationships and stalls on concurrencyControl = pessimistic locking it.
A traversal without a depth bound in the query effectively becomes a full scan of the graph: latency grows by orders of magnitude and indexes do not help.
availability = 0.999 is about 8.8 hours of downtime per year, the lowest value among the stores together with redis-store, so do not build a critical path on the graph.

nfs.summary: A network file system with POSIX semantics, mounted by several nodes at once: a shared directory with familiar paths and permissions. You need it where the application can only work with files and requires shared write access. There is no out port — the block emits no events, it only serves mounts.
nfs.capacity: The limiters are iops and throughput. IOPS: provisionedIops 35000 is consumed with the weights iopsPerRead 1 and iopsPerWrite 2, so on a 50-50 mix you get 35000 / 1.5 ≈ 23300 operations/s. Bandwidth: throughputMbs 300 as the baseline, on top of which burstCredits 2100000 operate — a reserve for peaks that refills slowly and runs out under sustained load.
practices: NFS is taken only for POSIX semantics and shared write access: if an object API is enough for the application, s3 or minio is cheaper and scales better.
Account for iopsPerWrite 2: a write costs twice as much as a read, so a write-heavy profile exhausts provisionedIops twice as fast as a naive calculation suggests.
latencyMs 2.5 against 0.2 ms for block: databases and any latency-sensitive files are not moved onto a network share.
Small files are the worst profile: every operation is charged at iopsPerRead while the bandwidth sits idle, and you hit the IOPS wall at 10 percent channel utilization.
storageGb 20000 at costPerGbMonth 0.3 USD is 6000 USD a month: keep on the share only what genuinely needs file access.
pitfalls: Running out of burstCredits looks like sudden degradation: throughput drops to the baseline 300 MB/s in the middle of a load, even though nothing changed in the application.
Network file locks do not behave like local ones: several nodes writing to the same file produce corrupted data rather than a clear error.
A shared mount is a shared point of failure: availability 0.9999 is about 53 minutes a year, but for that time every mounted node goes down at once.

notification.summary: A notification bus: one event fans out to fanoutPerEvent 20 recipients across channels 2 channels, i.e. 40 messages, and goes to an external provider with a delaySec 5 s delay. It sits between the domain services and the push/SMS providers so that fanout and retries do not live in business logic. The only outputs are http/grpc/internal.
notification.capacity: The limiters are rate-limit, workers and inflight. rate-limit = providerLimitRps 12,000 messages/s, which at 40 messages per event is only 300 events/s. workers = instances 3 × concurrency 200 = 600 slots ÷ serviceTimeMs 20 ms = 30,000 messages/s, so the hardware has three times more room than the provider; inflight = maxInflight 100,000, which is 8.3 s of buffer at 12,000/s.
practices: Count the load in messages, not in events: fanoutPerEvent 20 × channels 2 = 40, so 300 events/s already hits providerLimitRps 12,000.
delaySec 5 s is a legitimate trade-off: a notification does not have to be synchronous, and that delay lets you smooth out peaks through maxInflight 100,000.
retryPolicy once at errorRate 0.02 adds only 2% to the load; exponential-backoff is gentler on the provider but requires deduplication on the receiving side.
Put the block behind a queue instead of calling it synchronously from a service: a fanout of 40 inside an HTTP request means 40 external calls on the critical path.
Separate channels by priority: transactional push and marketing campaigns should not share one providerLimitRps 12,000.
pitfalls: costPerMessage $0.0002 across the fanout: 100 events/s is 4000 messages/s and $0.8/s, i.e. about $2880/hour, against which the 3 × 0.15 = $0.45/hour for instances is simply invisible.
fanoutPerEvent growing with the audience: an event on a popular object turns into thousands of messages and instantly eats up the provider's limit.
maxInflight 100,000 without backpressure: if the provider responds slower than 12,000/s the buffer is gone in 8 seconds and losses start after that.
No deduplication on retries: the user receives the same notification twice, and that is more noticeable than any outage.

outbox.summary: An implementation of the transactional outbox pattern: the service writes the event into a table in the same transaction as the business data, and a separate publisher reads the rows and sends them to a broker. It removes the dual-write problem — either both the data and the event are stored, or neither is. Use it between a database block (the in port is sql/internal) and kafka, amqp or sqs, when state and events must never diverge.
outbox.capacity: The limiters are poll-batch and depth. The publish rate is instances 2 × batchSize 200 per pollIntervalMs 100 ms, that is 2000 rows/s per instance and 4000 rows/s in total. depth is backlogRows 50000: that reserve is drained in 12.5 s at full speed, and with a larger inflow the backlog grows and the target publishLagMs 500 stops holding.
practices: Tune pollIntervalMs and batchSize as a pair: a batch above 1000 rows makes read transactions long, and an interval above 1 s breaks publishLagMs 500 ms.
Publishing here is fundamentally at-least-once: a row is marked published only after the broker acknowledges it, so the consumer must be idempotent on the event identifier.
Maintain ordering per aggregate: publish with the partitioning key set to the entity identifier, otherwise instances 2 will send two events for the same entity out of order.
An index on the unpublished flag and the timestamp is mandatory: without it every poll cycle turns into a full table scan.
Route the output into a single broker: two independent publishers reading the same table produce duplicates that cannot be told apart from retries.
pitfalls: Several instances without row locking (SKIP LOCKED or a lease) publish the same row twice — the classic bug that shows up exactly at instances 2.
retentionHours 24 at 4000 rows/s means up to 345 million rows in the table per day; without cleanup the indexes bloat and the source database itself degrades.
A publisher crash creates no divergence, but the lag grows silently: alert on the age of the oldest unpublished row, not on how many of them there are.

payment-external.summary: An external payment provider: a managed block with p50Ms 200 ms, p99Ms 3000 ms, a rateLimitRps 300 limit and mandatory idempotency. Put it in the design to make it explicit that money leaves for the outside, where someone else's timeouts, limits and SLOs apply. It has no out ports — nothing of yours lives beyond it.
payment-external.capacity: The limiters are rate-limit and concurrency. rate-limit = rateLimitRps 300 transactions/s. concurrency = maxConcurrency 200 simultaneous calls: at p50Ms 200 ms that is 1000 transactions/s, but in the tail at p99Ms 3000 ms it is only 67/s, four times below the provider's limit.
practices: timeoutMs 10,000 ms is set above p99Ms 3000 ms, which is the right order: a timeout below p99 would turn slow but successful payments into false failures.
idempotencyRequired true is not negotiable: an idempotency key per transaction is the only thing that separates a retry from a second charge.
webhookCallback true means the final status arrives asynchronously: do not hold the user's request until the end, show 'processing' and finish on the callback.
Put a queue and a rate limiter in front of the block: rateLimitRps 300 is somebody else's limit, and exceeding it produces failures, not graceful degradation.
Do the money math: costPerTransaction $0.029 at 100 transactions/s is $2.9/s ≈ $10,400/hour, next to which no infrastructure saving is worth anything.
pitfalls: Sizing concurrency by p50Ms 200 ms: when the provider degrades to p99Ms 3000 ms the same 200 slots yield 67 transactions/s and the payment backlog snowballs.
A retry without an idempotency key after a timeout is a double charge, the most expensive class of bug in the whole design.
errorRate 0.01 and availability 0.999 add up: roughly one attempt in a hundred has to be repeated, and retry logic must be part of the design rather than a patch.
A callback with no signature check and no duplicate handling: the provider sends the webhook several times, and naive handling flips the order status back and forth.

postgres.summary: A classic relational database with a single primary for writes and readReplicas = 2 asynchronous read replicas. It gives you transactions, joins and secondary indexes, which makes it the default first schema store at the mvp stage. Pick it where you need strict transactions over related entities rather than peak RPS.
postgres.capacity: The limits are cpu, connections and iops. cpu yields cpuCores = 8 / readServiceMs = 0.8 ms ≈ 10,000 reads/s or 8 / writeServiceMs = 2.5 ms = 3,200 writes/s, but iops caps writes earlier: provisionedIops = 12,000 at iopsPerWrite = 4 is 3,000 writes/s. connections bound concurrency: maxConnections = 200 with connectionsPerQuery = 1 and connectionPooler = none means two hundred concurrent queries, and everything beyond that queues.
practices: connectionPooler = none with maxConnections = 200 will not survive a hundred service instances: put pgbouncer-transaction in front, it holds thousands of client connections on the same 200 server-side ones.

bufferPoolGb = 8 GB is smaller than workingSetGb = 20 GB, so 60% of the working set is read from disk and burns iops; growing bufferPool to the size of the working set is cheaper than buying more IOPS.

readReplicas = 2 with readFromReplica = 0.3 take a third of the reads off the primary, but replicationMode = async and replicaLagMs = 200 ms mean you should route only queries that tolerate a 200 ms lag there.
A cdc output into Kafka relieves the consumers of changes: logical replication instead of polling queries against the table.
A backup output to S3 is mandatory: availability = 0.9995 and failoverSec = 45 s cover a node failure, but not data loss caused by an application bug.
pitfalls: consistencyModel = linearizable contradicts readFromReplica = 0.3 at stickyReadShare = 0: a third of the reads go to async replicas lagging 200 ms, and the user does not see their own write.
shardCount = 1 means the block does not scale writes: vertical growth stops at cpuCores = 192, and beyond that you need vitess or a different store.
isolationLevel = read-committed does not protect against lost updates under read-modify-write; for counters and balances use repeatable-read or explicit locks with concurrencyControl = pessimistic.
rowCount = 200 million × rowSizeBytes = 400 bytes × indexOverhead = 0.4 is 112 GB out of storageGb = 500, and WAL, table bloat and snapshots in the remaining space are usually forgotten.

probe-availability.summary: A measurement window for path availability: it multiplies the availability of every block in the chain over windowDays = 30 and, with showWeakest = true, highlights the weakest link. Hooked up through attach to the final block or to the entry edge of the path whose availability you want to assess. It reveals what per-block numbers hide: how sequential dependencies compound.
probe-availability.capacity: hasModel = false: the probe consumes no resources and does not enter the capacity calculation, it aggregates the availability parameters of the blocks already placed. targetAvailability = 0.999 only sets the comparison line against which it highlights the result.
practices: Sequential dependencies multiply: five blocks at 0.999 give 0.995, that is about 3.6 hours of downtime per month instead of the expected 43 minutes.
showWeakest = true tells you where to invest: improving a block at 0.9999 is pointless while the chain still contains one at 0.99.

Redundancy changes the formula from a product into 1 minus the product of failures: two independent instances at 0.999 give 0.999999, but only if they are genuinely independent and sit in different az.
Reducing the number of synchronous dependencies raises availability more reliably than improving each of them separately.
pitfalls: An inconspicuous managed block on the critical path: a single external service with availability = 0.99 cancels out the effort spent on the rest of the design.
Standby capacity that depends on the same component as the primary path: formally two instances, in fact one failure domain and no gain at all.
Comparing windowDays = 30 against annual commitments: monthly and annual downtime budgets differ by a factor of 12, and mixing them up is expensive.

probe-cost.summary: A cost measurement window: it shows spend over the selected period and, with breakdown = true, splits it into line items. Hooked up through attach to a single block or to an edge, so you can see the price of one specific node or one specific traffic leg. This is the probe you use to check an architectural decision against the budget.
probe-cost.capacity: hasModel = false: the probe consumes no resources and does not enter the capacity calculation, it sums the cost computed by the blocks of the diagram. period = month by default, with hour, day and year available, which is convenient both for talking about the monthly bill and about total cost of ownership.
practices: breakdown = true shows which line item dominates: for logs it is ingest at 0.5 USD per GB, for apm the subscription at 31 USD per host, for vpc the NAT traffic processing at 0.045 USD per GB.
Look at edges separately, not only at nodes: traffic through NAT, link-cross-az at 0.01 USD per GB and link-cross-region at 0.02 USD per GB belongs to no block and is therefore easy to lose.
Use period = year to compare alternatives: the difference in a region's costMultiplier or in the fixed 73 USD for the control plane only becomes visible over a horizon.
Compare cost against probe-rps on the same block: the price of a single request is more telling than an absolute sum and does not go stale when scale changes.
pitfalls: Optimizing the most visible line item instead of the largest one: on the defaults storing logs costs tens of dollars while ingesting the same data costs thousands.
Forgotten traffic line items: 1 Gbps through NAT is 14580 USD per month, which is usually more than the compute blocks themselves cost.
Reading the hourly cost as a small number: 0.15 USD per node per hour is 657 USD for six nodes per month.

probe-heatmap.summary: A measurement window for an overview: it colours the whole diagram with scope = scheme, or a subtree with scope = subtree, by the chosen metric, utilization or errors. Hooked up through attach to the root block of the part of the diagram you care about. This is the first-glance probe you use to find the hot spot before placing targeted probes.
probe-heatmap.capacity: hasModel = false: the probe consumes no resources and does not enter the capacity calculation, it reads the values computed by each block. The warnThreshold = 0.7 and alarmThreshold = 0.9 thresholds only set colour boundaries and match the thresholds of probe-utilization, so the readings are interpreted the same way.
practices: Start with metric = utilization and scope = scheme to see the overall picture, then narrow down to the subtree around the hot spot you found.
Switching to metric = errors answers a different question: utilization shows where the headroom is running out, errors show where it already has.
Once you find a hot block, attach probe-utilization to it with showBoundBy = true: the heatmap shows where, but not why.
Keep the 0.7 and 0.9 thresholds identical across every probe in the diagram, otherwise the same block will be a different colour on different screens.
pitfalls: A red block is not always the culprit: it may simply sit downstream of whoever sends the excess traffic, and the fix belongs further up the chain.
An evenly green map while the SLO is missed: the map shows utilization and errors but not latency, for which you need probe-latency or probe-waterfall.
Too broad a scope = scheme on a large diagram: dozens of blocks in the same shade carry no information, narrow the area down.

probe-latency.summary: A measurement window with a latency histogram: it shows the response time distribution of the block it is attached to, along with the p50, p95 and p99 percentiles. Hooked up through attach to any node or edge, most often to a service, a database or an external call. With showQueueWait = true it separates queue wait from service time.
probe-latency.capacity: hasModel = false: the probe does not affect the calculation, occupies no resources and adds not a single millisecond to the path it measures. What it gives you is the shape of the distribution: buckets = 40 buckets on a scale = log axis, enough to see both fractions of a millisecond and a second-long tail at once.
practices: Look first at the ratio of queueing to service: if with showQueueWait = true the wait exceeds the service time, the problem is capacity, not the code in the block.
scale = log was not chosen by accident: on a linear axis with 40 buckets the p99 tail collapses into a single edge column and becomes unreadable.
Compare p99 against targetP99Ms = 300 ms on probe-slo, not against the average: the average stays calm long after the tail has fallen apart.
The shape of the distribution matters more than the number: two humps usually mean two different branches, for example a cache hit and a miss.
pitfalls: Adding up the p99 of individual blocks into a p99 for the chain: that overstates latency, use probe-waterfall to break down the budget.
Judging by p50 when the conversation is about an SLO: the median stays quiet while every hundredth user already waits seconds.
showQueueWait turned off: without separating wait from service, growing p99 looks like a code problem when the cause is utilization.

probe-queue.summary: A queue measurement window: it shows accumulated depth, consumer lag and, with showTimeToDrain = true, an estimate of how long the backlog takes to drain. Hooked up through attach to brokers and queues, kafka, amqp, sqs, streams and pipelines, as well as to services with an internal queue. It answers whether processing is keeping up with arrivals.
probe-queue.capacity: hasModel = false: the probe consumes no resources and does not enter the capacity calculation, it displays the state computed by the broker or the worker itself. lagAlarmSec = 60 only sets the highlighting threshold for lag, not the behaviour of the queue.
practices: The main sign of health is convergence: if the drain time is not shrinking, arrivals exceed processing, and no queue size will fix that.
Match lagAlarmSec = 60 to the business meaning of the message: a minute of lag is harmless for sending emails and not harmless for a balance update.
A queue is a buffer for a burst, not for sustained overload: it converts failures into latency and buys you time that has to be spent adding consumers.
Read it together with probe-utilization on the consumer: growing lag at a utilization near 1 means too few workers, while growing lag at low utilization points to locking or partitioning.
pitfalls: Increasing the queue size instead of the number of consumers: messages stop being lost but start arriving hours late.
Judging by average depth: a queue can be almost empty on average and still produce many hours of lag once a day.
Ignoring the drain time after an incident: an hour of downtime accumulates a backlog that takes another hour to drain at the same processing rate.

probe-rps.summary: A measurement window rather than a piece of infrastructure: it shows the request flow in RPS arriving at the block or edge it is attached to. Hooked up through the attach port to any node or link of the diagram, from http and grpc to sql, kafka and telemetry. This is the first probe people place, because every other quantity is derived from load.
probe-rps.capacity: hasModel = false: the probe takes no part in the capacity calculation, consumes no resources, adds no latency and costs nothing. It only visualizes the flow the model has already computed, splitting it by operation when splitByOperation = true and averaging it over a five-minute window when windowSec = 300.
practices: windowSec = 300 smooths out bursts: to see the peak, lower the window to the minimum of 10 to 60 s, otherwise a brief threefold burst dissolves into the average.
splitByOperation = true shows which operation creates the bulk of the flow, while splitByFlow = true answers a different question, which user scenario generates it.
