Read it in pairs with probe-utilization: RPS on its own says nothing, what matters is the ratio of flow to the capacity of the block.
Place a probe on both sides of a cache: the difference between the readings is the actual hit rate, which otherwise has to be taken on faith.
pitfalls: Sizing capacity from the average RPS over a 300 s window: capacity has to cover the peak, and the peak is several times the average.
Attaching to the wrong edge: the flow before the load balancer, after the cache and at the database differ by multiples, and the numbers are easy to confuse.
Comparing RPS from probes with different windowSec: the numbers are comparable only under the same averaging window.

probe-slo.summary: A measurement window for target compliance: it compares the actual figures of a path against targetP99Ms = 300 ms and targetAvailability = 0.999 and shows how much of the error budget has been spent over errorBudgetDays = 30. Hooked up through attach to a user-facing path, that is to an entry edge or to the block that returns the response to the client. This is the probe that translates engineering metrics into commitments to users.
probe-slo.capacity: hasModel = false: the probe takes no part in the capacity calculation and does not affect the path it measures. What it gives the diagram is a scoring system: targetAvailability = 0.999 over a 30-day window is a budget of 43.2 minutes of downtime, and as it is spent you can see whether there is still room for change.
practices: Set the SLO on the user-facing path, not on internal blocks: the user does not care about the availability of one database, they care about the result of their request.
Count the budget in minutes, not in nines: 0.999 is 43.2 minutes per month, 0.9999 is 4.3 minutes, and the gap between them is the gap between an on-call rotation and automation.
targetP99Ms = 300 ms is the full budget, out of which the internet block already takes 40 ms per leg and up to 120 ms on a cold connection.
A spent error budget is the signal to stop changes and work on reliability, while the remaining headroom is permission to take risks.
pitfalls: An SLO stricter than the components allow: a target of 0.9999 on a chain of blocks with availability = 0.999 is unreachable by any amount of operational effort.
A single manual region failover with rtoTargetSec = 900 s spends 3.5 times the 0.9999 budget: 900 s against 259 s per month.
errorBudgetDays = 30 with a quarterly planning cycle: the windows have to line up, otherwise the budget either resets or carries over.

probe-storage.summary: A data volume measurement window: it shows how much space the store will occupy over a horizonYears = 3 horizon, growth included. Hooked up through attach to any block that stores data, from sql and nosql to s3, kafka and observability blocks. It answers what today's stream turns into three years from now.
probe-storage.capacity: hasModel = false: the probe stores nothing itself and does not enter the capacity calculation. It aggregates the volume computed by the block's model, adding the replication factor multiplier when includeReplicas = true and the backup volume when includeBackups = true.
practices: Keep includeReplicas and includeBackups switched on: useful volume and billed volume differ by a factor of two to three, and you have to plan by the second one.

Reconcile the readings with the retention of the source: retentionDays = 30 in logs, 400 in metrics, 7 in traces and retentionYears = 7 in audit-log produce completely different curves from one and the same traffic.
horizonYears = 3 with noticeable annual growth shows not today's pain but the pain the storage type is being chosen for right now.
Read it together with probe-cost: volume on its own is harmless, what matters is volume multiplied by the price per gigabyte per month.
pitfalls: Calculating from useful data without indexes and service structures: the real volume on disk is always larger than the sum of the records.
includeReplicas turned off: at a factor of 2 the estimate is exactly half of reality, at 3 it is a third.
Planning for one year when horizonYears = 3: a storage migration is usually longer and more expensive than choosing with headroom in the first place.

probe-traffic-inspector.summary: A measurement window for traffic composition: it shows the topN = 5 largest sources of load in the groupBy dimension, that is by operations, edges or user scenarios. Hooked up through attach to a node or an edge whose traffic you need to break down. With showBytes = true the request counts are accompanied by volume in bytes, and errorAlarmShare = 0.01 highlights edges where the error share has exceeded one percent.
probe-traffic-inspector.capacity: hasModel = false: the probe takes no part in the capacity calculation, adds no latency and does not affect the traffic it inspects. It only sorts and aggregates flows that are already computed, limiting the output to the top topN entries, 20 at most.
practices: groupBy = operation answers what exactly loads the block; groupBy = edge finds the expensive legs, and groupBy = flow ties the load to a user scenario.
showBytes = true converts traffic into money: the volume on an edge is multiplied by 0.01 USD per GB for link-cross-az, 0.02 USD for link-cross-region and 0.045 USD for NAT in vpc.
errorAlarmShare = 0.01 is a threshold, not a target: one percent of errors on an edge usually means the SLO budget is exhausted long before the window ends.
topN = 5 is enough for a first pass, raise it to 20 when the distribution is even and there is no obvious leader.
pitfalls: The top by request count does not match the top by bytes: one rare heavy operation can cost more than all the others combined, and without showBytes you will not see it.
Optimizing the top row without checking its share: if the first operation carries 12 percent of the traffic, making it twice as fast changes the picture by 6 percent.
Breaking traffic down only by operation when the problem is cost: the money lives on the edges, and you can only see it with groupBy = edge.

probe-utilization.summary: A utilization measurement window: it shows the ratio of incoming flow to the capacity of the block and, with showBoundBy = true, names the bound that saturates first. Hooked up through attach to any node that has a capacity model, for example a service, a database, a broker or an observability block. This is the main probe for finding the bottleneck in a design.
probe-utilization.capacity: hasModel = false: the probe consumes no capacity and takes no part in the calculation, it reads the utilization value that has already been computed. The warnThreshold = 0.7 and alarmThreshold = 0.9 thresholds only drive the colouring and do not change the behaviour of the block.
practices: The 0.7 and 0.9 thresholds come from queueing behaviour: the wait multiplier 1 / (1 - utilization) equals 3.3 at 0.7 and already 10 at 0.9, so past 0.9 latency grows faster than load.
showBoundBy = true matters more than the number itself: it tells you what to add, nodes, memory or ingest bandwidth, and protects you from scaling the wrong resource.
Design with headroom for the peak factor: if the target utilization at peak is 0.7, then with a threefold profile the average has to be around 0.23.
Check utilization on every block of the chain, not only on the suspect: the bottleneck usually turns out to be one step further along.
pitfalls: Deliberately running at 0.95 utilization to save money: no headroom is left for a burst, and queue wait grows twentyfold compared to an idle system.
Green colouring at 0.69 utilization reads as health, even though the block already slows the queue threefold compared to idle.
Ignoring the bound: adding nodes when the limit is memory or ingest bandwidth does not move utilization at all.

probe-waterfall.summary: A measurement window for the latency breakdown: it decomposes the selected percentile = p99 by the steps of the path, showing up to topHops = 12 of the most expensive hops. Hooked up through attach to the entry edge of a user-facing path, starting from the client. This is the probe that answers where exactly the response time budget went.
probe-waterfall.capacity: hasModel = false: the probe takes no part in the capacity calculation, consumes no resources and does not lengthen the path it measures. It decomposes latency that has already been computed into contributions, including the network legs when showNetwork = true and the cache miss branch when showCacheMiss = true.
practices: showNetwork = true is mandatory for an honest picture: 40 ms on internet, 1 ms per crossing on link-cross-az and 80 ms per leg on link-cross-region are contributions that belong to no service.
showCacheMiss = true reveals the real p99: cache hits shape the median, while the tail of the distribution consists almost entirely of misses.
Compare the sum of contributions against targetP99Ms = 300 ms on probe-slo and look for the step that eats more than a quarter of the budget; optimizing the rest is pointless.
Switching percentile to p50 is useful for comparison: a step that looks the same at p50 and p99 is stable, while a diverging one means queueing or misses.
pitfalls: topHops = 12 truncates long chains: in a design with many steps part of the contribution falls into the remainder and stops being visible.
Optimizing against a p50 breakdown while the commitment is on p99: queues are barely visible at the median, and it is queues that shape the tail.
Expecting the sum of hops to equal the end-to-end p99: parallel calls and retries contribute in ways that do not add up linearly.

prometheus.summary: A pull-model monitoring system: it scrapes the targets itself every scrapeIntervalSec = 15 s, holds activeSeries = 10 million series and samplesPerSec = 700,000, which is roughly those same 10 million / 15 s. It keeps retentionDays = 15 locally at bytesPerSample = 1.7 bytes. It is placed at v1 as the source of metrics and alerts, with long-term history offloaded to a separate store.
prometheus.capacity: The limits are cardinality, memory and query-slots. cardinality and memory are essentially one limit: memoryGb = 64 at memoryPerMillionSeriesGb = 4 holds 16 million series, while the current 10 million take 40 GB, that is 62% of the ceiling. query-slots: queryConcurrency = 20 at queryServiceMs = 5 ms gives 4,000 light queries/s, but a single heavy range query occupies a slot for seconds.
practices: Memory depends on activeSeries and disk on samplesPerSec: doubling scrapeIntervalSec from 15 to 30 s halves the disk and does not touch memory at all.
Compute disk as 700,000 × 1.7 bytes = 1.19 MB/s, that is 103 GB per day and 1.54 TB over retentionDays = 15; replicationFactor = 2 doubles that to 3.1 TB.
replicationFactor = 2 here means two independent scrapers, not replication: their series diverge slightly, and deduplication happens one layer up.
seriesPerQuery = 1000 is a workable number for a panel; a recording rule is cheaper than computing the same aggregate in every dashboard query.
retentionDays = 15 is a local window: hand long-term history to a remote-write store instead of raising retention to 3650.
pitfalls: A high-cardinality label (userId, a path with an identifier, trace_id) is the primary way to kill Prometheus: at 10 million series against a ceiling of 16 million there is only 60% of headroom left.
Heavy queries clog queryConcurrency = 20: a couple of dozen dashboards running a month-long range query take alerting down, because rules and queries share the very same slots.
consistencyModel = eventual and availability = 0.99: Prometheus is not the source of truth for billing or SLA reports, missing samples are normal by design.
scrapeIntervalSec = 15 s sets the lower bound on resolution: an alert on a 5-second event physically cannot fire before two scrapes.

pulsar.summary: A log broker with compute and storage separated: brokers serve clients, the data lives on bookies, and cold segments are offloaded to object storage. Delivery is at-least-once with acknowledgements, ordering holds within a partition and, with subscriptionType key-shared, within a key. Take it instead of kafka when you need long retention, many topics and subscriptions with different semantics.
pulsar.capacity: Three limiters. partitions 12 sets write parallelism. broker-network: brokers 3 × throughputMbsPerBroker 250 = 750 MB/s, of which every write is copied replicationFactor 3 times. retention-disk: bookies 4 × diskGbPerBookie 2000 = 8000 GB raw, about 2.7 TB usable at RF 3, and with tieredOffloadHours 24 only one day sits on local disk — that is roughly 31 MB/s of sustained flow.
practices: Pick subscriptionType by the job: exclusive and failover give strict ordering inside a partition, shared gives maximum parallelism with no ordering, and key-shared gives per-key ordering even when consumers outnumber partitions.
Unlike kafka, consumersPerGroup 6 is not capped by partitions 12 on a shared subscription: consumers scale independently of partitions.
tieredStorage true with tieredOffloadHours 24 is the main argument for Pulsar: storage older than a day costs costPerGbMonthOffload 0.023 USD instead of costPerGbMonth 0.1 USD, four times cheaper.
Keep minInsync 2 with replicationFactor 3: a write is acknowledged by two bookies and survives the loss of one.
Bookies scale storage and brokers scale client serving; grow them separately, according to which limiter is on fire.
pitfalls: Running it costs more than kafka: brokers 3 plus bookies 4 at costPerInstanceHour 0.45 USD is about 2300 USD a month against 985 USD for kafka on three brokers, and that is before the metadata store.
retentionHours 168 with tieredStorage disabled means keeping everything on local disks: 2.7 TB of usable space runs out at a stream of only about 4.5 MB/s.
The default shared subscription gives no ordering whatsoever: porting logic over from kafka without changing subscriptionType silently breaks everything that relied on ordering within a partition.
There are more moving parts: a bookie failure is not visible to the client straight away, but it eats the minInsync headroom and eventually stops writes.

rabbitmq.summary: A queue broker with exchange-based routing: a message goes to one consumer of a queue, not to everyone at once. With ackMode manual and quorumQueues true delivery is at-least-once and ordering is FIFO within a queue. Use it for background jobs, commands and retry chains, where a reliable handoff of work matters more than a history of events.
rabbitmq.capacity: The limiters are queues and nodes. The ceiling is queues 20 × throughputPerQueue 20000 rps, but nodes 3 have to digest all of it, and quorumQueues true forces every write to replicate to a majority of nodes. Depth is capped by maxQueueDepth 100000 messages per queue: at messageSizeKb 2 that is about 200 MB per queue and on the order of 4 GB across all 20 against memoryGb 16.
practices: A single queue lives on a single leader node, so you scale by adding queues: 20 queues at 20000 rps each work, one queue at 400000 rps does not.
prefetch 32 with ackMode manual is the working point: a large prefetch piles up invisible work inside one consumer, while prefetch 1 sinks throughput on the round-trip.
Leave dlqEnabled true and wire the dlq port into the dlq block, otherwise rejected messages and ones expired by ttlSec vanish without a trace.
Take quorumQueues true for anything you cannot afford to lose; switch lazyQueues to true if a queue regularly runs tens of thousands of messages deep.
priorityLevels 1 means no priorities at all; more than 5 levels is rarely justified and makes the resulting order hard to predict.
pitfalls: ackMode auto is effectively at-most-once: a message counts as delivered before it is processed and is lost when the worker crashes.
FIFO breaks with multiple consumers and on redelivery: requeue puts the message back at the head of the queue and reorders it relative to its neighbors.
ttlSec 3600 quietly kills everything not consumed within an hour: during a consumer outage the queue does not grow, it drains, and that looks perfectly normal.
With lazyQueues false a queue of 100000 messages lives in memory rather than on disk; exhausting memoryGb 16 triggers publish blocking for every producer.

rate-limiter.summary: A rate limiting block: it counts requests by a chosen key and rejects everything above the limit using the configured algorithm. It exists to protect the services from surges and to share capacity fairly between clients. Place it at the entrance, next to api-gateway, either before or after it.
rate-limiter.capacity: The limits are counter-store and concurrency. With backingStore=redis the ceiling is set by maxOpsPerSec=120,000 operations per second: at limitCheckPerRequest=1 that is 120,000 RPS, but with three checks (global, per user, per IP) it is already down to 40,000 RPS. The concurrency limit does not bind with the defaults: instances=3 × concurrencyPerInstance=256 = 768 simultaneous checks at networkRttMs=0.4 ms plus serviceTimeMs=0.05 ms works out to roughly 1.7 million RPS.
practices: backingStore=redis is mandatory with scope=global or per-user across several instances: local keeps counters independently, so the effective limit becomes instances × rateLimitRps, that is 3 × 2,000 = 6,000 RPS instead of 2,000 RPS.
algorithm=token-bucket with burst=200 lets short surges through; sliding-window is stricter but costs more operations, and gcra gives the smoothest shaping.
rateLimitRps=2000 RPS is the enforced limit, not the block's capacity: capacity is set by maxOpsPerSec=120,000 and does not depend on the limit value you chose.
rejectMode=http-429 is preferable because the client sees an explicit rejection and can back off; queue pushes the overload deeper into the diagram, and shed drops requests silently.
Keep limitCheckPerRequest as close to 1 as possible: every extra check divides the counter-store capacity by that number.
pitfalls: Choosing backingStore=local for speed and getting an effective limit several times higher than the configured one, and the more instances there are the worse it gets.

Treating the block as safe in the critical path at availability=0.999 (about 8.8 hours per year) without deciding in advance whether to let traffic through or reject it when the counters are unavailable.
burst=200 at rateLimitRps=2000 RPS is only 0.1 s worth of traffic: clients with burstiness=2 do not have enough headroom and get 429s on a perfectly normal profile.
Choosing scope=per-ip for a public API, so that every user behind a single NAT or PoP shares one common limit.

redis.summary: An in-memory cache and data structure store: key-value, lists, sorted sets. Placed in front of the database to take hot reads off it and to hold counters, sessions and rate limits.
redis.capacity: Capacity is bounded by shard operations and by how resident the working set is: if the data does not fit in memory, eviction devalues the cache long before the operations ceiling is reached.
practices: Derive the hit ratio from the size of the working set and zipfAlpha instead of assigning the number you wish for.
Keep TTL shorter than the window of acceptable divergence from the source of truth.
Shard by key and watch that a hot key does not pull all the traffic onto one shard.
pitfalls: A cache with no fallback turns the database into a single point of failure when the cache goes down.
Event-based invalidation without a key version creates the 'stale value overwrites the fresh one' race.

redis-store.summary: Redis used as the primary store rather than a cache: shards = 6, replicasPerShard = 1, evictionPolicy = noeviction and persistence = aof. It gives serviceTimeMs = 0.25 ms per operation, an order of magnitude faster than any disk-based database, at the price of keeping the whole dataset in memory. It is placed at v1 under high-RPS state: sessions, counters, leaderboards, rate limits.
redis-store.capacity: The limits are ops, memory, connections, hot-key and iops: ops is maxOpsPerSec = 120,000 per shard (the ceiling of a single-threaded process) × shards = 6 = 720,000 operations/s. memory is computed as uniqueKeys = 50 million × (keySizeBytes = 64 + valueSizeBytes = 1024 + overheadPerKeyBytes = 64) = 57.6 GB against memoryGb = 26 per shard, that is 156 GB per cluster. hot-key at hotKeyShare = 0.05 loads one shard about 1.25 times above average, and iops is driven by persistence = aof on provisionedIops = 20,000.
practices: evictionPolicy = noeviction is the right choice for a store: when it fills up Redis returns an error on writes instead of silently dropping data, but memoryGb = 26 needs an alert.
persistence = aof at durabilityRisk = 0.02 means a loss window of about 2% of acknowledged writes on a crash; if that is unacceptable you need rdb-aof with more frequent fsync at the cost of iops.
pipelining = true is mandatory: without it every operation pays a full round-trip and serviceTimeMs = 0.25 ms drowns in network latency.
Take the overhead seriously: at valueSizeBytes = 1024 the key and overheadPerKeyBytes = 64 add 128 bytes, that is 11% on top, and on small values they start to dominate.
Sharding does not save you from a hot key at hotKeyShare = 0.05: that is cured by read replicas or a local cache in front of Redis.
pitfalls: consistencyModel = eventual with replicationMode = async and replicaLagMs = 5 ms: a shard failover loses the most recent writes, which is why Redis does not fit where commit durability is required.
conflictResolution = lww: WATCH and MULTI give optimistic control, but a plain SET from concurrent writers simply overwrites the value.
memoryGb = 26 per shard at replicasPerShard = 1 is 312 GB of paid-for memory for 57.6 GB of data: replicas are billed at full price.
One large structure (a list, hash or set) lives entirely on one shard: a million elements in a key makes it both hot and blocking on O(n) commands.

redis-streams.summary: A stream inside Redis built on the stream data structure with consumer groups: an in-memory append-only log with acknowledgements and a pending list. Delivery is at-least-once, and ordering holds within a single stream. Use it when Redis is already in the design and you need a sub-millisecond queue (serviceTimeMs 0.3) without standing up a separate broker.
redis-streams.capacity: Four limiters. ops: maxOpsPerSec 120000 rps is split between XADD on write and XREADGROUP plus XACK for each of consumerGroups 4, so the useful message rate is several times below the raw 120000. partitions: write parallelism equals shards 3. inflight: pendingLimit 10000 unacknowledged messages per group, which at processingTimeMs 20 ms gives a ceiling of 500000 messages/s along that axis. memory: maxLen 10000000 entries at messageSizeKb 1 is about 10 GB against memoryGb 8, so memory runs out before the declared stream length does.
practices: Bring maxLen and memoryGb into agreement: 10 million entries of 1 KB need at least 10 GB plus headroom for pending lists and internal structures.
Always set MAXLEN trimming: an unbounded stream grows until maxmemory eviction kicks in and drags the whole instance down with it.
Spread the load across shards 3: one stream lives on one shard, and replicas serve reads but add no write capacity.
Watch the pending list and use XAUTOCLAIM: a stuck consumer keeps up to pendingLimit 10000 messages invisible to everyone else.
Redis Streams is about latency, not history: count retention in hours, and for a day or more take kafka or kinesis.
pitfalls: The data lives in memory: at availability 0.999, a node failure without AOF or a replica loses the entire unacknowledged tail.
Every new consumerGroup multiplies read and acknowledge operations against the same maxOpsPerSec budget — four groups cost four times as much as one on the read side.
maxLen trimming removes entries regardless of whether the groups have read them: a slow consumer silently loses messages with no error at all.

redshift.summary: A managed MPP warehouse: nodes split a table by the distribution key and run SQL in parallel. The classic enterprise data warehouse on a fixed cluster.
redshift.capacity: disk-scan binds first: 8 managed-storage nodes give 19.2 GB/s against 4.2 GB scanned per query. network depends on distKey, query-slots on queryConcurrency = 15, and ingest-bandwidth on the load process.
practices: distKey = key leaves 10% of the data to redistribute, even leaves 50%: the distribution key takes the shuffle off the network.
sortKey compound cuts the scan to 25%, interleaved to 40%, and none does not cut it at all.
vacuumNeeded adds 35% to the scan: keep VACUUM and ANALYZE on a schedule.
queryConcurrency 5–50 is about WLM queues; more queues will not add disk bandwidth.
pitfalls: distKey = even moves the limit onto network for joins: half of everything scanned gets redistributed.
Eight nodes at $3.26/h is about $19,000 a month — the cluster is billed even with no queries.
sortKey = none removes range pruning and quadruples the scan over the same data.

region.summary: A geographic region container: everything placed inside it counts as living in one provider point of presence. It sets the geography used to compute latency to clients, the cost multiplier and the data residency requirements. Placed first in any diagram, because it defines the coordinate system for az, vpc and links.
region.capacity: hasModel = false: the region serves nothing itself and does not enter the capacity calculation, it has neither ports nor bounds. Instead it gives the diagram three things: availability = 0.9999 as the ceiling for everything inside it, costMultiplier = 1 within the 0.5 to 3 range as a cost multiplier for those blocks, and geo = europe for computing the leg to clients.
practices: isPrimary = true with an empty mirrorOf means a single primary region; when you add a second region, reconcile mirrorOf with writeRegion in multi-region-policy, otherwise the diagram describes two independent products.

costMultiplier changes the bill for everything inside the region: the same design in a region with a multiplier of 3 costs three times as much, and picking a different region is often cheaper than optimizing blocks.
dataResidency = gdpr or local-only restricts where you may replicate: check it against dataResidency = strict in multi-region-policy and against the direction of link-cross-region.
Choose geo to match the bulk of your users: it is what drives clientRttMs on the internet block, and a 40 ms leg is the baseline that everything else adds on top of.
availability = 0.9999 is about 4.3 minutes per month and 52.6 minutes per year: a single region cannot deliver an SLO above that ceiling, no matter how much redundancy sits inside.
pitfalls: Expecting a region to provide fault tolerance by itself: without az inside and without multi-region-policy outside it is just a frame on the diagram.
Choosing a region by price while ignoring geo: the costMultiplier = 0.5 you saved is easily eaten by clientRttMs growing from 40 ms to 150 ms.
dataResidency = none while handling personal data of European users: the model will allow replication, the regulator will not.

reverse-cache.summary: A caching reverse proxy in front of the services: it keeps hot responses in memory and serves them without reaching the origin. Unlike cdn it runs inside your own perimeter and caches internal API responses as well. Place it between the load balancer and the services wherever reads repeat.
reverse-cache.capacity: There are four limits: memory, cpu, proxy-rps and network. With the defaults CPU binds first: cpuCores=4 at serviceTimeMs=0.8 ms gives 5,000 RPS per instance and 15,000 RPS across three instances, against roughly 10,000 RPS per instance on the network side (networkMbps=10,000 with a 120 KB object) and a nominal proxy-rps of 3 × maxRpsPerInstance=30,000 = 90,000 RPS. Memory determines not the RPS but the hit ratio: cacheSizeGb=50 with avgObjectKb=120 KB holds about 437,000 objects out of uniqueKeys=5,000,000, which at zipfAlpha=1 is exactly what produces the stated cacheHitRatio=0.85.
practices: Size the cache from uniqueKeys and avgObjectKb: 50 GB with a 120 KB object is about 437,000 keys, less than 9% of the 5,000,000-key space.
zipfAlpha=1 implies a pronounced head in the distribution; at a zipfAlpha of around 0.6 the same amount of memory yields a noticeably lower hit ratio and cacheHitRatio=0.85 has to come down.
varyHeaders=2 multiplies the key space: every additional header in Vary cuts the effective hit ratio by a multiple at the same cacheSizeGb.

staleWhileRevalidateSec=30 s and purgeApi=true are a mandatory pair: the first protects the origin at the moment ttlSec=600 s expires, the second lets you invalidate selectively without flushing the whole cache.
serviceTimeMs=0.8 ms with cpuCores=4 is 5,000 RPS per instance; scale instances from that figure, not from maxRpsPerInstance=30,000 RPS.
pitfalls: Planning around maxRpsPerInstance=30,000 RPS and getting a real ceiling several times lower, because cpu (5,000 RPS per instance) and network (about 10,000 RPS per instance) bind first.
Setting cacheHitRatio=0.95 with a cacheSizeGb that only covers a few percent of the keys, understating the calculated origin load several times over.
Adding headers to Vary (varyHeaders above 3 is outside the realistic range) and then being surprised by the falling hit ratio once memory is full.
Forgetting that after an instance restart the cache is empty: a 15% miss rate instantly becomes 100% and the origin takes an almost sevenfold spike.

s3.summary: Managed object storage: a flat key space, HTTP access to the whole object, durabilityNines 11. It is not a file system — no partial writes, no renames, no locks — but capacity is unbounded. Use it for user files, media, backups, logs and as the cold layer under analytics.
s3.capacity: The limiters are prefix-requests and prefix-throughput, both counted per prefix. Requests: prefixCount 10 × maxGetRpsPerPrefix 5500 = 55000 GET/s and × maxPutRpsPerPrefix 3500 = 35000 PUT/s. Bandwidth: prefixCount 10 × throughputPerPrefixMbs 400 = 4000 MB/s, which at avgObjectSizeMb 2 gives only 2000 objects/s — bandwidth becomes the wall more than an order of magnitude earlier than the request limit.
practices: Lay keys out across prefixes deliberately: the limits apply per prefix, so a date at the start of the key funnels all of today's load into one prefix out of ten.
firstByteLatencyMs 30 is not suitable for hot reads: put a CDN or a cache in front of s3 and keep the block itself as the source of truth.
Enable multipartThresholdMb 100 for anything large: a single-request upload that fails means retransmitting the whole object.
lifecycleDays 90 moves cold data into infrequent-access or glacier — across objectCount 50000000 of 2 MB each (about 100 TB, 2300 USD a month at costPerGbMonth 0.023) the saving is substantial.
Wire the event port into kafka or sqs: processing an uploaded file should be triggered by an event, not by polling the bucket.
pitfalls: Small objects are expensive in request terms: costPerMillionPut 5 USD against costPerMillionGet 0.4 USD — a million files of 10 KB costs more than a hundred files of 100 MB.
costPerGbEgress 0.09 USD easily outweighs storage: serving 100 TB outbound costs 9000 USD against 2300 USD for storing the same volume.
versioning false means an overwrite destroys the object irreversibly, while versioning enabled without lifecycleDays inflates the bill with forgotten old versions.
crossRegionReplication false: 11 nines of durability save you from neither a region outage nor an accidental mass delete.

s3-table.summary: A parquet-formatted table on object storage with a snapshot manifest: rawGbPerDay = 2000 GB per day, partitioning = day, fileSizeMb = 128, compaction = scheduled. This is the analytical layer, where a read costs a scan and a write costs a manifest commit rather than a row in an OLTP database. It is placed at v2 as long-term event storage and the source for batch analytics.
s3-table.capacity: The limits are manifest, compaction, throughput and ingest-bandwidth. throughput caps writes first: commitServiceMs = 200 ms per commit is 5 commits/s, and only batchSize = 200 files per commit turns that into 1000 files/s. The manifest grows with the number of files: 2 TB per day at fileSizeMb = 128 yields 15,625 files per day and about 5.7 million over lifecycleDays = 365, compactionSlots = 8 must keep up with merging them, while ingest-bandwidth (maxIngestMbs = 2000 against an average of 23 MB/s) has enormous headroom.
practices: fileSizeMb = 128 inside the 64–512 band is the main lever: 8 MB files would produce 250,000 files per day and drown the manifest together with the query planner.
partitioning = day at 2 TB per day is right: hourly gives 24 partitions per day and small files, monthly makes it impossible to prune anything at read time.

compaction = scheduled with compactionSlots = 8 has to keep up with the write stream; if the queue of small files grows day after day, there are not enough slots, and queries degrade gradually without a single error.
bytesScanned = 200 MB per query holds only thanks to partition pruning and the columnar format: a query without a date filter reads the whole table and is billed at costPerMillionRequests = 0.4.

compression = zstd and format = parquet are the right defaults, but lifecycleDays = 365 at 2 TB per day is 730 TB and about 16,800 USD per month at costPerGbMonth = 0.023, so the retention period is agreed before launch.
pitfalls: Consistency here is snapshot-based, not transactional in the OLTP sense: readers only see a committed manifest snapshot, and two concurrent commits are resolved optimistically with one of them retrying.

The cost of a write is measured in hundreds of milliseconds (commitServiceMs = 200 ms plus writeServiceMs = 50 ms), so you cannot write here synchronously from a service, only in batches through Kafka or a batch job.
The small file problem is the typical failure mode: manifestOverhead = 0.02 is harmless at 15 thousand files per day and becomes dominant at millions of small ones.
lifecycleDays = 365 without a real deletion policy turns into storing forever: costPerGbMonth = 0.023 looks small until 730 TB becomes a noticeable budget line.

saga-orchestrator.summary: An orchestrator for distributed transactions: it drives workflowsPerSec 2000 sagas of stepsPerWorkflow 8 steps each, persisting every state change in stateStore database and keeping history for retentionDays 30. Use it where a business operation touches several services and you need compensations instead of two-phase commit. The only outputs are http/grpc/internal to the saga participants.
saga-orchestrator.capacity: The limiters are state-transitions, quotaRps and workers. state-transitions = 2000 × 8 = 16,000 transitions/s against quotaRps (maxOpsPerSec 20,000 on the state store) — only 20% headroom, and it disappears if a transition costs a read plus a write. workers = instances 3 × concurrency 100 = 300 slots ÷ serviceTimeMs 6 ms = 50,000 transitions/s, but a slot is held for the whole time a step is awaited: with a 200 ms step that is already 1500 transitions/s, i.e. 187 sagas/s.
practices: Count the load in transitions, not in sagas: stepsPerWorkflow 8 multiplies everything at once — the state store's ops, costPerStateTransition $2.5e-05 and the volume of history.
Keep steps short and asynchronous: a concurrency slot waiting on an external call is an order of magnitude more expensive than the 6 ms of processing itself.
Every step must have a compensation and be idempotent: the orchestrator guarantees that a step is retried, not that it runs exactly once.

retentionDays 30 at rowSizeBytes 512 and 16,000 transitions/s is 708 GB per day and about 21 TB of history, i.e. roughly $2100/month at costPerGbMonth $0.1; shorten the retention or archive to object storage.
stateStore database gives durability and queries over state; redis is faster, but losing a saga's state means a business operation stuck forever with no chance of recovery.
pitfalls: The orchestrator as a single point of failure: availability 0.999 is 43 minutes a month during which every multi-step operation hangs halfway.
16,000 transitions/s against maxOpsPerSec 20,000: any spike, or a saga growing to 10 steps (20,000 transitions), pins the block against the state store's ceiling.
A compensation that fails itself: without retries and a DLQ on the compensating steps the saga stays inconsistent forever.
costPerStateTransition $2.5e-05 at 16,000/s is $0.4/s ≈ $1440/hour, incomparable with the 3 × 0.2 = $0.6/hour for the instances.

scheduler-queue.summary: A queue of deferred jobs: the task is accepted now and handed to the consumer at the scheduled moment through the due port. It covers delayed retries, timeouts, reminders and expiry-driven cancellation. Put it in front of an ordinary queue — the block does not process jobs itself, it releases them once they come due into amqp, sqs or internal.
scheduler-queue.capacity: The limiters are poll-batch, depth and memory. poll-batch: instances 2 × batchSize 500 per pollIntervalSec 1 = 1000 due jobs per second. depth: pendingJobs 20000000 deferred jobs. memory: those same 20 million at messageSizeKb 2 need about 40 GB against memoryGb 32, so memory becomes the wall before the declared depth does.
practices: Reconcile pendingJobs with memoryGb: 20 million jobs of 2 KB is 40 GB, so either keep only a reference inside the job or add memory.
pollIntervalSec 1 sets the firing precision: with that polling interval you cannot promise the user better than second-level accuracy.
delayDistribution flat with maxDelayHours 24 gives 20000000 / 86400 ≈ 231 jobs per second on average — four times below the 1000/s ceiling, so there is headroom.
Do not schedule on round moments: delays rounded to the minute or to midnight pile into a spike that poll-batch cannot digest.
Release is at-least-once: a job can fire twice across a restart, so the handler must check whether the action has already been performed.
pitfalls: delayDistribution long-tail with maxDelayHours up to 720 accumulates millions of jobs aimed far into the future and turns the block into a database with durability requirements.
Cancelling a scheduled job is the most commonly forgotten part: the user unsubscribed and the reminder still goes out — you need a relevance check at release time.
Polling with instances 2 without a lease or an atomic claim hands the same job to both instances, and the repeat looks like a duplicate on the consumer side.
availability 0.999 is about 8.8 hours a year during which nothing fires on time, and everything accumulated is released in one burst right after recovery.

scylla.summary: A Cassandra-compatible database on a thread-per-core architecture: shardsPerCore = 1 at cpuCores = 16 gives 16 independent shards per node, and throughputMultiplier = 4 reflects the gain from having no JVM and from sharded execution. The data model, consistencyModel = eventual and conflictResolution = lww are the same as in cassandra. It is taken at v1 as a Cassandra replacement where nodes are expensive.
scylla.capacity: The limits are shard-cpu, node-ops and iops. shard-cpu: nodes = 6 × cpuCores = 16 × shardsPerCore = 1 = 96 shards, each single-threaded, and one partition is served by exactly one shard. node-ops: maxOpsPerSecPerNode = 20,000 with throughputMultiplier = 4 is 80,000 operations/s per node and 480,000 per cluster before dividing by replicationFactor = 3, while iops at provisionedIops = 300,000 assumes NVMe and rarely binds.
practices: throughputMultiplier = 4 only holds with an even spread across the 96 shards: a hot partition sits on one shard and gets 1/96 of the cluster's power.
provisionedIops = 300,000 is a local NVMe profile, not a network volume; on network storage the ceiling drops by an order of magnitude and writeAmplification = 4 starts to dominate.
quorumR = 2 and quorumW = 2 at quorumN = 3 give overlapping quorums, and storageGbPerNode = 4000 against 167 GB of actual data per node leaves room for compaction.
Tune compactionStrategy = stcs to the workload the same way as in cassandra: twcs for time series with TTL, lcs when reads dominate.
Keep partitionSizeMb = 64 inside the 1–100 MB band: in Scylla a large partition hurts a single core, not the whole node.
pitfalls: shardsPerCore above 1 buys no throughput: it is the same cores sliced finer, plus extra context switching.
conflictResolution = lww and concurrencyControl = none are the same as in cassandra: a concurrent write is lost silently.
costPerInstanceHour = 0.9 against 0.5 for cassandra means the same 6 nodes cost 1.8 times more, and that is justified only if throughputMultiplier = 4 really lets you remove nodes.
readServiceMs = 1.5 ms against writeServiceMs = 0.3 ms: the same LSM asymmetry, a read is five times more expensive than a write.

search-indexer.summary: An indexing pipeline: it reads a change stream and writes documents into a search index at docsPerSec 2000 with docSizeKb 2. It sits between the data source (CDC, a queue) and the search cluster so that the index stays fresh without loading the primary database. Its output is restricted to the search/olap/internal ports — this is not a general-purpose service.
search-indexer.capacity: The limiters are indexing, cpu, throughput and memory. indexing is set directly: docsPerSec 2000. cpu = instances 4 × cpuCores 8 ÷ (indexServiceMs 5 ms × cpuShare 0.6) ≈ 10,700 documents/s, throughput = mergeThroughputMbs 100 MB/s against an actual 2000 × 2 KB × indexExpansionRatio 1.4 = 5.6 MB/s. So at the defaults the declared indexing rate binds first, not the hardware.
practices: indexLagSec 30 s plus refreshIntervalSec 5 s means up to 35 s from a change in the database to visibility in search; agree that number with product expectations up front.
indexExpansionRatio 1.4 means the index is 40% larger than the source data: 2000 documents/s × 2 KB × 1.4 = 5.6 MB/s ≈ 484 GB per day on the search cluster's disk.
Raise docsPerSec together with cpuCores: at the defaults there is 5× cpu headroom, so a reindex can run much faster than the normal stream.
Feed the block from a queue or a CDC stream rather than from a synchronous call inside a service: indexing should lag behind writes, not block them.
Keep a document idempotency key: the stream is at-least-once, so re-indexing must overwrite rather than duplicate.
pitfalls: A full reindex at the defaults: 100 million documents at 2000 documents/s takes about 14 hours, and for all that time half the index is stale.
refreshIntervalSec 5 s at the peak of a reindex kills throughput: frequent refreshes spawn small segments and push merging into the mergeThroughputMbs 100 MB/s wall.
Indexing from the same service that writes to the database: a search outage starts taking transactions down, even though the block exists precisely to prevent that.
memoryGb 16 × 4 = 64 GB is sized for buffers, not for the whole index: assuming the index is held in the indexer's memory makes the capacity estimate wrong.

secrets.summary: A secrets store: it hands out keys, passwords and certificates in serviceTimeMs 4 ms plus encryptionMs 2 ms, with a hard rateLimitRps 1200 and a client-side cache of ttlSec 300 s. Put it next to any block that needs credentials, instead of keeping passwords in environment variables. It has no out ports.
secrets.capacity: The limiters are rate-limit and cpu. rate-limit = rateLimitRps 1200 requests/s — a hard wall rather than degradation. ttlSec 300 s determines how many requests actually reach it: 1200 RPS × 300 s = 360,000 instance-secret pairs can be refreshed without exceeding the limit.
practices: ttlSec 300 s is the main lever: 1000 instances with 5 secrets each give 5000 ÷ 300 ≈ 17 requests/s, i.e. 1.4% of the limit.
Read secrets at startup and on TTL expiry, not on every request: with ttlSec 0 any service above 1200 RPS hits the limit immediately.
costPerCall $3e-06 looks trivial, but at the 1200 RPS limit it is $12.96/hour ≈ $9500/month — almost 29 times more than the 3 × 0.15 = $0.45/hour for the instances themselves.
Keep the last successfully fetched secret in the client: availability 0.9995 (22 minutes a month) is survivable with a cache, but only if the TTL does not expire at that same moment.
Rotation has to be two-phase: the old and the new secret stay valid together for at least ttlSec 300 s, otherwise some instances will still authenticate with the old one.
pitfalls: Fetching the secret in the request handler instead of at startup — the symptom is exactly 1200 RPS and an avalanche of failures the moment you try to scale.
Restarting the whole fleet at once: 1000 instances start simultaneously and the volley of 5000 requests is four times rateLimitRps 1200.
Putting secrets into the config block: it has no encryption, no auditing and no hard limit — that is precisely why a separate block exists.
encryptionMs 2 ms on every operation: bulk-decrypting data through this block instead of with a local key costs 6 ms per item and hits the limit at just a few thousand items.

serverless.summary: Function as a service: the platform spins up executions to match the load and you pay per invocation. Use it for uneven traffic, rare jobs and glue logic where permanently running instances cost more than paying per call. It is a managed block — the only knobs are memoryMb 512, the timeouts and maxConcurrency 1000.
serverless.capacity: The only limiter is concurrency: maxConcurrency 1000 simultaneous executions divided by the hold time. At serviceTimeMs 80 ms that is 12,500 RPS, and once coldStartShare 0.02 × coldStartMs 400 ms is taken into account the average hold grows to 88 ms and the ceiling drops to ~11,400 RPS.
practices: provisionedConcurrency 0 means every spike pays coldStartMs 400 ms; for latency-sensitive paths set provisioned concurrency to the level of baseline traffic.
memoryMb 512 sets both the CPU share and the price: doubling memory usually halves serviceTimeMs while costPerGbSecond 1.66667e-05 per GB-s stays the same, so the bill often does not change.
timeoutMs 30,000 ms must be below maxDurationSec 900 s and below the caller's patience: 30 s on a synchronous HTTP path is a failure, not a response.
For background work wire the consume port to a queue, and for synchronous work wire the in port to a gateway; with maxConcurrency 1000 both shapes give you up to 1000 parallel executions.
logLinesPerRequest 3 × logBytesPerLine 400 bytes = 1.2 KB per invocation: at 1000 RPS that is 1.2 MB/s, and in serverless logs are usually billed separately from invocations.
pitfalls: The cost of steady traffic: 512 MB × 80 ms = 0.04 GB-s, i.e. $0.667 per million invocations plus costPerMillionInvocations $0.2; at 1000 RPS that is 86.4 million invocations a day and about $75 a day.
maxConcurrency 1000 is a hard wall: exceeding it produces failures rather than degradation, so the limit on the calling block has to be lower, not higher.
Long-running work under maxDurationSec 900 s combined with queue retries leads to re-execution — without idempotency that means duplicate records.
1000 simultaneous executions open up to 1000 database connections: without a pool or a proxy the database hits its session limit before the function hits its concurrency.

service.summary: A general-purpose stateless application service: it accepts HTTP/gRPC/WS or queue messages, runs its own logic in serviceTimeMs = 20 ms and talks to databases, caches and brokers. This is the basic building block of a design once the monolith has been carved up. It sits behind a load balancer or a gateway and scales horizontally up to autoscaleMax = 20 instances.
service.capacity: The limiters are workers, cpu and network. workers = instances 3 × concurrencyPerInstance 200 ÷ serviceTimeMs 20 ms = 30,000 RPS, but cpu binds far earlier: 3 × cpuCores 4 ÷ (0.02 s × cpuShare 0.15) ≈ 4000 RPS. network gives 3 × networkMbps 1000 = 3000 Mbps, so at 4000 RPS each request gets 0.75 Mbit ≈ 94 KB.
practices: Autoscaling is enabled up to autoscaleMax 20 at autoscaleTargetUtilization 0.65, but scaleUpLagSec 60 s means the first minute of a spike is absorbed by the instances 3 already running — size the baseline for the peak minus that minute.
cpuShare 0.15 at serviceTimeMs 20 ms is 3 ms of CPU per request; if the logic computes rather than waits on I/O, raise cpuShare to 0.4-0.5, otherwise the model overstates capacity threefold.
queueLimit 1000 against a capacity of 4000 RPS adds 250 ms of waiting and still fits inside timeoutMs 1000 ms; a queue of 10,000 would mean 2.5 s of waiting and turn all the work into timeouts.
azSpread 3 means losing one zone removes a third of the capacity: keep 1.5× headroom so that two zones out of three can carry full traffic.
Wire the telemetry port to the logging and metrics blocks: logLinesPerRequest 4 × logBytesPerLine 400 bytes = 1.6 KB per request, which at 4000 RPS is 6.4 MB/s ≈ 550 GB of logs per day.
pitfalls: callMode sequential adds the latency of every downstream call into p99: three calls of 40 ms each add 120 ms on top of the service's own 20 ms and eat into timeoutMs 1000 ms.
concurrencyPerInstance 200 with cpuCores 4 is eightfold CPU oversubscription: the queue fills up, p99 climbs, and RPS stays pinned at the cpu limit of 4000.
availability 0.999 is 43 minutes a month; a chain of three such services gives 0.997 ≈ 2.2 hours, which is already below a typical 99.9% SLO.
The default 3 instances × $0.17/hour = $372/month, but scaled out to autoscaleMax 20 the bill becomes $2480/month — check the cost at the peak, not at the average.

service-mesh.summary: A service mesh: a sidecar proxy next to every service, providing mTLS, retries, circuit breaking and uniform telemetry for east-west traffic. It is not an entry point; it serves calls between services inside the perimeter. Place it between internal blocks when there are several services and you need uniform policies.
service-mesh.capacity: The limits are cpu and network. The mesh does not so much cap the stream as consume resources: cpuOverheadPercent=12 of instances=10 × cpuCores=4 = 40 cores means about 4.8 cores spent on the proxies. On latency, latencyOverheadMs=0.7 ms is multiplied by hopsPerRequest=2, so roughly 1.4 ms is added to every request, and 2.8 ms at 4 hops.
practices: hopsPerRequest=2 (realistically 2-4) is the main multiplier: both latency and CPU overhead grow linearly with the hop count, so shortening the call chain pays off more than any proxy tuning.
Leave mtls=true enabled, it is the main reason to run a mesh at all; turning it off saves CPU but removes encryption of service-to-service traffic.
retryPolicy=idempotent-only at every hop is safer than exponential-backoff: with 2 hops and three attempts at each, the amplification reaches 9x.
circuitBreaker=true with circuitBreakerErrorThreshold=0.5 opens the circuit once half the calls fail; for critical dependencies it is worth lowering the threshold so degradation is spotted sooner.
observabilityExport=true sends the data to the telemetry port; connect it to an observability block, otherwise metrics and traces go nowhere.
pitfalls: Adding a mesh for the sake of tidiness to a two-service diagram and paying 1.4 ms of latency and 12% CPU overhead for no real benefit.
Not reconciling retryPolicy between the mesh and lb-l7: two independent retry policies multiply and turn a local failure into a storm.
Reading cpuOverheadPercent=12 as being per service rather than across all instances: the real price is 4.8 cores out of 40, which have to come from somewhere.
availability=0.9995 (about 4.4 hours per year) applies at every hop, so with hopsPerRequest=2 the mesh's contribution is twice as significant as the single number suggests.

session-store.summary: Server-side session storage: activeSessions 20,000,000 records of sessionSizeKb 4 with ttlSec 1800 on backend redis. Put it next to auth when you need instant session invalidation, a server-side cart or a list of active devices. It has no out ports — the block only answers reads and writes.
session-store.capacity: The limiters are ops and memory. ops = maxOpsPerSec 90,000 operations/s at readServiceMs 0.3 ms and writeServiceMs 0.6 ms, so a write costs twice as much as a read. memory: 20,000,000 × 4 KB = 80 GB against instances 3 × memoryGb 32 = 96 GB is 83% full, and that is before replicas.
practices: ttlSec 1800 s directly determines the number of live sessions: 20 million records accumulate at roughly 11,000 logins/s, which makes shortening the TTL the cheapest way to cut memory.
sessionSizeKb 4 is already a lot for a session: store the identifier and the permissions and pull the profile from its own service, otherwise 20 million sessions become 80 GB.
Count writes separately: every session extension costs writeServiceMs 0.6 ms, and the habit of updating last_seen on every request doubles the ops load.
backend cookie-jwt removes the block from the design entirely but gives up instant revocation — that is a deliberate trade-off, not an optimization.
Connect it to auth and to the services that need session checks; at 90,000 ops/s, checking on every request caps the whole system at that number.
pitfalls: 80 GB of data in 96 GB of memory with no headroom: a single replica doubles the requirement to 160 GB and the block no longer fits.
Losing session-store logs every user out; availability 0.999 here means 43 minutes a month when nobody can work.
backend database instead of redis: readServiceMs 0.3 ms turns into single-digit milliseconds and the ceiling of 90,000 ops/s drops by an order of magnitude.
No TTL discipline: sessions without ttlSec pile up forever, and memory runs out with time rather than with load.

snowflake.summary: A managed warehouse that separates storage from compute: the warehouse spins up under load and shuts down when idle. You pay in credits for the time the cluster runs.
snowflake.capacity: credits is the limit: capacity equals (creditsPerHour / credits per size) × queryConcurrency / S. On medium with creditsPerHour = 4 that is a single cluster and 8 concurrent queries; ingest-bandwidth binds later.
practices: Warehouse size divides query time: medium (4 credits) turns 4,000 ms into 1,000 ms and costs four times more than x-small.
creditsPerHour divided by the credits of the size gives the number of clusters: that is how you grow concurrency, not the speed of a single query.
autoSuspendMin 1–60: idle time is not billed, but the first query after a sleep pays 2 s to resume.
queryConcurrency is realistically 4–20 — the warehouse queue is short by design, so plan the peak around that number.
pitfalls: Constant background traffic never lets the warehouse fall asleep: you pay creditsPerHour × $3 × 730 h whether it is useful or not.
Snowflake on the user's synchronous path: 1 s on medium plus up to 2 s to wake up.
Growing the warehouse size for concurrency: it speeds up a single query, while the queue is still governed by queryConcurrency.

sns.summary: A publish-subscribe bus: one message goes out to every subscriber at once, and no history is kept. Delivery is at-least-once per subscription, and ordering between messages is not guaranteed. Use it when an event has to reach several recipients and nobody needs to re-read it — the standard pairing is sns at the front with one sqs queue per subscriber.
sns.capacity: The limiters are fanout and broker-network. Every publish turns into subscribers 6 deliveries, so rateLimitRps 30000 on the way in means 180000 deliveries/s on the way out. At messageSizeKb 4 that is about 5.8 Gbps out of networkMbps 10000, so the headroom is less than two-fold, and each new subscriber adds roughly another 1 Gbps.
practices: Do not subscribe service HTTP endpoints directly: put an sqs queue between sns and the consumer, otherwise a slow subscriber holds up delivery to everyone else.
filterPolicy attributes drops what is not needed on the bus side; with none all 6 subscribers receive every message and pay for it.
maxRetries 3 plus the dlq port wired into the dlq block — otherwise anything undelivered to a subscriber is gone for good.
Keep subscribers in the realistic 2-50 range: fanout multiplies both traffic and the bill at costPerMillionRequests 0.5 USD linearly.
messageSizeKb 4 against a 256 KB limit: an event should be a notification carrying a reference, not a way to move data around.
pitfalls: There is no history: a subscriber unavailable past maxRetries 3 loses the event forever — for replay you need kafka or kinesis.
Ordering is not guaranteed at all: two events about the same entity arrive in arbitrary order, so the body must carry a version or a timestamp.
Fanout cost is counted in deliveries, not in publishes: a million publishes with 6 subscribers is 6 million deliveries.

solr.summary: A Lucene-based search cluster sharded through SolrCloud: full-text search, facets and filters. The alternative to Elasticsearch where mature faceting and a Java stack matter.
solr.capacity: cpu binds first: nodes × cpuCores / (S × fanout), where every read request touches all shards. search-threads (24 per node) bind later than the 16 cores, and indexing is loaded only by writes.
practices: softCommitMs is the price of freshness: 1,000 ms adds 20% to query time for cache warm-up, 15,000 ms adds 1%.
queryType aggregation (facets) costs 3× of queryServiceMs = 20 ms, term costs 0.4×.
Keep heapGb between 8 and 31 GB and leave the rest of memory to the page cache for Lucene segments.
Replicas are asynchronous with replicaLagMs = 1,000 ms: a reader may not see a document that was just indexed.
pitfalls: Adding shards for scale makes every read request more expensive: fanout hits all of them.
softCommitMs = 50 ms for the sake of freshness cuts throughput fivefold on cache warm-up.
Solr and Elasticsearch in the same design duplicate the index: pick a single search layer.

spanner.summary: A managed globally distributed SQL database: nodes = 3, regions = 3, replicationFactor = 5, isolationLevel = serializable and external consistency backed by TrueTime with trueTimeUncertaintyMs = 3 ms. It is the only block with availability = 0.99999, about 5 minutes of downtime per year. Taken at v2 when you need global transactions and the price tag is not a blocker.
spanner.capacity: The limits are vendor-units, commit-wait and connections. vendor-units: maxReadsPerSecPerNode = 22,500 × 3 nodes = 67,500 reads/s and maxWritesPerSecPerNode = 13,900 × 3 = 41,700 writes/s. commit-wait caps writes earlier: commitConcurrency = 300 concurrent commits, with the quorum crossing crossRegionRttMs = 70 ms plus about 6 ms of TrueTime wait, yields on the order of 3,900 commits/s, while connections stop at maxSessions = 10,000.
practices: partitionKey = userId has to spread the load evenly: a monotonic key such as a timestamp funnels every write into one split and wipes out the 41,700 writes/s ceiling.

partitionStrategy = global-table at regions = 3 means the quorum of 5 replicas always crosses regions; if the data is regionally separable, geo-partitioned removes crossRegionRttMs = 70 ms from writes.
indexCount = 2: every secondary index is an extra write inside the same commit, which multiplies the cost of a write directly.
maxSessions = 10,000 is sized for a client pool, not for a session per query, and connectionsPerQuery = 1 assumes exactly that reuse.
costPerInstanceHour = 3 USD × 3 nodes is about 6,600 USD per month for compute alone, plus costPerGbMonth = 0.3 for 1.12 TB of data, so do the math before adopting, not after.
pitfalls: readServiceMs = 1.5 ms and writeServiceMs = 3 ms are measured before the network and before commit-wait; the real write p99 in a multi-region setup is tens of milliseconds.
readFromReplica = 0.3 at replicaLagMs = 10 ms: stale reads work, but consistencyModel = linearizable is guaranteed only for strong reads, so choose the read mode explicitly.
transactionScope = distributed-2pc: a transaction touching two splits in different regions pays two cross-region round-trips; keep related rows together via interleaving.
commitConcurrency = 300 is a hard queue: a write spike turns into growing latency rather than errors, and the error counter shows nothing.

sqlite.summary: An embedded database in a single file: no network, no server, journalMode = wal and exactly one writer. It gives isolationLevel = serializable and linearizable semantics for free, simply because there is no write concurrency here at all. It is placed at v2 as node-local storage — a cache, a queue, edge state, configuration — and not as a shared database for a service.
sqlite.capacity: single-writer binds first: at writeServiceMs = 0.3 ms and fsyncMs = 2 ms per commit, one writer gives about 435 transactions/s, and at writesPerTransaction = 1 that is the same number of rows; batching 100 rows per transaction raises it to 43,500 rows/s. cpu (cpuCores = 4 / readServiceMs = 0.05 ms = 80,000 reads/s) and iops (provisionedIops = 8000 at iopsPerWrite = 4, that is 2,000 writes/s) stay far ahead.
practices: journalMode = wal is mandatory for a mixed workload: readers do not block the writer, whereas in rollback mode any write stalls all reads.
Batch your writes: writesPerTransaction = 1 means an fsync per row, while raising it to 100–1000 moves the ceiling by two orders of magnitude.
synchronous = normal in WAL is a sensible compromise (fsync at checkpoint rather than at commit); full is needed where the last transactions must not be lost on power failure.
databaseSizeMb = 2000 against rowCount = 5 million × 200 bytes with indexOverhead = 0.3 is 1.3 GB, so headroom is thin, and cacheSizeMb = 64 keeps only about 5% of the file in memory.
The backup output to S3 is the only real protection: availability = 0.99 is roughly 3.6 days of downtime per year, and the block has no replica at all.
pitfalls: Serving several service instances from one file over a network filesystem is the classic way to corrupt the database; the block is designed for exactly one process.
synchronous = off speeds writes up several times over and loses acknowledged transactions on power failure, which is acceptable only for a rebuildable cache.
linearizable and serializable are free here, but the price is zero availability when the node fails: the file dies together with the machine.
A long transaction under concurrencyControl = pessimistic stalls every writer: the single writer is also the single queue.

sqs.summary: A managed queue with no nodes and no maintenance: the producer sends a message, the consumer pulls it in a batch and deletes it after processing. queueType standard gives at-least-once with no ordering guarantee, while fifo gives ordering within a MessageGroupId and deduplication at the cost of throughput. Use it as a buffer between services when you do not want to operate a broker of your own.
sqs.capacity: The only limiter is inflight: maxInflight 120000 messages taken by consumers and not yet deleted. Little's law turns that into a rate: if processing takes the full visibilityTimeoutSec 30, you get 120000 / 30 = 4000 messages/s; if it takes 1 s, the same 120000 per second. For queueType fifo, fifoThroughputLimit 3000 rps applies on top.
practices: Set visibilityTimeoutSec 30 with headroom over your processing p99: a short timeout hands the same message to a second consumer and breeds duplicates.
maxReceiveCount 5 and dlqEnabled true are a mandatory pair: after the fifth failed delivery the message goes to the DLQ instead of looping forever.
longPollingSec 20 is both the maximum and the right default: billing runs at costPerMillionRequests 0.4 USD for every request, empty polls included.
batchSize 10 is the SQS ceiling; receive and delete in batches, otherwise both the bill and p99 grow linearly with the message count.
messageSizeKb 8 against a hard limit of 256 KB: put large payloads in s3 and pass a reference in the message.
pitfalls: standard gives no ordering and allows duplicates, so the handler must be idempotent; switching to fifo for the sake of ordering cuts the rate to 3000 rps and demands a carefully chosen MessageGroupId.
Processing that runs longer than visibilityTimeoutSec means the message has already been redelivered, and the delete at the end of processing applies to somebody else's attempt.
retentionHours 96 is a hard deadline: whatever is not consumed within 4 days disappears without a trace and without an event.
delaySec 0 makes messages visible immediately; build delayed retries through a redrive from dlq or through scheduler-queue, not by delaying the whole queue.

stream-processor.summary: Stateful stream processing: parallelism 24 tasks read partitions 24 and hold stateSizeGb 120 of state for windows and aggregates. It sits between the broker and a data mart when you need continuous aggregates, enrichment and joins in real time. The only input is consume; the output goes to a database, to search, to analytics or back into a topic.
stream-processor.capacity: The limiters are partitions and memory. partitions caps parallelism at the number of partitions in the input topic: 24 tasks × recordsPerSecPerTask 20,000 = 480,000 records/s, and any parallelism above 24 simply leaves tasks with no work. memory: stateSizeGb 120 against instances 4 × memoryGb 32 = 128 GB is 94% full, with essentially no headroom.
practices: Keep parallelism equal to partitions or to a divisor of it: with 24 partitions and parallelism 32, eight tasks idle and the ceiling stays at 480,000 records/s.
checkpointIntervalSec 60 s with exactlyOnce true sets the cost of recovery: after a crash up to a minute of data is replayed, and lag doubles for that period.
watermarkLagSec 30 s is a promise to the user: tumbling windows close with a 30 s delay, and anything that arrives later goes down the late branch.
Plan state with headroom: 120 GB in 128 GB of memory means OOM on the first key skew; either raise memoryGb or spill the state to disk.
exactlyOnce true requires a transactional broker and idempotent writes into the sink, otherwise the guarantee ends the moment data leaves the block.
pitfalls: Key skew: one hot key funnels all the traffic into a single task and the ceiling falls from 480,000 to 20,000 records/s while 23 tasks are formally free.
Switching windowType from tumbling to session with watermarkLagSec 30 s inflates state unpredictably: sessions do not close while events keep arriving.
exactlyOnce makes every write more expensive and ties result visibility to checkpointIntervalSec 60 s — turn it on only where duplicates really are unacceptable.
Increasing partitions after the fact is cheap, decreasing them is not: build in 2-3× headroom up front, otherwise the parallelism ceiling is fixed forever.

timescale.summary: A Postgres extension for time series: a hypertable is cut into chunks of chunkIntervalHours = 24, old chunks are compressed after compressionAfterDays = 2 with compressionRatio = 10 and dropped at retentionDays = 90. It absorbs metricsPerSec = 100,000 at insertBatchRows = 1000 and still allows ordinary SQL with joins to reference tables. It is placed at v1 when you need metrics or events specifically with SQL queries.
timescale.capacity: The limits are cpu, iops, connections and throughput, and everything rests on batching: 100,000 metrics/s at insertBatchRows = 1000 is 100 inserts/s at writeServiceMs = 3 ms, a third of a core. Without batching (insertBatchRows = 1) those same 100,000 rows would need 300 cores against cpuCores = 16. On reads, queryRangeHours = 168 at chunkIntervalHours = 24 touches 7 chunks, and cpu gives about 16 / (readServiceMs = 5 ms × 7) ≈ 457 queries/s.
practices: insertBatchRows = 1000 is the key parameter of this block: dropping it to 1 multiplies the cost of a write by 1000 and saturates cpu instantly.
Choose chunkIntervalHours = 24 so that a typical queryRangeHours touches a handful of chunks and the newest chunk fits into memory: 7 chunks for a weekly query is fine, 168 hourly ones is not.

compressionAfterDays = 2 at compressionRatio = 10: the two uncompressed days are 1.7 TB, the other 88 days compressed are 7.6 TB, about 9.3 TB in total at retentionDays = 90, so size the disk from those numbers.
maxConnections = 300 with readReplicas = 1 requires a pool: writers and dashboards compete for the very same connections.
Set retentionDays = 90 from the very start: dropping a chunk is a DROP of a table, whereas deleting rows by WHERE on time series is prohibitively expensive.
pitfalls: consistencyModel = linearizable does not hold with replicationMode = async, readFromReplica = 0.3 and replicaLagMs = 200 ms: dashboards on the replica lag behind, and it looks like missing metrics.
Compressed chunks are effectively not updatable: a point arriving later than compressionAfterDays = 2 requires decompressing the chunk, so plan the late-arrival window in advance.
queryRangeHours = 168 is the default, but a user will ask for 90 days: such a query touches 90 chunks and eats the whole cpu, so bound the range in the UI or build continuous aggregates.
rowSizeBytes = 100 at 100,000 metrics/s is 864 GB of raw data per day, and one extra 20-byte column adds another 173 GB per day.

traces.summary: A distributed trace store: it assembles the spans of one request into a tree and shows exactly where the time went along the service chain. Added in wave v1, once there are more than three services and logs can no longer reconstruct the path of a request. It is what gives probe-waterfall its meaning: without traces the p99 breakdown by hops rests on the model alone.
traces.capacity: Two bounds apply: ingest-bandwidth at maxIngestMbs = 400 MB/s and span-ingest at maxSpansPerSec = 2000000. On the defaults bandwidth saturates four times earlier: 400 MB/s at spanBytes = 800 bytes is 500000 spans per second, which at spansPerRequest = 20 and samplingRate = 0.1 corresponds to roughly 250000 application RPS against the 1 million RPS allowed by the span limit.
practices: samplingRate = 0.1 is not a decorative default: at 10000 RPS and spansPerRequest = 20 the stream is 20000 spans per second and 16 MB/s, which at costPerGbIngest = 0.4 USD works out to about 16600 USD per month.
The realistic sampling range is 0.01 to 0.2; below 0.01 rare errors stop landing in the sample, above 0.2 the bill grows without added value.

tailSampling changes the decision scheme: sampling happens after the trace is assembled, so rare slow and failing requests are kept in full, but the collector still has to accept the entire stream before filtering.
retentionDays = 7 within the realistic range of 3 to 30 is enough: traces are for investigating a fresh incident, keep history in metrics.
Control spansPerRequest = 20 through instrumentation: a chain of 60 spans per request costs three times as much as the same design with 20.
pitfalls: samplingRate = 1 on production traffic: at 100000 RPS that is 2 million spans per second and 160 MB/s, meaning 40 percent of maxIngestMbs and a six-figure bill at costPerGbIngest.
Turning on tailSampling expecting to save bandwidth: it saves storage but does not relieve the ingest path, because the decision is made after all spans of the trace have been accepted.
Expecting traces to replace metrics: retentionDays = 7 and sampling at 0.1 mean you cannot build monthly trends from them.
Estimating load in spans without accounting for spanBytes = 800 bytes: bandwidth saturates before the span counter does.

transcoder.summary: A media transcoder: one job takes sourceMinutes 10 of source material and produces renditions 5 quality variants with codec h264 at speedFactor 1 (real time). It sits behind an upload queue in video and audio services. The block is heavy on both CPU and outbound traffic, which is why it is always kept off the synchronous API.
transcoder.capacity: The limiters are cpu and network. One job costs 10 min × 5 renditions ÷ speedFactor 1 = 50 minutes of encoding = 3000 core-seconds, while instances 8 × cpuCores 16 = 128 cores, i.e. about 0.043 jobs/s ≈ 154 jobs per hour. network gives 8 × networkMbps 2000 = 16 Gbps for downloading sources and uploading results.
practices: hardwareAccel false with gpuCount 2 means the GPUs are paid for but unused: either turn acceleration on or drop the GPUs from the configuration.
The codec changes speed by an order of magnitude: h265 and especially av1 need many times more core-seconds than h264 at the same speedFactor — lower speedFactor when you change the codec.
renditions 5 is a direct work multiplier: a ladder of three variants instead of five immediately raises capacity to 256 jobs per hour.
maxQueueDepth 5000 at 0.043 jobs/s is more than 32 hours of backlog; either cut the depth or count the queue as part of the publishing delay you promise.
Put a queue in front of the block and object storage plus a CDN behind it: 16 Gbps of outbound traffic cannot be pushed through an ordinary service.
pitfalls: queuePriority fifo lets a four-hour movie go first and every short clip waits behind it; mixed traffic needs weighted.
Estimating capacity in jobs without accounting for duration: sourceMinutes 10 on average versus sourceMinutes 120 for one user is a 12× difference in core-seconds.
8 × 0.9 = $7.2/hour ≈ $5250/month runs continuously, even when the queue is empty: without scaling on queue depth the block is billed at peak.
availability 0.99 (7.3 h a month) on the content publishing path: without retries and a DLQ the uploads that arrive during the outage are simply lost.

trino.summary: A distributed SQL engine with no storage of its own: it runs queries over the data lake and external sources, federating them behind a single SQL interface.
trino.capacity: disk-scan binds first: workers × cpuCores × scanThroughputMbsPerCore gives 24 GB/s against 12.5 GB per query. network carries the shuffle (30% of what is scanned), and query-slots cap concurrency at 20.
practices: pushdown leaves 25% of the scan: filtering and projection at the source are the main lever, not the number of workers.
workers 2–200 scale the scan linearly: each one adds cpuCores × 150 MB/s of reads.
The shuffle counts as 30% of the bytes scanned: at 10 Gbps per worker the network becomes the second limit.
queryConcurrency = 20 — Trino is for heavy analytical queries, not for thousands of small ones.
pitfalls: Trino has neither its own storage nor a cache: speed is determined entirely by the source and the file format.
Availability is 0.99 by default: there is a single coordinator, and losing it kills every running query.
Disabling pushdown quadruples both the scan and the shuffle — the network binds before the disks do.

vector-db.summary: An embedding store with approximate nearest-neighbour search (HNSW or IVF): semantic search, recommendations and similar-item lookup by vector proximity.
vector-db.capacity: memory is the limit: the index has to stay resident. 100 million vectors at 768 dimensions is 921 GB (dimensions × 4 B × 1.5 × (1 + replicas)) against 163 GB of cluster RAM, and capacity drops proportionally.
practices: Budget memory as dimensions × 4 B × 1.5 per vector: 768 dimensions is 4.6 KB, 1536 is 9.2 KB.
recallTarget gets expensive non-linearly: 0.95 costs 1.3 of the baseline work, 0.99 costs twice as much. The realistic range is 0.9–0.99.
topK = 10 is the baseline cost and topK = 100 doubles it; never ask for more than you display.
hnsw versus ivf is a 2.2× difference in query time; pick ivf when a compact index matters more.
pitfalls: replicas double index memory, not just durability: size RAM with the (1 + replicas) multiplier.
Vector search does not replace filters: exact field predicates are cheaper served by a regular index.
recallTarget = 0.999 without a quality metric: query time triples for a difference nobody will notice.

vitess.summary: A sharded layer on top of MySQL: vtgateInstances = 4 proxies route queries across shardCount = 8 shards spread by shardKey = customerId with shardStrategy = hash. It provides the horizontal write scaling a single mysql lacks, at the price of forbidding arbitrary cross-shard joins. It is introduced at v1 when one MySQL instance can no longer absorb the write load.
vitess.capacity: vtgate binds first: vtgateInstances = 4 × vtgateMaxRps = 12,000 = 48,000 queries/s, whereas 8 shards of cpuCores = 8 at readServiceMs = 0.6 ms give roughly 107,000. Next come cpu, connections (maxConnections = 500 per shard, 4,000 in total) and iops (provisionedIops = 12,000 at iopsPerWrite = 3, that is 4,000 writes/s per shard).
practices: crossShardQueryShare = 0.1 means every tenth query goes scatter-gather to all 8 shards: an average query costs 0.9 × 1 + 0.1 × 8 = 1.7 shards, so keep the share below 0.2.
shardKey = customerId has to appear in the WHERE clause of the vast majority of queries, otherwise vtgate cannot pick a shard and falls back to a scatter.
vtgateLatencyMs = 0.4 ms is added to every query on top of readServiceMs = 0.6 ms, which is plus 67% on the p99 of a point read, so budget for it in the SLO.
Grow vtgateInstances proportionally to RPS: they are stateless and this is the cheapest way to lift the 48,000 queries/s ceiling.
replicasPerShard = 2 with readFromReplica = 0.5 and replicaLagMs = 500 ms means half the reads are half a second stale, and consistencyModel = sequential states that honestly.
pitfalls: transactionScope = single-shard: a transaction spanning two shards is either forbidden or splits into two, so invariants across shards have to be maintained with sagas.
Hash sharding on customerId is uniform across keys but not across volume: a large customer creates a hot shard, and resharding 4 billion rows is weeks of work.
vtgate is a single point of failure for throughput: losing one of the four instances costs 12,000 queries/s, a quarter of the ceiling.
In total 4 billion rows × 300 bytes × 1.35 = 1.6 TB; storageGb = 4000 looks like headroom until you remember replicasPerShard = 2 holding the very same data.

vpc.summary: A private network container inside a region: the cidr address space, egress to the internet through NAT and interconnection with other networks through peering. It determines how much egress traffic costs and how many addresses are available to pods and nodes. Appears in wave v1, when the design outgrows a single flat network.
vpc.capacity: hasModel = false: the network serves no application requests and does not enter the capacity calculation of the blocks. Instead it adds natGatewayCount = 1 gateway with natThroughputGbps = 45 Gbps as the egress ceiling, costPerGbProcessed = 0.045 USD for every gigabyte that passes through, and peeringLatencyMs = 0.1 ms on calls between networks.
practices: NAT is the single most expensive line on the network bill: 1 Gbps of steady egress is 324000 GB per month and 14580 USD at costPerGbProcessed = 0.045, four times more expensive than the same bandwidth over link-cross-region.
Route everything you can around NAT: private endpoints to object storage and internal calls over peering at 0.1 ms never hit that line item.
Keep natGatewayCount = 1 only in designs with no availability requirements: a single gateway is both a point of failure and a source of cross-zone traffic for blocks in neighbouring zones.

cidr = 10.0.0.0/16 is 65536 addresses; with a CNI that gives every pod an address and a k8s-cluster of 6 nodes at podsPerNode = 110 you occupy 660 addresses, but grow to hundreds of nodes and addresses run out before compute does.
flowLogsEnabled = false by default: turn it on deliberately, because the flow log stream lands in the logs block and is billed there at costPerGbIngest = 0.5 USD per GB.
pitfalls: All egress through a single NAT: on top of the bill you hit natThroughputGbps = 45 Gbps and degrade every external call at once.
