A gateway in one zone while blocks sit in three: traffic from the neighbouring zones goes over link-cross-az and is billed twice, at 0.01 USD per GB and at 0.045 USD per GB.
Planning addresses from the node count instead of the pod count: 6 nodes is 660 addresses, and a /24 runs out on the second node.
flowLogsEnabled turned on for a busy network quietly becomes the largest source of volume in logs.

waf.summary: An application-layer filter in front of the application: it inspects requests against a rule set, cuts off bots and provides a coarse rate limit at the entrance. A self-managed block where you choose the instance and core counts yourself. Place it between the external entry point (cdn or glb) and the load balancer or the gateway.
waf.capacity: The limits are cpu, rate-limit and network. With the defaults CPU binds first: instances=4 × cpuCores=8 = 32 cores, and at inspectionMs=1.2 ms one core handles about 833 RPS, so the whole block does roughly 26,700 RPS, almost 19 times below rateLimitRps=500,000 RPS. Growing rulesCount=250 increases inspectionMs and lowers that figure proportionally.
practices: Check the inspectionMs and cpuCores pair before touching rateLimitRps: with the defaults the binding constraint is not the limit but 32 cores at 1.2 ms per request.
rulesCount=250 sits in the realistic 100-800 range; every doubling of the rule set roughly doubles inspectionMs and halves throughput.
instances=4 across azSpread=3 spreads unevenly (2+1+1), and losing the busiest zone removes half the capacity; pick an instance count that is a multiple of the zone count.
botScore=0.6 is the bot cut-off threshold; connect the block to client-bot so the diagram shows exactly which traffic it filters.
Wire the upstream output to lb-l7 or api-gateway rather than directly into a service: a WAF does no routing and no load balancing.
pitfalls: falsePositiveRate=0.001 looks tiny, but at 26,700 RPS it is about 27 legitimate requests blocked every second, which means a constant stream of complaints.
Seeing rateLimitRps=500,000 RPS and treating the block as practically unlimited, when the real ceiling with the defaults is about 26,700 RPS on CPU.
Adding rules in batches without recomputing inspectionMs=1.2 ms: latency creeps up unnoticed while capacity falls linearly.
availability=0.9999 (about 53 minutes per year) is lower than that of the cdn and glb in front of it, which makes this block the weakest link at the entrance.

webhook.summary: Outbound webhook delivery: it dispatches events to subscribers 20 subscribers with deliveryTimeoutMs 5000 ms and maxRetries 3 at retryBackoffMs 1000 ms. It sits at the platform boundary when external systems need to learn about events and polling your API does not work for them. The only outputs are http/grpc/internal.
webhook.capacity: The limiters are concurrency and ops. concurrency = instances 3 × concurrency 256 = 768 slots: at serviceTimeMs 80 ms that is 9600 deliveries/s, but slowConsumerShare 0.05 holds a slot for the full deliveryTimeoutMs 5000 ms, raising the average hold to 0.95 × 80 + 0.05 × 5000 = 326 ms and dropping capacity to ~2350 deliveries/s. ops = maxOpsPerSec 5000 deliveries/s and becomes the limiter only when there are no slow consumers.
practices: Isolate slow subscribers into a separate pool: 5% of consumers that answer in 5 seconds take 77% of the slots and cut capacity fourfold.
Keep deliveryTimeoutMs 5000 ms as low as you can: dropping it to 2000 ms cuts the average hold from 326 to 176 ms and nearly doubles throughput.
subscribers 20 is a multiplier: 100 events/s becomes 2000 deliveries/s, and the ops ceiling of 5000 is reached at just 250 events/s.
maxRetries 3 with retryBackoffMs 1000 ms needs a separate retry queue: otherwise retries occupy the same 768 slots as fresh deliveries.
Sign the payload and give the subscriber an idempotent event identifier — retries guarantee duplicates, and that is normal.
pitfalls: Sizing by serviceTimeMs 80 ms: the promised 9600 deliveries/s is never reached, because some subscribers are always an order of magnitude slower.
A dead subscriber with no circuit breaker: 20 subscribers × 3 retries of 5 seconds each, and one downed consumer slows the entire dispatch.
An ordering guarantee that does not exist: retries and parallel slots deliver events out of order, so the subscriber has to sort them itself.
Growing subscribers from 20 to 200 without changing capacity: the same 100 events/s becomes 20,000 deliveries/s — four times maxOpsPerSec 5000.

webrtc-sfu.summary: A Selective Forwarding Unit for calls: it accepts participants' streams and forwards them to everyone else without transcoding. At participantsPerRoom 8 and simulcastLayers 3 a single room produces 8 publications and 56 forwarded streams at bitrateKbps 800. Use it in video conferencing, streaming and voice rooms instead of an MCU when latency matters more than saving the client's traffic.
webrtc-sfu.capacity: The limiters are cpu and media-egress. cpu = instances 4 × cpuCores 16 = 64 cores ÷ (cpuPerStream 0.01 × 56 streams per room) ≈ 114 rooms, i.e. about 910 participants. media-egress binds later: 4 × egressGbps 10 = 40 Gbps ÷ 44.8 Mbps per room ≈ 890 rooms.
practices: The number of streams grows quadratically: participantsPerRoom 8 means 56 forwards, while 50 participants means 2450 — that is 24.5 cores for a single room at cpuPerStream 0.01.
simulcastLayers 3 exist precisely so that weak clients can be sent the lowest layer: without simulcast, bitrateKbps 800 is multiplied across every receiver with no way to degrade.
sessionDurationMin 25 drives concurrency: 100 new calls a minute with 25-minute sessions means 2500 concurrent rooms, not 100.
Pin a room to a single instance and route participants by geography: forwarding between SFUs doubles egress and adds latency.
For rooms larger than 20 participants turn on active-speaker mode — otherwise the cpu ceiling of 114 rooms falls by an order of magnitude.
pitfalls: Computing egress from the number of participants rather than from the number of pairs: 8 participants is not 8 streams of 800 kbps but 56, i.e. 44.8 Mbps per room.
Losing an instance takes down all of its rooms at once: availability 0.999 is 43 minutes a month, and every one of those minutes means dropped calls that cannot be retried.
cpuPerStream 0.01 is accurate for pure forwarding; turning on recording or transcoding raises it 5-20× and moves the block into the transcoder class.
4 × 0.6 = $2.4/hour across 114 rooms is $0.021 per room-hour, but with only ten rooms occupied a single room costs $0.24/hour.

worker.summary: A background message processor: it reads from a queue or a topic and handles a task in processingTimeMs 120 ms. Put it behind a broker to move everything that can be asynchronous off the synchronous path — notifications, recalculations, integrations. It accepts no HTTP: the only entry point is the consume port.
worker.capacity: The limiters are workers and cpu. workers = instances 4 × concurrency 16 ÷ processingTimeMs 120 ms ≈ 533 messages/s, but cpu = 4 × cpuCores 2 ÷ (0.12 s × cpuShare 0.5) ≈ 133 messages/s and binds four times earlier. In other words, 16 slots on 2 cores at cpuShare 0.5 is fourfold CPU oversubscription.
practices: Match concurrency to cpuCores: at cpuShare 0.5 two cores honestly sustain 4 slots, not 16 — either lower concurrency or raise cpuCores to 8.
prefetch 32 against concurrency 16 gives a 2× buffer per instance; a larger prefetch hoards messages on one instance and gets in the way of rebalancing.
idempotent true is mandatory with retries 3: the broker gives at-least-once, so a single message will be processed up to four times.
dlqEnabled true is a mandatory default: without a DLQ a poison message returns to the queue forever and burns retries × capacity.
batchSize 1 suits heterogeneous tasks; for writes into a database or into analytics raise it to 100-500 to amortize the round trip.
pitfalls: Sizing capacity by workers instead of cpu: the arithmetic promises 533 messages/s, the block actually delivers 133, and queue lag grows linearly.
retries 3 against a systematic downstream error quadruple the load at exactly the moment downstream is already down.
No rate limiting on the output: four instances can throw a spike at a database or at an external API that has its own rateLimitRps.
Measuring lag in messages when it should be measured in seconds: at 133 messages/s a backlog of 1 million takes more than two hours to drain.

ws-gateway.summary: A persistent-connection gateway: it holds clients' WebSocket sessions and pushes messages to them, receiving those messages from a bus through the fanout port. Use it wherever updates flow from server to client rather than by polling. Place it behind lb-l4 or lb-l7 and subscribe it to kafka, amqp, redis or stream.
ws-gateway.capacity: The limits are connections, memory and network. On connections the ceiling is instances=6 × connectionsPerInstance=100,000 = 600,000 against a target of concurrentConnections=400,000, but memory binds sooner: memoryGb=8 at memoryPerConnKb=120 KB is enough for roughly 70,000 connections per instance, about 420,000 for the block. The network is not in the way with the defaults: 400,000 connections × messagesPerConnMin=6 per minute gives 40,000 messages per second at messageBytes=400 B, on the order of 128 Mbps against networkMbps=10,000.
practices: Cross-check connectionsPerInstance=100,000 against memoryGb=8 and memoryPerConnKb=120 KB: with the defaults the real limit is about 70,000 connections per instance, and the declared hundred thousand cannot be backed by that memory.
fanoutMode=pub-sub is what you want when one event goes to many recipients; with direct the delivery scales with the number of recipients and runs into the gateway's outbound throughput.
heartbeatSec=30 s with idleTimeoutSec=120 s allows four missed pings before a disconnect; shrinking the heartbeat to a few seconds is expensive in both traffic and CPU.
Connect the fanout port to a broker or a stream and the upstream port to the services for commands coming from the client; do not route all the client HTTP traffic into this block.
azSpread=3 with instances=6 gives exactly two instances per zone; keep that multiple, otherwise a zone failure cuts connection capacity disproportionately.
pitfalls: Counting only useful messages and forgetting heartbeats: at 400,000 connections and heartbeatSec=30 s that is another 13,300 messages per second, a third of the useful 40,000.
Not budgeting for a reconnect storm: losing one instance out of six sends about 70,000 clients reconnecting at once, and the remaining instances hit their limits instantly.
Running concurrentConnections=400,000 with instances=6 and no per-zone headroom: losing one zone leaves four instances, roughly 280,000 connections, 30% short of what is needed.
Leaving memoryPerConnKb=120 KB at its default and never recomputing it for larger buffers: raising it to 200 KB drops the limit to 42,000 connections per instance.

yugabyte.summary: A distributed SQL database with a Postgres-compatible layer on top of Raft: nodes = 6 across regions = 3, replicationFactor = 3, transactionScope = distributed-2pc. It differs from cockroach in defaulting to isolationLevel = snapshot instead of serializable and in being half the cluster size. It is chosen at v2 when you need a distributed database with the Postgres dialect and its extensions.
yugabyte.capacity: raft-quorum comes first: maxOpsPerSecPerNode = 6000 × 6 nodes = 36,000 operations/s, and divided by replicationFactor = 3 that is about 12,000 client writes/s, with iops following right behind (provisionedIops = 16,000 at iopsPerWrite = 3 is 5,300 per node, roughly 10,700 after replication). cpu (6 × 16 cores / writeServiceMs = 1.8 ms ≈ 53,000) and connections (maxConnections = 300 per node, 1,800 in total) bind later.
practices: maxConnections = 300 per node is the tightest connection limit in the whole SQL family; connectionPooler = proxy-managed is on by default, do not turn it off.
partitionStrategy = geo-partitioned with partitionKey = region is mandatory at regions = 3: otherwise the write quorum travels over crossRegionRttMs = 70 ms.
isolationLevel = snapshot is cheaper than serializable but allows write skew, so for invariants across rows raise the level explicitly or use SELECT FOR UPDATE.
partitionSizeMb = 256 over 840 GB of logical data gives about 3,300 tablets; define split points for large tables up front so you do not hit splits under load.
readFromReplica = 0 is correct for consistencyModel = linearizable; enable follower reads only with an explicit tolerance for staleness.
pitfalls: snapshot instead of serializable is a silent difference from cockroach: code written for serializable will let write skew through here without a single error.
Data with replicationFactor = 3: 840 GB logical becomes 2.5 TB on disk, that is 420 GB per node out of storageGbPerNode = 2000.
concurrencyControl = optimistic: conflicting transactions are rolled back, and without a retry in the application the user simply sees an error.
6 nodes over 3 regions means 2 per region: losing a region leaves 2 replicas out of 3 and quorum survives, but losing two nodes in different regions already kills some tablets.
